papers.title: Toward a Robust Crowd-labeling Framework using Expert Evaluation and Pairwise Comparison
papers.abstract: Crowd-labeling emerged from the need to label large-scale and complex data, a tedious, expensive, and time-consuming task. One of the main challenges in the crowd-labeling task is to control for or determine in advance the proportion of low-quality/malicious labelers. If that proportion grows too high, there is often a phase transition leading to a steep, non-linear drop in labeling accuracy as noted by Karger et al. [2014]. To address these challenges, we propose a new framework called Expert Label Injected Crowd Estimation (ELICE) and extend it to different versions and variants that delay phase transition leading to a better labeling accuracy. ELICE automatically combines and boosts bulk crowd labels supported by labels from experts for limited number of instances from the dataset. The expert-labels help to estimate the individual ability of crowd labelers and difficulty of each instance, both of which are used to aggregate the labels. Empirical evaluation shows the superiority of ELICE as compared to other state-of-the-art methods. We also derive a lower bound on the number of expert-labeled instances needed to estimate the crowd ability and dataset difficulty as well as to get better quality labels.
papers.summary: When large datasets are labeled by crowds of workers, too many low-quality or malicious labelers can trigger a sudden, steep drop in labeling accuracy. The proposed framework, `ELICE` (Expert Label Injected Crowd Estimation), uses expert labels on a small number of instances to estimate each crowd worker's ability and each instance's difficulty, then uses those estimates to combine the crowd labels. Variants of the method **delay this sudden drop in accuracy** and outperform other state-of-the-art aggregation methods in experiments. The authors also derive a lower bound on how many expert-labeled instances are needed to estimate worker ability and instance difficulty reliably.

papers.title: LLM-Enhanced Self-Evolving Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Step E-Commerce Payment Fraud Risk Detection
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to e-commerce payment fraud detection by integrating reinforcement learning (RL) with Large Language Models (LLMs). By framing transaction risk as a multi-step Markov Decision Process (MDP), RL optimizes risk detection across multiple payment stages. Crafting effective reward functions, essential for RL model success, typically requires significant human expertise due to the complexity and variability in design. LLMs, with their advanced reasoning and coding capabilities, are well-suited to refine these functions, offering improvements over traditional methods. Our approach leverages LLMs to iteratively enhance reward functions, achieving better fraud detection accuracy and demonstrating zero-shot capability. Experiments with real-world data confirm the effectiveness, robustness, and resilience of our LLM-enhanced RL framework through long-term evaluations, underscoring the potential of LLMs in advancing industrial RL applications.
papers.summary: E-commerce payment fraud detection is framed as a multi-step Markov Decision Process (MDP), so that reinforcement learning (RL) can optimize risk decisions across several payment stages. Because good RL reward functions usually take a lot of expert effort to design, the authors use large language models (LLMs) to refine the reward function over repeated rounds. In experiments on real-world transaction data, **the LLM-refined rewards improve fraud detection accuracy**, show zero-shot capability, and stay robust in long-term evaluations.

papers.title: Relic and Gumi: Governing Memory, Safety, and Continuity in Diegetic Relational Agents
papers.abstract:
Longitudinal relational agents rely on memory for continuity, but remembering can lead to intrusion, clinical overconfidence, emotional manipulation, and opacity. We present Relic, a governance architecture for diegetic relational agents, and Gumi, a subject-specific companion agent initialized and governed through Relic. The architecture separates what the system can observe, what researchers can review, what Gumi can remember, and what Gumi can say.
  We describe three mechanisms. Relic represents sensitive safety signals as researcher-facing governance objects rather than user-facing explanations or agent memories. Shared Continuity Memory organizes relational markers around subject-confirmed wording, corrections, explicit follow-up permissions, and recall limits. We specify a runtime mediation layer for delivery, proactivity, session identity, output transformation, and platform allowlists; adoption across live paths remains partial. These mechanisms aim to preserve relational continuity without turning Gumi into a clinical assistant, mood tracker, general-purpose assistant, or opaque profiling system.
  We contribute the architecture, object model, researcher workbench design, and a proposed evaluation framework for governed relational memory. An exploratory pilot involved the author as P1 and one external participant as P2. Weekly self-reports from P1 and researcher-led interviews with P2 provide descriptive observations of early use and perceived naturalness. The pilot does not support claims about clinical efficacy, diagnosis, therapeutic outcomes, general usability, or deployment safety. Relic provides research infrastructure intended to make relational memory, safety constraints, and agent behavior inspectable and testable.
papers.summary: Long-term companion agents need memory to stay consistent from one conversation to the next, but remembering can become intrusive, overconfident in clinical matters, manipulative, or opaque. `Relic` is a governance architecture that keeps four things separate: what the system can observe, what researchers can review, what the companion agent `Gumi` can remember, and what it can say. Sensitive safety signals are kept as objects only researchers can see, and a Shared Continuity Memory stores only wording the user has confirmed, along with their corrections and recall limits. An exploratory pilot with two participants, one of whom is the author, provides only descriptive observations, and **the authors explicitly make no claims about clinical efficacy or deployment safety**.

papers.title: MeshRT: Compile-Time Governed Wafer-Scale Runtime for Low-Latency High-Throughput Inference
papers.abstract:
Wafer-scale accelerators promise ultra-low-latency AI inference, but current system stacks still carry an unsustainably high cost premium. The reason is that many current and emerging inference techniques, such as batching and MoE, introduce runtime dynamism that existing wafer-scale systems cannot support efficiently. As a result, they must choose between two unsatisfactory options: accept suboptimal latency, or preserve low latency by restricting dynamic techniques, thereby limiting the models they can support and reducing aggregate throughput. This tradeoff significantly increases the cost of low-latency serving.
  We present MeshRT, the first wafer-scale system to achieve both ultra-low latency and high throughput for LLM inference. MeshRT achieves this via a novel system architecture, which we call compile-time governance of runtime dynamism. This architecture features new system abstractions and mechanisms that enable MeshRT to compile dynamic events arising from LLM inference directly into per-core schedules, enabling asynchronous and decentralized execution with low runtime overhead. Implemented on a commodity wafer-scale accelerator, MeshRT preserves ultra-low latency while improving throughput by up to 56$\times$ over the state-of-the-art system for wafer-scale accelerators. Against measured single-instance SGLang results on H200, MeshRT achieves 4.5-7.0$\times$ lower latency. Under ideal linear scaling of those GPU measurements to an approximately power-matched H200 cluster, MeshRT achieves 1.7-13.0$\times$ higher decode system throughput in the low-latency regime.
papers.summary: Wafer-scale accelerators can serve AI models with very low latency, but they handle runtime variability poorly, including the variability introduced by request batching and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. As a result, they have had to trade throughput for latency. `MeshRT` compiles dynamic events from large language model (LLM) inference directly into a schedule for each core, so that execution is asynchronous and decentralized with little runtime overhead. On a commodity wafer-scale accelerator it keeps ultra-low latency while improving throughput by **up to 56× over the previous state-of-the-art wafer-scale system**. It also reports 4.5–7.0× lower latency than `SGLang` running on a single H200 GPU.

papers.title: MorphSched: Workload-Aware Adaptive Scheduler Generation for Linux
papers.abstract: Modern Linux scheduling increasingly requires workload-specific policies to meet the dynamic performance needs of heterogeneous applications. The recent sched_ext framework enables custom BPF schedulers, but building practical policies still requires coordinating Rust user-space control logic, BPF scheduling callbacks, generated user-kernel interfaces, and strict eBPF verifier constraints. This paper presents MorphSched, an LLM-driven system for synthesizing complete Rust+BPF sched_ext schedulers. MorphSched profiles target workloads under Linux EEVDF to construct dynamic, workload-specific optimization objectives, and uses a scaffold-constrained generation pipeline to translate scheduling intent into deployable scheduler implementations. To improve synthesis reliability, MorphSched separates implementation repair from strategy search: verifier, build, and runtime failures are handled through a DAG-structured repair process, while performance feedback is accumulated in an evolutionary memory pool to refine high-level scheduling strategies across iterations. We evaluate MorphSched across 120 machine/workload/interferer configurations on a real Linux kernel. The generated schedulers compile, pass eBPF verification, load successfully, and remain stable throughout our benchmark runs without manual edits to generated scheduler source code. Across these configurations, MorphSched improves the primary foreground metric over EEVDF by 26.5% on average and up to 87.3%. In selected comparisons, the generated schedulers are also competitive with representative hand-written sched_ext schedulers. These results show that scaffold-constrained, system-grounded LLM generation can be a practical tool for exploring workload-specific Linux scheduling policies.
papers.summary: Writing a custom Linux scheduler with the `sched_ext` framework means coordinating Rust user-space code, eBPF kernel callbacks, and the strict eBPF verifier. `MorphSched` uses a large language model (LLM) to generate complete Rust and BPF schedulers tailored to a profiled workload. It fills in a fixed code scaffold, fixes verifier, build, and runtime failures through a separate repair process, and refines scheduling strategies over iterations using a memory of past performance results. Across 120 configurations on a real kernel, every generated scheduler compiled, loaded, and stayed stable without manual edits, and **improved the primary foreground metric by 26.5% on average (up to 87.3%) over Linux's default `EEVDF` scheduler**.

papers.title: Subliminal Learning in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Subliminal learning is a phenomenon in large language models (LLMs) where a teacher passes a hidden preference to a student through training data unrelated to that preference. We study whether subliminal learning also occurs in vision-language models (VLMs). We finetune a teacher VLM to prefer a specific animal or facial attribute and use a control teacher from the same base model. Both teachers generate numbers for an unrelated visual task involving geometric shapes. Two students initialized from the same base VLM are finetuned on the same images, using numbers generated by either the biased or control teacher. Across VLMs ranging from 2B to 7B parameters, we find that both animal and facial preferences can transfer through this unrelated task. Students trained on biased-teacher outputs select the target more often than control students, with a difference of up to $\sim$10 percentage points in the animal preference task. Transfer can become stronger with more training data and varies with the target preference, model, and how the numbers are generated. Beyond preferences, we show that the biased student's explanations use more of the same words and phrases as the biased teacher's explanations than those of the control student, even when all three models select the same image. These results matter for training VLMs and show that training on unrelated data may change both a VLM's image preferences and how it explains its choices, and that transfer can become stronger with more training samples.
papers.summary: In large language models, subliminal learning is when a teacher model passes a hidden preference to a student through training data that has nothing to do with that preference. The authors test whether the same happens in vision-language models (VLMs). A teacher fine-tuned to favor a particular animal or facial attribute produces numbers for an unrelated geometric-shape task, and students are then trained on those numbers. Across VLMs from 2B to 7B parameters, the preferences do transfer, with students choosing the target **up to about 10 percentage points more often** than control students. The effect grows with more training data, and the students' explanations also pick up the biased teacher's wording.

papers.title: SAFTAC: Simulation-Augmented Fine-Tuning of Open-Source LLMs for Analog Circuit Design
papers.abstract: Circuit design for analog integrated circuits (ICs) is challenging because circuit topology, device sizing, and circuit performance are tightly coupled. Existing large language model (LLM)-based methods either rely on inference-time correction around frozen models or train on limited circuit types without directly using simulation outcomes as training signals. A key bottleneck is that existing datasets do not provide sufficient task information for training LLMs on end-to-end specification-conditioned design. To fill this gap, we first construct a large-scale simulation-grounded dataset with 8,626 design tasks across 10 different types of analog circuits, where each task includes a textual description, labeled I/O ports, loading condition, target specifications, a testbench, and a reference netlist. Using this dataset, we present SAFTAC, a simulation-augmented fine-tuning framework that trains LLMs to generate and revise analog circuit design. SAFTAC combines three-stage supervised fine-tuning, which progressively builds the capabilities required for analog circuit design and feedback-guided correction, with simulation feedback-augmented reinforcement fine-tuning, which further optimizes models using simulation-grounded rewards. We evaluate SAFTAC under single-pass generation and two-pass generation with simulation feedback, showing improvements over the strongest closed-source LLM by 15.9% and 7.8%, respectively.
papers.summary: Designing analog integrated circuits with large language models (LLMs) has been held back by a lack of training data tied to circuit specifications, and by methods that never use simulation results as a training signal. The authors build a dataset of 8,626 simulation-grounded design tasks covering 10 circuit types, each with specifications, a testbench, and a reference netlist. Their framework, `SAFTAC`, fine-tunes open-source LLMs in three supervised stages and then applies reinforcement fine-tuning with rewards computed from circuit simulations. The resulting models **outperform the strongest closed-source LLM by 15.9% in single-pass generation** and by 7.8% when given one round of simulation feedback.

papers.title: PINNeval: A Comprehensive Evaluation Standard for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.abstract: The Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) literature has produced a rapidly expanding catalogue of methods. We divide a PINN training pipeline systematically into four components and observe that many existing benchmarks study these components in isolation. These components are domain-importance adaptation, loss balancing, neural network architecture, and optimization scheme. Moreover, the studies set the surrounding and not considered components of the pipeline to a minimal default that is no longer representative of current best practice approaches. Conclusions drawn under such conditions may not transfer to competitive pipelines. In this work, we propose a new evaluation protocol that (1) treats the four components as an integrated system; (2) crucially requires competitive implementations of the components not under investigation; (3) specifies the metrics and reporting format; and (4) is accompanied by structured documentation that ensures the traceability of evaluations across studies. Based on this comprehensive protocol, we release PINNpipe, an innovative JAX package containing 18 different methods from the current literature as well as nine efficiently implemented benchmark problems. Using PINNpipe, we illustrate our evaluation protocol in relation to established benchmark studies and report results that challenge common assumptions.
papers.summary: Benchmarks for Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) usually study one part of the training pipeline in isolation and leave the other parts at outdated minimal defaults, so their conclusions may not hold for competitive pipelines. The authors propose an evaluation protocol that treats four components as one system: domain-importance adaptation, loss balancing, network architecture, and optimizer. The protocol requires strong implementations of every component not under study, and it fixes the metrics and reporting format. They release `PINNpipe`, a JAX package with 18 methods and nine benchmark problems, and use it to report **results that challenge common assumptions in prior benchmark studies**.

papers.title: Towards Label-Efficient Geospatial Foundation Model Adaptation via Positive-Unlabeled Learning for Building Damage Mapping
papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are reshaping remote sensing by shifting the field from task-specific modeling toward general-purpose geospatial intelligence. Mapping the damage to buildings stands to benefit substantially from this shift, as GFMs pretrained on large-scale Earth observation data provide generalizable geospatial representations that can facilitate effective responses to sudden-onset disasters. Although parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) facilitates GFM adaptation, parameter efficiency does not necessarily translate into label efficiency. Building damage mapping remains challenging due to scarce pre-existing labeled data or limited time for annotation. When weak supervision is introduced to alleviate the labeling bottleneck, we identify the difficulty of learning sufficiently discriminative representations as a key challenge for label-efficient GFM adaptation. To address this challenge, we propose a Positive-Unlabeled GFM Adaptation (PUMA) framework that requires annotations for only a small number of damaged buildings. More specifically, PUMA integrates non-contrastive weakly supervised representation refinement to mitigate the impact of noisy supervision on representation learning from a gradient perspective, and latent-state-based label disambiguation to enable reversible supervision refinement without requiring class prior estimation. Extensive experiments on disaster benchmark datasets from around the world demonstrated the effectiveness and robustness of PUMA. A real-world application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires further highlighted its potential to accurately map damage under highly limited supervision. More broadly, these findings suggest that weakly supervised PEFT offers a label-efficient pathway from GFMs to real-world applications.
papers.summary: Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) can be adapted to map building damage after disasters, but parameter-efficient fine-tuning still needs labels that are scarce in an emergency. `PUMA` (Positive-Unlabeled GFM Adaptation) needs labels for only a small number of damaged buildings and treats everything else as unlabeled. It combines a non-contrastive refinement step that limits the damage noisy supervision does to the learned representations with a way of revising uncertain labels that does not require estimating class proportions. Experiments on disaster benchmarks from around the world, and an **application to the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires**, show accurate damage mapping from very limited supervision.

papers.title: CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive rerankers for recommendation. Running an expensive model on every request is costly, and for users with sparse interaction histories it often lowers quality. We present CascadeRec, a two-tier LLM reranking cascade deployed in production at a large financial planning and analysis (FP&A) SaaS provider. It serves content recommendations to enterprise tenants on AWS EKS and GKE. A lightweight Tier-1 model reranks every request. A router escalates only the requests where extra inference-time compute is likely to help, and sends them to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure (self-consistency sampling, multi-path reasoning, or a larger model). The system has run in a production A/B experiment for over a month. Compared with uniform use of the expensive tier, CascadeRec has reduced inference cost by about 10%, with minimal latency impact and no quality regression observed to date. Tenant data cannot be released, so we also evaluate the pipeline on public benchmarks (MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Electronics). Segment-level analysis with paired-bootstrap confidence intervals shows that uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and its only statistically significant gain appears on the segment with the longest histories. Escalating cold users can make the loss larger instead of repairing it. Which segments benefit from escalation depends on the domain, and this motivates the segment-gated rollout we use in production. We describe the deployment architecture, the measured benefits, and lessons learned, including inter-tenant load imbalance as a driver for cascading and the handling of LLM output-parsing failures at the serving layer.
papers.summary: `CascadeRec` is a two-tier system for reranking recommendations with large language models (LLMs), deployed in production at an enterprise financial-planning SaaS provider. A cheap model reranks every request, and a router sends only the requests likely to benefit to a costlier second tier, such as self-consistency sampling or a larger model. In a month-long production A/B test, it **cut inference cost by about 10% with no observed quality loss**. On the public `MovieLens-1M` and `Amazon-Electronics` benchmarks, uniform LLM reranking lowered `NDCG@10` by up to 30% for users with short interaction histories, and sending those users to the costlier tier made the loss worse rather than fixing it.

papers.title: Enhancing Academic Advisement with Case-Based Reasoning
papers.abstract:
This research involved the study of an application of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) in the field of academic advising. Academic advisement has been recognised as an important function of higher education. However, there is a widespread desire to improve the advisement services provided by many educational institutions (e.g., colleges and universities) around the world. In the last ten years, CBR expert systems have made important contributions in many domains by applying CBR methodology to a variety of areas of human problem solving. However, to date, expert advisement systems have not been successfully applied to academic advisement, which seems to be a very appropriate domain for this technology.
  Academic advising is an important and time consuming task, and different tools and techniques must be used to make it an effective and efficient process. This thesis describes the design, development, and validation of a prototype case-based academic advisement recommender system that supplements the conventional advising process, and could eventually evolve to replace human academic advisors when its full potential is realised.
papers.summary: This thesis applies Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) to academic advising in universities, an area where expert advisement systems have not yet been used successfully. It describes the design, development, and validation of **a prototype case-based recommender system that supports conventional human advising**. The author argues that the system could eventually replace human advisors.

papers.title: Q-OIL: Optimistic Exploration in Learning from Human Interventions
papers.abstract: As robots are deployed in the real world, they will inevitably make mistakes. Human interventions provide valuable feedback for improving their behavior, enabling them to adapt online to new scenarios. However, studying human-in-the-loop robot learning is difficult: real-world experiments are slow and expensive, so most algorithm development relies on simulated human models. We show that common human modeling assumptions do not match how real people intervene in practice. Through analyzing intervention data from human participants, we find that humans tend to intervene when agent progress stalls, and that their corrective actions are often suboptimal. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a progress-based model of human intervention that achieves higher rank correlation with real-user algorithm rankings, enabling realistic algorithm benchmarking and development in simulation. Building on these insights, we propose Q-OIL, a method that adds optimistic bonuses to intervention transitions in reinforcement learning and softly guides exploration toward human corrections. We find that decoupled critics are critical for stability because they prevent the bonuses from backing up to pre-intervention states. As a result, Q-OIL learns more efficiently than competitive baselines, achieving 10-50% higher success in simulation and on real robots, and improving pretrained VLAs on two bimanual manipulation tasks. As we ground both evaluation and algorithms in realistic human behavior, this work provides a practical path toward scalable robot learning from interventions.
papers.summary: Studying how robots learn from human interventions usually relies on simulated humans, but data from real participants shows that people tend to step in when the robot's progress stalls, and their corrections are often suboptimal. The authors propose a progress-based model of human intervention that ranks algorithms more like real users do. Building on it, `Q-OIL` adds optimistic reward bonuses to intervention transitions in reinforcement learning, and uses separate critics so the bonuses do not spread back to the states before an intervention. The method achieves **10–50% higher success than competitive baselines** in simulation and on real robots, and it improves pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models on two two-armed manipulation tasks.

papers.title: HaNDF: Object-Conditioned Geometric Neural Hand Distance Fields
papers.abstract: We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand-object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations. While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand-object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.
papers.summary: Generative priors for human pose usually ignore the objects that hands are holding, even though hand poses depend heavily on the object. `HaNDF` learns a neural distance field conditioned on the object, so that plausible hand articulations lie on the field's zero-level set. It uses tools from Riemannian geometry to project any given hand pose onto that set. The prior can also infer which object is being held, and it is **useful for pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and synthesizing physically plausible manipulation**.

papers.title: NormGym: Evaluating Normative Competence through Social Interaction
papers.abstract: Normative competence, the ability to infer socially enforced expectations from interaction and adjust behavior accordingly, is essential for agents operating in unfamiliar human communities. Yet existing evaluations largely test whether agents can recognize or apply norms they may already know, rather than whether they can acquire previously unknown norms from social interaction. We introduce NormGym, an interactive benchmark for normative competence in which a newcomer must infer a hidden, arbitrary norm while pursuing its own task in a multi-agent community. Success requires distinguishing what is possible from what is permitted, inferring the norm from observed behavior and sanctions, and applying it in new situations. NormGym contains diverse norms and distinct environments, allowing systematic evaluation of current agents, including large language model (LLM) agents. We find that normative competence remains challenging: the strongest evaluated LLM achieves a joint task-and-compliance success rate of 55.3%. Our analysis reveals that models can sometimes revise their behavior following sanctions for their own actions, but struggle to use other agents' behavior and the sanctions they receive to infer the underlying norm. We further find that fine-tuning models may be insufficient to improve normative competence. These results suggest that current models lack a robust, transferable capability for acquiring normative knowledge through social interaction.
papers.summary: `NormGym` is an interactive multi-agent benchmark that tests whether an agent can learn an unfamiliar, arbitrary social norm from interaction, rather than apply norms it already knows. A newcomer agent must pursue its own task while inferring the hidden norm from how other agents behave and how they are sanctioned. The strongest large language model (LLM) agent tested reaches **only 55.3% joint task-and-compliance success**. Models sometimes adjust after being sanctioned themselves but rarely learn from sanctions applied to other agents, and fine-tuning did not reliably help.

papers.title: s$^3$: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL
papers.abstract: Groups can achieve more than individuals in the same amount of time, but only if their members coordinate: they must decide who works on what and what to share. However, this organization in multi-agent systems today usually comes from arbitrary, static harnesses designed a priori without adapting to agent behaviors or task specifications. We ask whether agents can instead learn to organize themselves. We introduce s$^3$, the first multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents decide for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read teammates' messages, with no predefined organization or roles. Our s$^3$ agents learn to take different approaches, read each other's work, exhibit emergent roles that complement each other in the swarm, and generalize to bigger teams. We study both coordination, where agents must combine private information, and parallel exploration, where sharing discoveries can make search more efficient. With matched training and inference budgets, s$^3$, swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25$\times$ more coordination problems than the strongest baseline, and in exploration, communicating agents reduce repeated work by nearly 50% and outperform best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points. Rather than being designed in advance, s$^3$ enables organization to emerge from a shared goal. This opens the door to capable systems built from many models that learn to work together.
papers.summary: Multi-agent systems are usually organized by fixed, hand-designed setups that decide who works on what and what gets shared. `s³` instead uses cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning to let agents decide for themselves how long to work alone, when to share findings, and when to read teammates' messages, with no predefined roles. The agents develop complementary roles on their own and generalize to larger teams. With matched training and inference budgets, swarms twice the training size **solve over 25× more coordination problems than the strongest baseline**, and in exploration tasks communication cuts repeated work by nearly 50% and beats best-of-N sampling by up to 9.4 points.

papers.title: LLM-Based Feature Extraction for Multi-Criteria Inventory Classification
papers.abstract: E-commerce supply chains generate large volumes of customer feedback and operational data that remain underutilized in inventory management. Traditional inventory classification techniques such as ABC analysis rely primarily on annual dollar usage, while multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) methods extend this but still depend on structured quantitative data and do not utilize unstructured information available in modern supply chains. This paper proposes an LLM-based feature extraction approach that transforms unstructured sources such as customer reviews into quantitative features using vector embeddings and LLM-generated evaluation criteria. The enriched feature set is incorporated into an MCIC framework based on the Hadi-Vencheh model. Experimental results show measurable reclassification effects when customer sentiment signals are included, demonstrating that integrating unstructured data into MCIC can enhance inventory prioritization.
papers.summary: Multi-criteria inventory classification (MCIC) methods rank products using structured quantitative data and ignore unstructured sources such as customer reviews. The authors use vector embeddings and evaluation criteria generated by a large language model (LLM) to turn reviews into numeric features, and they feed those features into an MCIC model based on the `Hadi-Vencheh` method. Adding customer-sentiment signals **measurably changes how items are classified**, which the authors argue improves inventory prioritization.

papers.title: Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments for Test-Time Selection
papers.abstract: Scaling test-time compute has proven highly effective at improving LLM reasoning. A popular method is best-of-n sampling, where a model generates many candidate solutions and one is selected. This motivates the question: how can we select the best candidate? When humans make choices, we find it more natural to compare two options than judge each in isolation. Additionally, when the options become complex, we like to judge the options one aspect at a time, such as comparing two job candidates on experience, communication, etc. In the test-time setting, candidate solutions should be judged in the same way. Here we introduce Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments (APT), which verifies by comparison and compares by aspect. Each matchup of a single elimination tournament is decided by a vote over multiple off-the-shelf aspect verifiers, each expressing a pairwise preference along its own aspect. Across five domains and three generator LLMs, APT improves over binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency and reward model verification, with the largest gains on open-ended tasks. We find that both components matter; neither binary approval over the same aspects nor a generic pairwise judge at a matched budget matches APT. Because aspects are specified in natural language, APT also lets users steer selection toward properties they care about, better aligning with user preferences without needing to regenerate solutions. No component is trained, so APT transfers to new domains by simply rewriting prompts.
papers.summary: When a model samples many candidate answers (best-of-n), picking the best one is the bottleneck. Aspect-wise Pairwise Tournaments (`APT`) runs a single-elimination tournament in which each matchup between two candidates is decided by a vote among off-the-shelf verifiers, each judging one aspect such as correctness or clarity. Across five domains and three generator models, APT beats binary multi-aspect approval, self-consistency, and reward-model verification, with **the largest gains on open-ended tasks**. Ablations show that both the pairwise comparison and the per-aspect breakdown are needed, and because nothing is trained, users can steer selection simply by rewriting the aspect prompts.

papers.title: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction
papers.abstract: Financial institutions construct knowledge graphs (KGs) from shared SEC 10-Ks to serve risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment research, whose analytical needs differ. Extraction must adapt without fragmenting shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules. Hand-authored persona prompts and fine-tuning add cost. Weight-free prompt optimization offers an alternative, but unconstrained evolution of a monolithic prompt can rewrite shared rules alongside persona guidance, obscuring changes and complicating review. We introduce FinEvolveKG, a KG-construction harness separating reusable general and persona-policy blocks and mechanically confining GEPA, a reflective prompt optimizer, to the designated block. During persona adaptation, the approved general block remains byte-stable and every optimizer edit is localized to a separately versioned persona policy. A dual objective balances generic temporal-KG quality with persona-relevant facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity. We evaluate five mutation scopes on ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, with three seeds for the persona-conditioned arms (v3-v5) across three personas. On the three-seed mean, the complete two-stage block-constrained workflow (v4) improves over the frozen prompt baseline (v1) by 19.4-30.9% and over the tested unconstrained full-prompt workflow (v5) by 2.2-6.4%, leading v5 on both objective components and winning all nine paired-seed comparisons with the lowest seed variance in every persona. Without further optimization, v4 also exceeds v5 across all evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. An SME audit supports using the generated triplets as ground truth; a blinded two-SME audit favors v4 over v5 in 70.1% of contrast-enriched judgments. These results show that mechanically attributable evolution can coexist with strong empirical performance, without attributing the gains causally to the boundary.
papers.summary: Financial firms build knowledge graphs from SEC 10-K filings for different analyst personas, but letting a prompt optimizer rewrite a single monolithic prompt can silently change the extraction rules that all personas share. `FinEvolveKG` splits the prompt into a fixed general block and a separately versioned persona block, and restricts the `GEPA` prompt optimizer to editing only the persona block. The full two-stage constrained workflow **improves over the frozen baseline prompt by 19.4–30.9%** and over unconstrained whole-prompt optimization by 2.2–6.4%. It also performs better under out-of-distribution shifts and is preferred by subject-matter experts in a blinded audit.

papers.title: Decision Context: Persistent Behavioral Learning for AI Agents
papers.abstract:
LLM agents do not learn from corrections across sessions. A user fixes the same mistake at the start of every conversation. Existing agent memory systems primarily handle facts, such as preferences, entities, and conversational history, rather than procedural knowledge.
  We present Forge Decision Context (forge_dc), a system that captures behavioral signals from human corrections and self-assessed tool-call failures, compiles them into imperative RULE directives, and injects them at the decision points where they apply. We evaluate forge_dc alongside four predecessor approaches on DC-Bench, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios across nine behavioral dimensions, built from real executed agent traces in a deterministic mocked-tool environment. forge_dc reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval, while injecting approximately 10 times fewer tokens per query.
  Across the five-stage progression, the strongest systems represent behavioral memory as explicit directives and deliver it at the decision points where it applies. The results identify representation, activation, and placement as central design choices for persistent behavioral learning.
papers.summary: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) repeat the same mistakes in every new session, because existing memory systems store facts rather than lessons about how to behave. `forge_dc` collects human corrections and failed tool calls the agent identifies itself, turns them into imperative rules, and injects each rule at the decision point where it applies. On `DC-Bench`, a new benchmark of 71 scenarios built from real agent traces, it **reaches 95% compliance, up from 55% with naive retrieval**, while injecting about 10 times fewer tokens per query. The authors identify representation, activation, and placement as the key design choices for this kind of behavioral memory.

papers.title: From Geometry to Function: A Multi-Task LiDAR Benchmark Dataset for Semantic and Functional Parsing of Urban Facades
papers.abstract: Understanding building facades is central to urban digital twins, heritage modelling, and sustainable city analysis, yet existing LiDAR benchmarks stop at geometry and semantic segmentation and offer little support for reasoning about the functional role of each architectural element. We introduce HFX3D, a large-scale urban facade benchmark of approximately 492 million LiDAR points from 26 buildings in Halifax, Canada, captured across four seasons, day and night, and varied weather. Each facade is annotated at three tiers, semantic, instance, and per-instance functional attributes, making it, to our knowledge, the first facade dataset to pair geometry and semantics with functional labels. Annotations are produced by a semi-automatic pipeline that combines geometry-guided heuristics with expert validation. We benchmark representative point-based, graph-based, convolutional, and transformer architectures and find that semantic segmentation is already challenging under severe class imbalance, while instance separation of repetitive structures and functional reasoning from geometry are substantially harder. The benchmark establishes a new foundation for function-aware 3D urban understanding. Project page: https://jijup.github.io/hfx3d-benchmark/ ; code: https://github.com/jijup/hfx3d-benchmark
papers.summary: Existing LiDAR benchmarks for building facades cover geometry and semantic labels but say nothing about what each architectural element is for. `HFX3D` provides about 492 million LiDAR points from 26 buildings in Halifax, Canada, captured across seasons, times of day, and weather, with semantic, instance, and per-instance functional labels. Benchmarks of point-based, graph-based, convolutional, and transformer models show that semantic segmentation is already hard because of severe class imbalance, and that **separating repetitive structures into instances and inferring function from geometry are substantially harder**.

papers.title: IWIBench: Evaluating Gradient-Free Model Driven Intra-weight Injection
papers.abstract: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. Such edits can range from altering lexical associations to enforcing output formats or updating factual knowledge. Despite growing interest in these approaches, there has been no systematic way to evaluate how well models perform them. We introduce IWIBench, which measures a large editor model's ability to modify the weights of a smaller target model (typically Gemma 3 4B IT) to achieve one of ten classical text-editing objectives while preserving its other capabilities. Editors are limited to four tools for reading and writing weights, with bounded tensor access and a fixed budget for generating and inspecting rollouts. A validator applies each proposed patch in a clean environment and compares the edited model against the unmodified target. Evaluating frontier closed- and open-weight models reveals sharply diverging capabilities, both across models and across tasks. A small number of models, most notably Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, perform far ahead of the rest. The recency of this ability (little of it is evident in GPT-5.6 Sol, for instance), together with qualitative analysis, suggests it has been acquired through recent training. Tasks also vary widely: structured response resisted every attempt, and answer-length control yielded only one successful solution, whereas alias acquisition and recoding proved most amenable. Success in one task family correlated poorly with success in others, indicating an early and uneven capability frontier. We discuss strategies that editors repeatedly adopted and conclude with an outlook on intra-weight injection as an emerging but already potent approach to gradient-free behaviour modification.
papers.summary: Intra-weight injection is the practice of one model changing another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. `IWIBench` measures how well a large editor model can do this to a smaller target model, usually `Gemma 3 4B IT`, across ten text-editing objectives while keeping the target's other capabilities intact. Editors get four weight read/write tools, bounded tensor access and a fixed rollout budget, and a validator checks each patch in a clean environment. **Only a few recent frontier models, notably `Astra` and `GPT-6.1 Sol`, succeed to any real degree**, while older models such as `GPT-5.6 Sol` show little of the ability. Success also varies widely by task: structured-response edits never succeeded, alias acquisition and recoding were the easiest, and skill on one task family predicted little about another.

papers.title: VoluCompose: Constructing Compact Volumetric Visual Representations for Medical Image Understanding
papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models can interpret volumetric images, but processing full volumes is costly because hundreds of slices produce long, redundant visual-token sequences. Existing compression methods often couple content selection with budget determination. We observe that neighboring slices share visual features and that attention concentration varies across visual encoders. We propose VoluCompose, a training-free, model-agnostic framework that separates what visual content to retain from how many tokens to allocate. Its hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units and uses the Lorentz distance to account for feature magnitude and direction during token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement. Its capacity control module uses visual-encoder attention entropy to allocate more tokens when attention is more dispersed. We evaluate VoluCompose on two tasks across three datasets and four backbones. Across nine calibrated settings, VoluCompose attains the highest mean quality--retention hypervolume among the compared methods. It achieves a mean relative quality of 121.68\% against the uncompressed references while retaining 22.78% of visual tokens on average. Compression remains robust even at a 10% token budget. Across settings, the lowest ROUGE-L ratio to the uncompressed reference is 96.4\% for VoluCompose. The corresponding minima for the compression baselines range from 15.0% to 70.5%. Code is available at https://github.com/yezanting/VoluCompose.
papers.summary: Medical vision-language models that read volumetric scans produce long, redundant visual-token sequences, because each volume has hundreds of slices. `VoluCompose` is a training-free, model-agnostic compression framework that decides which content to keep separately from how many tokens to spend. It groups neighbouring slices and uses the hyperbolic Lorentz distance to allocate tokens and choose anchors, then sets the token budget from the attention entropy of the visual encoder. Across three datasets and four backbones it **reaches 121.68% mean relative quality against uncompressed inputs while keeping only 22.78% of visual tokens**, and its worst `ROUGE-L` ratio is 96.4%, compared with 15.0–70.5% for baseline methods.

papers.title: Scoring, Not Learning: Decomposing Catalog-Consolidation Gains in Web-Scraped Retail Product Recognition
papers.abstract: Retail product catalogs assembled from web image search are cheap to build and pervasively noisy: queries return packaging shots instead of products, and entries proliferate under names that cannot be distinguished visually. Consolidating such a catalog can look like an alternative to scaling the model. We show this is not a comparison between two ways of improving a recognizer, but between improving a recognizer and changing what counts as correct. We study a public archive of 165,769 cheese images across 1,824 query-named entries. A packaging filter and near-duplicate removal reduce it to a 998-class recognition set on one fixed, group-aware split. Canonicalizing entries to their base type (844 classes) raises top-1 accuracy by 4.0 points. Scoring the unchanged model against the merged label space, by summing its predicted probability within each canonical group, recovers +4.27 points with no retraining (+4.25 over six seeds). Retraining on the consolidated catalog then adds -0.10$\pm$0.53, +0.08$\pm$0.65 and -0.10$\pm$0.65 points at 28, 50 and 88 M parameters, indistinguishable from zero at every capacity ($\pm$ is the across-seed standard deviation). That component is specific, not mechanical: random merges with the identical size profile yield only +0.68 points, and the three backbones agree to within 0.1 points. But it is overwhelmingly category coarsening, not alias correction: across the 37 merged groups, type coarsenings supply 94% of the gain and alias collapses only 7%. We also detect no interaction between consolidation and backbone size: tripling backbone parameters is worth +1.50$\pm$0.57 points on the raw catalog and +1.42$\pm$00.44 on the canonical one, a within-seed interaction of -0.08 [-0.79,+0.63]. On this archive, the reported consolidation gain primarily reflects the evaluation label space, and separating that out costs one evaluation
papers.summary: Retail product catalogs built from web image search are noisy, and consolidating their entries is often presented as an alternative to scaling the recognition model. Using a 998-class cheese-image dataset scraped from the web, the authors show that canonicalizing labels raises top-1 accuracy by 4.0 points. However, simply scoring the unchanged model against the merged label space recovers +4.27 points without retraining, while **retraining on the consolidated catalog adds a gain indistinguishable from zero at all three model sizes**. Nearly all of the gain comes from coarsening product types rather than from correcting aliases. The study concludes that the reported benefit mostly reflects a change in what counts as a correct answer, not a better recognizer.

papers.title: JEPAhead: From Inpainting to Causal Forecasting for Urban Driving
papers.abstract: We fine-tune a pre-trained V-JEPA1 predictor from bidirectional latent inpainting to action-free causal forecasting while keeping the encoder frozen. Using contiguous past observations, horizon-aligned targets, and group-level causal attention, the model forecasts eight future token groups, corresponding to sixteen frames, in one forward pass. On CARLA Town12, it retrieves the correct future among 591 candidates in 69.0% of cases, compared with 55.3% for persistence, with greater gains at longer horizons and on tokens exhibiting greater change. It also outperforms a compact predictor trained from scratch with six times fewer parameters. Semantic analysis indicates driving-relevant information in predicted features: a fixed linear probe trained on real encoder tokens achieves 0.16 mIoU on patches undergoing semantic-class changes, versus 0.13 for persistence. Vehicle-conditioned retrieval improves over persistence by 15 percentage points at the longest horizon. Pixel-space evaluation shows modest L1 gains but little improvement under LPIPS, motivating direct evaluation through latent and semantic measures alongside an oracle reconstruction reference. These findings support further investigation of latent forecasting for driving perception, while downstream utility remains unverified.
papers.summary: The authors fine-tune a pretrained `V-JEPA` predictor, originally trained for bidirectional latent inpainting, to forecast future latent video features causally without action inputs, while keeping the encoder frozen. Working from past observations, the model predicts eight future token groups, covering sixteen frames, in a single forward pass. On `CARLA` Town12 it **picks the correct future out of 591 candidates 69.0% of the time, compared with 55.3% for a persistence baseline**, with larger gains at longer horizons, and it beats a smaller predictor trained from scratch. Linear probes show that the predicted features carry driving-relevant semantic information, but pixel-space gains are modest and the benefit for downstream driving tasks has not yet been verified.

papers.title: Pdb or Not to Be: Comparing Debugging Interfaces With Pass$_{X}$@$k$
papers.abstract: Interactive debuggers are indispensable to human software development, yet coding agents overwhelmingly rely on edit-execute-observe loops, using common bash tools, test scripts, and print statements to debug via repeated shell commands. Stepping through a debugger provides live access to runtime state, which may enable different problem-solving capabilities. However, prior work typically introduces the debugger as an additional tool or through a new subagent, making its individual contribution difficult to isolate from the associated scaffold changes. To address this, we compare a debugger-only agent against a bash-only agent on all 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, holding the rest of the scaffold fixed. We evaluate both architectures on two models, GPT-OSS-120B and Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B, with three independent runs per architecture $\times$ model configuration. Crucially, to distinguish interface specialization from expanded coverage under repeated sampling, we introduce pass$_X$@$k$, a cross-agent pass@$k$ that provides an unbiased estimator of the probability that at least one of $k$ agents is successful. Although the bash and debugger agents solve partially disjoint subsets of the benchmark in any single pair of runs, our pass$_X$@$2$ estimator reveals that this is largely due to run-to-run variance rather than tool complementarity. Across both models, we find that two bash rollouts outperform the combination of one bash and one debugger rollout. Our findings highlight the importance of accounting for stochastic variance in evaluating agent and tool diversity, and we hope that pass$_X$@$k$ will serve as a useful framework for the community.
papers.summary: Coding agents mostly debug by running shell commands and adding print statements, and earlier attempts to give them interactive debuggers also changed the surrounding scaffold, so the debugger's own effect was never isolated. Here a debugger-only agent and a bash-only agent are compared on all 500 `SWE-bench Verified` instances with the rest of the scaffold held fixed, using `GPT-OSS-120B` and `Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B` with three runs each. The authors introduce `pass_X@k`, an unbiased cross-agent version of pass@k that estimates the chance at least one of k different agents succeeds. The two agents solve partly different problems, but this turns out to be mostly run-to-run variance, and **two bash rollouts beat one bash plus one debugger rollout on both models**.

papers.title: ChainFlow: Few-Step Latent Flow Matching for Speculative Decoding
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has become a standard way to accelerate LLM inference: a lightweight drafter proposes tokens that the target verifies in one parallel pass. Existing drafters face trade-offs that limits their speedups: autoregressive drafters generate tokens one at a time, so drafting cost grows with draft length, while diffusion drafters generate tokens in parallel but predict each position independently, ignoring inter-token dependencies. We introduce ChainFlow, a new speculative decoding paradigm and the first flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target's hidden states. ChainFlow treats drafting as a short transport over hidden states, needing one or two flow steps instead of the many denoising steps of generation from noise. A variational autoencoder compresses these states so drafting cost barely grows with target size, lightweight feedback heads restore inter-token dependencies, and tree drafting raises acceptance. On Qwen3.5 models, at matched drafter size and training data, ChainFlow outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash in vLLM by 39% and 11%, respectively. These gains further widen as drafters are adapted to new languages sequentially. Our ablations cover drafter design and concurrent serving, and we open-source our code and drafter models.
papers.summary: In speculative decoding, a small drafter proposes tokens that the large model then verifies in parallel. Autoregressive drafters slow down as drafts get longer, and diffusion drafters ignore dependencies between tokens. `ChainFlow` is a flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target model's hidden states that drafts in one or two flow steps. It uses a variational autoencoder to keep drafting cost nearly constant as the target model grows, lightweight feedback heads to restore inter-token dependencies, and tree drafting. On `Qwen3.5` models served in `vLLM`, at the same drafter size and training data, it **outperforms `EAGLE-3` by 39% and `DFlash` by 11%**, and the code and drafter models are open-sourced.
papers.highlight_summary:
Speculative decoding drafters face a trade-off: autoregressive drafters like `EAGLE-3` get slower as drafts get longer, while parallel diffusion drafters like `DFlash` predict each position independently and lose the dependencies between tokens. `ChainFlow` treats drafting as a short flow-matching transport over a compressed latent of the target model's own hidden states. Because the transport starts from an extrapolation of the recent hidden-state trajectory rather than from noise, a single integration step is enough.

- A transformer VAE compresses the target's final hidden states, and two "chunk expert" velocity networks cross-attend to 8 context latents to transport a linear extrapolation into 8 future latents in one Euler step; the target's frozen `lm_head` decodes these, a rank-256 Markov head and a path head restore dependence on the chosen prefix, and beam search emits the draft as a chain or an 8×4 tree.
- On `Qwen3.5-4B` in `vLLM` at batch one, the 8×4 tree reaches a pooled **1.87×** speedup against **1.69×** for `DFlash` and **1.35×** for `EAGLE-3`, with matched drafter size and training data (**11%** and **39%** faster); without tree verification the plain chain manages only 1.23× and trails both baselines.
- Because the flow runs in a fixed-width latent, drafting takes **0.30–0.38 ms** across 4B to 27B targets while one target decoding step grows from 3.1 to 11.2 ms, so the pooled speedup peaks at **2.12×** at 27B, with **3.23×** on math.
- Sequential adaptation to Turkish, German and French yields the largest gains of the three methods (Turkish tree speedup reaches 2.25× at 27B), but without replay adding German erases most of the Turkish gain; replaying about a fifth Turkish rows largely prevents this forgetting.
- The tree's advantage disappears under load: it is a net slowdown beyond 4 concurrent requests (**0.94×** at 8 and 0.45× at 128), whereas both baselines still speed things up at every batch size; tree verification also requires greedy decoding and a patched engine, 4–13% of outputs differ from plain greedy decoding because of fp16 near-ties, and only `Qwen3.5` targets were tested.

papers.title: Transporting the Past: An Optimal Transport View of Backtracking Counterfactuals
papers.abstract: We study backtracking counterfactual inference for Structural Causal Models (SCMs) through the lens of optimal transport. In SCMs, a factual observation generally induces a posterior distribution over exogenous variables, making counterfactual inference inherently distributional. We introduce two complementary frameworks that transport this posterior onto the set of exogenous configurations satisfying a desired counterfactual query. The first constructs a natural pointwise projection and is suitable when the transported exogenous distribution can be used directly. The second enforces mutual independence among counterfactual exogenous variables, so that the transported variables remain interpretable as genuine exogenous noises of the same SCM. We show that both frameworks are consistent with the original backtracking counterfactual principle, and we propose marginal, penalty-based, and hard-constrained solvers for finite-posterior settings. Synthetic experiments on non-bijective SCMs illustrate the geometry of the problem and reveal trade-offs among transport cost, counterfactual constraint satisfaction, and preservation of exogenous independence.
papers.summary: In Structural Causal Models (SCMs), a factual observation induces a posterior distribution over the unobserved exogenous variables, so backtracking counterfactual inference is inherently a question about distributions. The paper treats it as optimal transport of that posterior onto the exogenous configurations that satisfy the counterfactual query. It proposes two frameworks: a pointwise projection, and a variant that keeps the transported variables mutually independent so they remain valid exogenous noise for the same SCM. **Both are shown to be consistent with the original backtracking counterfactual principle**, and the authors provide marginal, penalty-based and hard-constrained solvers for finite posteriors. Synthetic experiments on non-bijective SCMs show trade-offs between transport cost, satisfying the counterfactual constraint and preserving independence.

papers.title: Compression of Emotion in Language Model Representations
papers.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) have been evaluated on their ability to identify emotions expressed in text and produce fluent emotional language. However, output predictions alone do not reveal how fine-grained emotion distinctions are organized internally. We study seven LLMs on GoEmotions, an English Reddit dataset annotated with 27 fine-grained emotion categories plus neutral. We compare model predictions and emotion-prompted final-token representations with the 28 GoEmotions categories and with coarser emotion-family and sentiment groupings.
  We find a consistent pattern of $\textit{overcompression}$ relative to the fine-grained GoEmotions taxonomy. Under the tested KMeans protocol, when we cluster their hidden representations without using emotion labels, the clearest split is into two groups that largely separate positive from negative emotion. Coarser emotion groupings are also recovered with fewer clusters than the full 28-category taxonomy. Yet linear probes retain substantial fine-grained predictive information. These results suggest that fine-grained emotion information remains accessible even though broader affective structure more strongly organizes the unsupervised geometry.
papers.summary: Seven large language models (LLMs) are studied on `GoEmotions`, a Reddit dataset labelled with 27 fine-grained emotions plus neutral, to see how emotion distinctions are organized inside the models. Both the models' predictions and their final-token representations are compared against the fine-grained labels and against coarser emotion-family and sentiment groupings. When the hidden representations are clustered with `KMeans` without labels, **the clearest split is into just two groups that largely separate positive from negative emotion**, a pattern the authors call overcompression. Linear probes, however, still recover substantial fine-grained information, which suggests the detail is present even though broad sentiment dominates the representation geometry.

papers.title: Cancellation Is Not Enough: What Retries Leave Behind in an Overloaded LLM Engine
papers.abstract: Clients and proxies in front of an LLM engine retry calls that time out. After a transient overload, these retries can keep the engine from recovering even when calls arrive below its capacity. Since the engine may keep computing for clients that have left, propagating cancellation looks like the natural remedy. In this paper, we test it on vLLM with overload experiments on three open models, and with scheduler traces of one that follow each client attempt to the execution it creates in the engine. We find that with retries on, cancellation alone did not restore service in any run, and only 12-38% of the calls that arrived after the overload were delivered. The traces suggest why: retries that vLLM ran typically started prefill less than half a second before they timed out. Executions that vLLM later aborted took 79-85% of the prompt tokens it computed, and vLLM's prompt-token counter missed a third to half of all computed prompt tokens. A retry budget restored service by shedding retries but left many of the overload's calls undelivered. Request coalescing delivered every call from the overload onward, some late, unless cancellation had already aborted the running execution. Overload controls should thus be judged by the executions that retries add and the calls that clients receive.
papers.summary: Clients and proxies retry LLM calls that time out, and after a brief overload these retries can keep an inference engine from recovering even once traffic falls below its capacity. Overload experiments on `vLLM` with three open models, together with scheduler traces, show that **with retries enabled, cancelling abandoned requests never restored service, and only 12–38% of calls arriving after the overload were delivered**. The traces show that retries typically started prefill less than half a second before timing out, aborted executions consumed 79–85% of computed prompt tokens, and vLLM's prompt-token counter missed a third to a half of them. A retry budget restored service but still dropped many calls, while request coalescing delivered every call unless cancellation had already aborted the running execution.
papers.highlight_summary:
Retries of timed-out LLM calls can keep an engine overloaded long after a transient spike has passed, even when new calls arrive below capacity. Passing each client's disconnect through to the engine (cancellation) looks like the obvious fix, but on `vLLM` it never restored service; attaching each retry to the call's still-running execution did.

- The testbed runs `vLLM` 0.30.0 on one H100 with `Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct`, `Qwen3-14B` and `Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, using ~12K-token synthetic prompts, a 107-s pulse at **2.7× capacity** followed by a 720-s hold at 0.6×, and clients with a 120-s timeout and up to 3 retries, routed through a proxy that can propagate cancellation, enforce a retry budget, or coalesce retries.
- With retries on and cancellation off, no model delivered a single hold-period call, and with cancellation added only **12–38%** were delivered and no run recovered; with retries off, every model recovered within the hold.
- Scheduler traces show why: retries reached prefill a median **0.22–0.47 s before their own deadline**, so aborted executions took **79–85% of computed prompt tokens**, and vLLM's prompt-token counter missed **a third to half** of that work because it records a prompt only at the first output token.
- A retry budget restored service but delivered pulse calls at about the no-control rate (~51–54%), while `request coalescing` delivered **every pulse and hold call** (some late), unless cancellation took effect immediately and left nothing to attach to; deferring cancellation by 10 s restored the coalescing behavior.
- Limitations: the evidence comes from one vLLM version, one GPU type, random-token single-turn prompts and one open-loop client policy, and in these runs deferred cancellation never actually cancelled anything, so its cleanup path was not tested.

papers.title: FoleyForge: Free-form, Controllable, Rectified-flow Editing of Sound Effects
papers.abstract: We present FoleyForge, a generative model for instruction-based editing of sound effects. Given an input clip and a free-form instruction describing the desired change, it applies the edit while preserving the input's identity. A single model handles semantic, stylistic, and DSP-like changes. We introduce a data pipeline that guides an audio language model to author both DSP-based acoustic edits and similarity-preserving semantic edits, thus addressing the lack of publicly available audio editing data. Such data is then used to fine-tune a rectified-flow audio generation model, which we extend to expose attribute controls for loudness change, edit strength, and an input-derived contour envelope, each tunable via classifier-free guidance, yielding a more expressive editing model. FoleyForge achieves state-of-the-art instruction adherence at competitive audio quality and source faithfulness.
papers.summary: `FoleyForge` is a generative model that edits a sound-effect clip according to a free-form text instruction while preserving the clip's identity, and it handles semantic, stylistic and signal-processing-style changes in one model. Because public audio editing data is scarce, the authors build a pipeline in which an audio language model writes both signal-processing edits and semantic edits that preserve similarity to the source. This data is used to fine-tune a rectified-flow audio generator, extended with controls for loudness change, edit strength and an input-derived contour envelope, each tunable through classifier-free guidance. The model reports **state-of-the-art instruction adherence** with competitive audio quality and faithfulness to the source.

papers.title: Dual-Stream LLM-Guided Reward Design for Reject-Inference-Aware Reinforcement Learning in E-Commerce Payment Fraud Detection
papers.abstract: Production fraud-detection models learn from a censored slice of their own traffic: transactions a legacy system blocked never receive fraud labels, so models train on a biased, approved-only distribution. We extend LLM-guided reward design, the framework of Qu et al. (2025) in which an LLM evolves the reward of a two-step REINFORCE fraud-blocking policy, to attack this reject-inference problem inside the reward. A single LLM designs a dual-stream reward: stream 1 applies the standard dollar-weighted precision objective to labeled transactions; stream 2 scores legacy-blocked, unlabeled transactions by contrasting the newest gradient-boosted risk signal against the legacy scores that drove the original block. Rather than prescribe which signals matter, we expose a superset of evidence and let the LLM decide for itself which to use, guided by evaluation feedback alone; because it writes the reward as code, that choice is directly auditable. On a held-out four-month out-of-time test, the dual-stream agent beats the prior labeled-only agent at every target recall, by +4.7, +2.4 and +3.0 points of dollar-weighted precision at 80%, 85% and 90% recall, and the production baseline by +6.8 points on average. The resulting policy is architecturally identical to that of Qu et al. (2025) and adds no inference cost.
papers.summary: Fraud-detection models learn only from transactions their legacy system approved, because blocked transactions never receive fraud labels, which biases the training data. This work extends an approach in which an LLM evolves the reward function of a two-step `REINFORCE` fraud-blocking policy, and has the LLM write a dual-stream reward. One stream scores labelled transactions by dollar-weighted precision, and the other scores unlabelled blocked transactions by comparing a newer gradient-boosted risk signal with the legacy scores that triggered the block. Because the reward is written as code, the LLM's choice of evidence can be audited. On a four-month out-of-time test, it **beats the labelled-only agent by 2.4–4.7 points of dollar-weighted precision at 80–90% recall** and the production baseline by 6.8 points on average, with no added inference cost.

papers.title: An Educated Guess: Deriving Statistically Aligned Gradient Estimates for Zeroth-Order Optimisation
papers.abstract: As novel hardware architectures are explored for the purposes of machine learning, including neuromorphic chips, asynchronous systems, and ASICs, effective learning algorithms are highly desirable. While backpropagation is the standard for differentiation on standard hardware, its requirement for global synchrony and exact differentiability limits the exploration of exotic algorithms on non-traditional substrates and devices. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimisation methods, such as SPSA and weight perturbation, offer a compelling alternative by estimating gradients through inference-only passes; however, these methods have historically suffered due to the `curse of dimensionality', where random perturbations become increasingly misaligned with the true gradient in high-dimensional spaces. In this work, we move beyond blind random noise by deriving zeroth-order search directions from activation geometry available during the forward pass. This leads to a family of Spectral Zeroth-Order methods, SZO-$\kappa$, whose directions solve local response-based gradient-guessing objectives under explicit stochastic assumptions. These methods explore feature-supported directions that are more likely to produce informative loss responses. Using multilayer and convolutional networks, we analyse gradient alignment, bias-variance structure, and training stability of these methods relative to standard perturbation baselines and backpropagation.
papers.summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization estimates gradients using only forward passes, which suits neuromorphic and other non-traditional hardware where backpropagation is impractical. However, random perturbations become poorly aligned with the true gradient as the number of dimensions grows. The proposed `SZO-κ` family of Spectral Zeroth-Order methods instead derives perturbation directions from the geometry of activations in the forward pass, solving gradient-guessing objectives under explicit stochastic assumptions. **These directions favour feature-supported subspaces that are more likely to produce informative loss responses**, and the methods are compared with standard perturbation baselines and backpropagation on gradient alignment, bias-variance structure and training stability in multilayer and convolutional networks.

papers.title: Patching the Blind Spots: Reversible LLM Rule Overlay for Frozen Fraud Detectors
papers.abstract: In industrial tabular fraud classification, gradient-boosted trees remain state-of-the-art, but even a well-trained model has blind spots, and retraining the deployed model is not always safe. We propose a framework that patches such a model without modifying it: LLMs propose rules anchored on features the model underweights by SHAP, and the resulting noisy pool is screened for empirical support and calibrated into an additive, reversible log-lift overlay that runs at the production cut-off. Single-LLM benefit is high-variance and inverts between datasets, so we pool three diverse backbones by equal-weight logit averaging, trading peak gain for a bounded worst case. On a real-world e-commerce fraud detector trained on selection-biased data, continued training regresses even when carefully tuned, whereas the overlay gains on average +2.26% recall at equal precision ($\Delta$R@P) and +1.60% precision at equal recall ($\Delta$P@R) over production cut-offs spanning 30-57% precision and 23-63% recall. On a public benchmark of seven designed bias-shift variants it raises $\Delta$P@R on every variant and keeps $\Delta$R@P near neutral. Each amendment is a readable predicate naming the fraud pattern it covers.
papers.summary: Gradient-boosted tree fraud detectors have blind spots, and retraining a deployed model is not always safe. In this framework, LLMs propose rules built on features that `SHAP` shows the model underweights; rules that lack empirical support are filtered out, and the rest are calibrated into an additive, reversible log-lift overlay applied at the production threshold. Because a single LLM's benefit varies widely between datasets, rules from three different LLMs are pooled by averaging, which lowers the peak gain but bounds the worst case. On a real e-commerce fraud detector, where continued training made results worse, **the overlay gained +2.26% recall at equal precision and +1.60% precision at equal recall**, and each added rule is a readable predicate naming the fraud pattern it covers.

papers.title: Memory-Aware Multi-Agent Architecture with LLM-based Orchestration for Conversational Recommendation
papers.abstract: Conversational recommender systems often treat user sessions in isolation, limiting their ability to capture how user intent evolves over time. While large language models (LLMs) have improved semantic understanding, they are typically used as isolated components, without addressing how memory, retrieval, and decision-making should be integrated at the system level. In this work, we propose a memory-aware multi-agent architecture for conversational recommendation, in which LLMs act as orchestration layers that coordinate intent refinement, query construction, and interaction flow. A key design principle is the integration of long-term memory as a first-class component, influencing both routing decisions and semantic query formation. We evaluate the system through cross-session memory experiments, multi-turn conversational simulations, and supervisor-driven interaction studies on the Amazon Reviews dataset. Results show that memory-enabled interactions recover up to 63\% of the gap toward explicit-query scenarios and prevent semantic degradation in extended dialogues.
