In addition, supervisory orchestration increases user acceptance by +28.9 percentage points, highlighting the importance of structured orchestration in guiding interaction and output quality. We also observe an exposure bottleneck between retrieved candidates and displayed recommendations. While LLM-reranking does not improve Hit@K, it consistently enhances semantic consistency and diversity. To capture these effects, we introduce the Semantic Consistency Score (SCS), a complementary evaluation measure. Overall, the results emphasize the importance of system-level design choices, suggesting that effective conversational recommendation benefits from explicit memory integration, orchestration, and evaluation beyond traditional ranking metrics.
papers.summary: Conversational recommender systems usually treat each session in isolation and use LLMs as standalone components. The authors propose a multi-agent architecture in which LLMs orchestrate intent refinement, query construction and dialogue flow, with long-term memory shaping both routing decisions and query formation. In experiments on the `Amazon Reviews` dataset, memory recovers up to 63% of the gap to scenarios where users state their query explicitly and prevents semantic drift in long dialogues, and **supervisory orchestration raises user acceptance by 28.9 percentage points**. LLM reranking does not improve `Hit@K` but does improve consistency and diversity, which the authors capture with a new Semantic Consistency Score (`SCS`).

papers.title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Evaluating Timing and Omission in Longitudinal AI Mental Health Support
papers.abstract: Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support commonly focus on the clinical appropriateness of individual responses, potentially overlooking failures that emerge across extended interactions. As AI assistants accumulate memory of users' circumstances and prior disclosures, this raises an accountability question: Do AI chatbots provide appropriate support as users' needs evolve? We investigate by analyzing 14,256 longitudinal simulations grounded in donated chatbot histories from 22 users, examining how a memory-equipped assistant responds to suicidal ideation, self-harm, and anxiety crises across recovery trajectories and communication styles. We introduce the Context-Aware and Readiness-Evaluative (CARE) framework, developed with mental health professionals, to assess the timing and quality of advice, including omissions. Advice was less aligned with users' readiness after a crisis than in matched control stretches of the same conversation, largely because of premature recommendations, which were most common when recovery stalled. Revisiting a crisis reduced premature advice but not lagging advice, and users' communication style changed how often and when the assistant gave recommendations. Although explicitly unproductive advice was rare, the assistant frequently omitted clinician-expected support such as follow-up and planning for next steps. These findings show the limits of single response-level safety evaluation and the need to assess timing, omission, and consistency across users when holding AI systems accountable for longitudinal support.
papers.summary: Evaluations of LLMs for mental-health support usually judge single responses and miss failures that only appear over long interactions. The authors ran 14,256 longitudinal simulations based on donated chatbot histories from 22 users and scored a memory-equipped assistant with the Context-Aware and Readiness-Evaluative (`CARE`) framework, developed with clinicians to rate the timing and quality of advice, including omissions. After a crisis, advice matched users' readiness less well than in matched control stretches, mainly because recommendations came too early, especially when recovery stalled. Explicitly unproductive advice was rare, but **the assistant frequently omitted support clinicians expected, such as follow-up and planning next steps**.

papers.title: AlterNet: Adaptive-Depth Mixture-of-Experts with Learned Halting for Elastic Inference
papers.abstract: Most LLM architectures have fixed compute demands determined at training time. We propose a novel architecture that combines the Mixture-of-Experts architecture with shallow experts and a novel dynamic-depth system to make the extent of a forward pass dynamically adjustable. Our approach lets the model automatically determine the compute needed for a given task, paired with a system to scale it down after training without retraining when the execution environment demands faster or cheaper inference. To achieve this, we introduce an iterative computation mechanism, sequence-level depth-based routing steered by a halting mechanism within the experts, a depth encoding that lets the model track its progress in the chain, and a regularization mechanism that incentivizes the model to use allocated compute efficiently. We present initial benchmarks and discuss future research directions.
papers.summary: Most LLM architectures fix their compute per token at training time. `AlterNet` combines a Mixture-of-Experts design using shallow experts with iterative computation, so the depth of a forward pass adapts to the input. Sequence-level depth routing is controlled by a learned halting mechanism, a depth encoding lets the model track its progress, and a regularizer encourages efficient use of compute. **The depth can also be scaled down after training without retraining** when the deployment environment calls for faster or cheaper inference. The paper presents only initial benchmarks.

papers.title: How are viral trends different from educational and commercial uses of LLM image generation and editing? A privacy-preserving descriptive analysis
papers.abstract: Gemini's Nano Banana models, first introduced in late 2025, led to a shift in the capabilities and use of image generation and editing. We utilize Urania, a Google-developed framework for generating insights about LLM chatbot interactions with rigorous differential privacy (DP) guarantees, to analyze use cases and intents, techniques and ways of prompting, without ever looking at a single image or individual prompt. We select a subsample of 2.1M conversations in early 2026 which utilized Nano Banana models, into roughly 800 clusters in five categories: (1) Social & Viral Sharing, (2) Brand & Marketing Collateral, (3) Educational & Technical Information Media, (4) Product Visualizations & E-commerce, and (5) Architectural & Spatial Designs. We then compare these clusters on 21 features of use, measuring aspects of prompts' (a) editing techniques, (b) artistic style requests, (c) composition, and (d) chatbot interactions. This allows us to describe a baseline of how people are using image generation and editing tools for different use cases---(including growing and emergent use cases which were not possible before Nano Banana)---in a privacy-preserving manner.
papers.summary: Researchers used `Urania`, a Google framework that extracts insights from chatbot conversations with differential privacy (DP) guarantees, to study how people use Gemini's `Nano Banana` image generation and editing models without viewing any individual image or prompt. **They grouped 2.1M conversations from early 2026 into roughly 800 clusters** across five categories: social and viral sharing, brand and marketing, educational and technical media, product visualization and e-commerce, and architectural and spatial design. The clusters are compared on 21 features covering editing techniques, requested artistic styles, composition and chatbot interaction patterns, giving a privacy-preserving baseline of how use differs across these categories, including uses that were not possible before.

papers.title: AttentionSwitch: Jailbreak Defense for LLMs via Joint Learning of Sparse Attention-Head Selection and Scaling
papers.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, yet they remain susceptible to jailbreak attacks that circumvent safety mechanisms and elicit harmful or unintended outputs. Although safety can be improved through model fine-tuning, such approaches can be computationally expensive and may degrade previously acquired capabilities through catastrophic forgetting. Recent jailbreak defenses have therefore explored targeted interventions on specific model components associated with unsafe behavior. However, existing approaches typically decouple two inherently related decisions: where to intervene and how to modify the selected components. Such sequential optimization may be suboptimal because the optimal intervention location can depend on the intervention applied there, and vice versa. In this work, we introduce AttentionSwitch, the first jailbreak defense to jointly optimize intervention sites and strengths within a frozen LLM. Specifically, AttentionSwitch learns a sparse set of attention heads together with query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors, allowing the outputs of the selected heads to be either attenuated or amplified without altering the directions of their representations. Across popular language models and jailbreak attacks, AttentionSwitch outperforms existing defenses, with particularly strong results when training data is scarce.
papers.summary: Jailbreak defenses that edit specific model components usually choose where to intervene and how strongly as two separate steps, even though the best choice of one depends on the other. `AttentionSwitch` learns both together inside a frozen LLM: it selects a sparse set of attention heads and learns query-conditioned multiplicative scaling factors for them. The selected heads can be weakened or strengthened without changing the direction of their representations. Across several popular models and jailbreak attacks it outperforms existing defenses, **especially when training data is scarce**.

papers.title: Random Symbolic Boosting: A Geometric Approach to Symbolic Regression
papers.abstract: Symbolic models offer interpretability, but their construction through generational evolution can be computationally expensive. This article presents Random Symbolic Boosting (RSB), a method that constructs explicit additive symbolic models via boosting over populations of randomly generated syntax trees, eliminating the need for generational evolution. The idea combines two observations: high-dimensional spaces can be spanned by enough linearly independent vectors, and the semantics of syntax trees can be directly manipulated as such vectors. It is shown that, for Ordinary Least Squares, the boosting process guarantees a monotonic reduction of the training error for both regression and classification. Furthermore, an adaptive geometric early stopping mechanism is introduced. It is based on the angle between the prediction and target vectors, is independent of the problems scale, and requires no adjustments across tasks. Evaluated on a standard benchmark for symbolic regression, the method is located at the Pareto-optimal point between predictive accuracy and training time, ranking first on the real-world datasets. Additionally, it was tested on a large tabular classification benchmark with 200 problems, achieving competitive results.
papers.summary: Symbolic regression produces interpretable formulas, but evolving them over many generations is computationally expensive. Random Symbolic Boosting (`RSB`) instead builds additive symbolic models by boosting over populations of randomly generated syntax trees, treating each tree's outputs on the data as a vector that helps span the target space. With ordinary least squares, the training error is guaranteed to decrease monotonically, and an early-stopping rule based on the angle between the prediction and target vectors needs no tuning across tasks. On a standard symbolic regression benchmark, **it sits at the Pareto-optimal trade-off between accuracy and training time and ranks first on the real-world datasets**, and it is competitive on a 200-problem tabular classification benchmark.

papers.title: AtariBench: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in Atari Gameplay
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.
papers.summary: `AtariBench` tests whether vision-language models (VLMs) can act in dynamic environments by having them play 20 Atari 2600 games from high-frame-rate gameplay, with game time decoupled from the model's inference speed. Even state-of-the-art VLMs **often fail to infer object motion and direction**, make brittle sequences of decisions and rely too heavily on the text history even when new visual feedback is provided. The authors also introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores reliably signal model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance.

papers.title: Debate to Deceive: Poisoning LLM's Fact-Checking via Game-Theoretic Multi-Agent Debate
papers.abstract: Knowledge attacks on Large Language Models, such as manipulating fact-checking judgments, pose significant risks to AI reliability. Existing approaches -- adversarial suffix/template injection and single-agent self-reflection -- lack robustness across diverse defenses and are prone to confirmation bias and costly trial-and-error, respectively. We propose Debate-to-Deceive (D2D), a multi-agent debate framework grounded in human debate structure and rhetorical style, enabling agents to generate adversarial passages that are semantically coherent, rhetorically effective, and resistant to early confirmation bias. D2D formalizes the adversarial process as an evolutionary game in which agents adaptively evolve their rhetorical strategies (Logos, Pathos, Ethos) through competition. To manage the intractably large LLM output space, we decouple agent behavior into a strategic layer, which selects a rhetorical action from a compact strategy space via evolutionary-inspired learning dynamics, and a generation layer, where the LLM produces a concrete passage conditioned on that strategy and the debate context. On four fact-checking benchmarks (FEVER, HealthVer, CLIMATE-FEVER, and SciFact), D2D substantially outperforms existing attacks and evades most defenses.
papers.summary: Existing attacks that push large language models (LLMs) into wrong fact-checking verdicts, such as adversarial suffix injection or single-agent self-reflection, hold up poorly against varied defenses and fall into confirmation bias or costly trial-and-error. `Debate-to-Deceive` (`D2D`) has multiple agents debate in the style of human debaters to produce adversarial passages that read coherently and persuade. The process is modeled as an evolutionary game: a strategic layer picks a rhetorical move (`Logos`, `Pathos`, or `Ethos`) through evolution-inspired learning dynamics, and a generation layer has the LLM write a passage conditioned on that move and the debate so far. On `FEVER`, `HealthVer`, `CLIMATE-FEVER`, and `SciFact`, `D2D` **substantially outperforms existing attacks and evades most defenses**.

papers.title: Goals as a Representational Layer for Human-AI Collaboration
papers.abstract: Goals are central to how people, teams, and organizations structure their work. Yet, while generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly operate across a worker's context, information about why a person is pursuing a task, beyond local prompts and interactions, is typically missing. We argue that goals should become an explicit representational layer mediating interactions among people, AI systems, and organizations. Because human goals are hierarchical, partially latent, and dynamically evolving, such a layer must be multidimensional, both grounded in human articulation and inferred from available evidence, and continuously updated. A goal layer could connect immediate requests to broader outcomes, improve the organization and retrieval of relevant context, support reflection and coordination, and provide a foundation for training, aligning, and evaluating AI systems in terms of human-centered outcomes. We highlight these opportunities while identifying open challenges involving goal inference, socio-cognitive frictions, alignment, privacy, and governance.
papers.summary: Generative AI tools usually see a worker's immediate prompts but not why the person is doing the task. This position paper argues that goals should become an explicit representational layer connecting people, AI systems, and organizations. Because human goals are hierarchical, partly unstated, and change over time, the authors say such a layer must be **multidimensional, both stated by people and inferred from evidence, and continuously updated**. They describe how it could link requests to broader outcomes, organize context, and anchor the training and evaluation of AI systems, and they list open problems in goal inference, alignment, privacy, and governance.

papers.title: CrowdDirector: Runtime Orchestration of Crowd Simulation through Natural-Language Directives
papers.abstract: Natural language offers an intuitive way to direct a virtual crowd while a simulation is running. Handwritten rules execute efficiently but cannot respond flexibly to varied instructions, whereas asking a large language model (LLM) to control the crowd at every update introduces repeated latency, cost, and the risk of unsupported actions. We present CrowdDirector, a framework that uses an LLM only when the user adds or changes an instruction. The LLM translates the request into a structured instruction, and a scene validator checks whether the entities and actions it references exist in the current Unity scene. Accepted instructions are stored and remain continuously active as the simulation is running. At each simulation tick, a graph neural network uses the current scene state and active instruction to choose an available action and target for each agent, while Unity handles movement, interactions, and animation. The network is trained offline on simulated scenarios, with LLM guidance on how agents should respond to instructions. Our evaluations show the scene validator's feasibility decisions matched human judgements more often than the LLM's own assessment, and on a behavioural benchmark CrowdDirector follows user instructions more closely than handwritten rules while avoiding repeated LLM calls. It therefore provides a practical middle ground between fixed rules and continuous LLM control.
papers.summary: Directing a virtual crowd with natural language while a simulation runs is hard: handwritten rules are rigid, and calling a large language model (LLM) on every update is slow, expensive, and can produce actions the scene doesn't support. `CrowdDirector` calls the LLM only when the user adds or changes an instruction, turns that instruction into a structured form, and has a scene validator check that the referenced entities and actions exist in the `Unity` scene. On every simulation tick, a graph neural network trained offline with LLM guidance picks an action and target for each agent. The validator's feasibility decisions matched human judgments more often than the LLM's own assessments did, and **the system followed instructions more closely than handwritten rules without repeated LLM calls**.

papers.title: Conflux: Preventing Privilege Escalation with Principal Contexts and System-Level Evaluation
papers.abstract: LLM agents combine information from multiple principals while acting externally. We formalise privilege escalation (PE) as the system-level security objective: an action may proceed only if every principal that influenced it would allow it. Model-level defences remain probabilistic, so enforcement must sit outside model judgement. We present Conflux, a principal-context defence. Its kernel, ITES, derives authority from provenance and the organisation's existing access-control system and intersects the permissions of every influencing principal. We prove a conditional authority-confinement theorem: under complete mediation, no-laundering provenance, a known non-empty decision context, fresh permission checks, and action binding, the kernel admits no action that escalates privilege with respect to any recorded influencing principal. The theorem covers the represented value-influence fragment; control influence from tool, branch, recipient, or plan-step selection remains a refinement obligation. Conflux extends the kernel with independent policy ports, argument-aware authorisation, disclosure, consent, delegation, restriction, and exposure planning. We describe two system- level evaluators. SLED is a black-box evaluator: it exhaustively explores a declared finite model of a defence up to a bound. SLED-V is a white-box evaluator: it checks a serialisable intermediate representation against security and provenance properties. The evidence is bounded and partial. The appendix reports retained AgentDojo, SLED, and SLED-V results, including the limits of those runs. No result in this paper is an unbounded deployment guarantee.
papers.summary: LLM agents mix input from several principals (the users, tools, and data sources that influence them) while taking real actions, so model-level defenses alone cannot guarantee that no action exceeds anyone's permissions. The authors define privilege escalation as an action that some influencing principal would not allow, and present `Conflux`, whose kernel `ITES` derives authority from provenance and the organization's existing access control and takes the intersection of the permissions of every influencing principal. They prove that, **under stated conditions such as complete mediation and fresh permission checks, the kernel admits no privilege-escalating action** for the influence it tracks, while noting that influence through tool or plan-step selection is not yet covered. Two evaluators, the black-box `SLED` and the white-box `SLED-V`, plus `AgentDojo` runs provide bounded evidence, and the authors make no claim of an unbounded deployment guarantee.

papers.title: Federated training performs as well as centralized for 3D Latent Diffusion for Diagnosis-Conditioned Brain MRI Synthesis
papers.abstract: Generative models of brain MRI are useful to understand brain conditions, and to enrich scarce and imbalanced neuroimaging data. However, training these models requires large, multi-site training sets, which is challenging. Federated learning (FL) allows for training deep learning models without sharing data. We show that training a 3D conditional latent model federatedly (where data is kept private at each site) performs similarly to centralized training (where all the data have been copied to a single site). We evaluate three metrics: conditional fidelity (how well generated MRIs perform in classification), diversity (how the generated images match the real data distribution, using MultiScale-SSIM), and realism (how close generated images are to real images, using Fr\'{e}chet Inception Distance). Our results show that federated training is a viable route to develop multi-site generative models of brain MRI.
papers.summary: Generative models of brain MRI need large multi-site datasets, which privacy rules make hard to pool. The authors train a 3D latent diffusion model conditioned on diagnosis using federated learning (FL), where each site keeps its data private, and compare it with centralized training on pooled data. They measure conditional fidelity through downstream classification, diversity with `MS-SSIM`, and realism with Fréchet Inception Distance (`FID`). **Federated training performs about as well as centralized training** on all three, which suggests FL is a workable way to build multi-site brain MRI generators.

papers.title: On Lipschitz Explosion in Deep Neural Networks with Normalization: Consequences for Optimization and Adversarial Robustness
papers.abstract: Can a network look stable at every layer and still be exponentially unstable as a whole? The Lipschitz constant of a neural network is a basic stability quantity appearing in optimization guarantees, generalization bounds, and robustness certificates. Deep networks naturally admit two such notions, input Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to data perturbations, and parameter Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to weight perturbations. We prove that, for deep networks with normalization layers, with batch normalization as the canonical example, both Lipschitz constants can grow exponentially with depth and hence with parameter dimension, even under strong per-layer norm control such as $\|W_\ell\|_2\le 1$, and already for linear activations. Thus, a mechanism widely used to stabilize training can create severe worst-case instabilities that are invisible locally, i.e., from layerwise norm bounds alone. Parameter-Lipschitz explosion turns Lipschitz-dependent nonsmooth optimization guarantees into exponential-in-dimension bounds for deep normalized networks, while input-Lipschitz explosion makes worst-case Lipschitz-based generalization and robustness certificates vacuous. The latter also yields a concrete rank-separation mechanism for adversarial vulnerability. The theory predicts that perturbations introducing new singular directions should be amplified much more strongly than perturbations at the same noise level that remain within the input's original singular subspace. Experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 support this prediction, showing that rank-creating perturbations cause substantially sharper drops in accuracy, confidence, and margins than same-subspace perturbations.
papers.summary: Can a network that looks stable at every layer still be exponentially unstable as a whole? The authors prove that in deep networks with normalization layers such as batch normalization, both the input Lipschitz constant (sensitivity to data perturbations) and the parameter Lipschitz constant (sensitivity to weight perturbations) **can grow exponentially with depth even when every weight matrix has spectral norm at most 1**, and even with linear activations. As a result, Lipschitz-based optimization guarantees become exponential in dimension, and worst-case generalization and robustness certificates become vacuous. The theory predicts that perturbations adding new singular directions should be amplified far more than equally sized perturbations within the input's existing subspace, and experiments on `MNIST`, `Fashion-MNIST`, and `CIFAR-10` confirm much sharper drops in accuracy and margins for these rank-creating perturbations.

papers.title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
papers.abstract: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.
papers.summary: Persistent-memory systems for language models decide not only what to retrieve but which stored information gets to change current outputs. Jacobian-causal memory control (`JCMC`) gives each authorized memory intervention a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, chooses interventions that reach a target effect within a side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects to decide whether to keep or roll back each one. Under smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, the authors prove local approximation, reachability, regret, and interaction bounds. **The paper reports no benchmark results**; it instead specifies an evaluation protocol against relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines, and states that the claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match it.

papers.title: Guardrail Erosion in Domain Fine-Tuned Large Language Models: A Paired Audit of Knowledge-Centric Abstention in Biomedical LLMs
papers.abstract: The number of domain fine-tuned models, particularly in the biomedical domain, is rapidly expanding. Fine-tuning promises high-performing models at a fraction of the cost of training a base model, but it can also produce unintended behavioral changes. Multiple studies have shown that safety guardrails can erode with fine-tuning, yet large-scale studies across model architectures, data mixtures, and fine-tuning methodologies remain limited. Where prior work in this space has studied value-centric refusal, this work focuses on knowledge-centric abstention. We audit 25 biomedical domain fine-tuned large language models against 11 paired base checkpoints on MedAbstain and ClinDet-Bench to evaluate the impact of fine-tuning on knowledge-centric abstention. We find that defined appropriate abstention measured by these benchmarks, already low in base models (median 8.3% on MedAbstain), falls further after fine-tuning (median 4.2%, decreasing in 21 of 25 pairs on MedAbstain), and that the magnitude and direction of change are heterogeneous across pairs. These results motivate fine-tuning methods that improve domain-specific capability while preserving appropriate caution.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning a model for a domain can erode its safety behavior, but large studies of this across architectures and training recipes are scarce, and most look at value-based refusal rather than knowledge-based abstention (declining to answer when the model lacks the information). The authors audit 25 biomedical fine-tuned large language models against 11 matching base checkpoints on `MedAbstain` and `ClinDet-Bench`. Appropriate abstention was already low in base models and **fell from a median of 8.3% to 4.2% on `MedAbstain` after fine-tuning, dropping in 21 of 25 pairs**, though the size and direction of change varied between pairs. The authors argue this calls for fine-tuning methods that keep appropriate caution while adding domain capability.

papers.title: Aligning, Fast and Slow: A Control-Theoretic Oversight Framework for Long-Horizon Trajectories and Maintained Deployments
papers.abstract: AI agents can pass checks on individual tasks while retaining memory or code changes that alter their later behavior. We introduce a control-theoretic framework that couples a fast loop controlling proposed actions with a slow loop reviewing persistent changes and reassessing configurations after model or tool updates. When measurement errors and changes between checks are bounded and controllers can enforce their decisions, we derive a deployment-level bound and a rule for dividing review effort. In simulation, dividing a fixed review budget between both loops reduces mean maximum departure from intended behavior roughly twelvefold compared with review confined to individual runs. In coding stress tests with authored memories and five matched seeds, combined controls reduce mean severity on a 0-3 scale from 0.325 without gates to 0.117, resolving 33 of 120 issues versus 35 without gates; in trading stress tests, combined controls reduce mean shortfall in low-emission purchases from 0.892 without gates to 0.107. The overall framework helps developers and auditors compare and enforce oversight designs, while the agent studies test component controls rather than the full deployment-level guarantee.
papers.summary: AI agents can pass checks on individual tasks while accumulating memory or code changes that alter how they behave later. The authors propose a control-theoretic oversight framework with a fast loop that gates proposed actions and a slow loop that reviews persistent changes and re-checks configurations after model or tool updates, and they derive a deployment-level bound and a rule for dividing review effort between the two loops. In simulation, splitting a fixed review budget across both loops **cuts the mean maximum drift from intended behavior roughly twelvefold** compared with reviewing only individual runs. In coding stress tests with planted memories, combined controls reduced mean severity from 0.325 to 0.117 while resolving 33 of 120 issues versus 35 without gates, and trading stress tests showed similar gains.

papers.title: Learning from How Users Interpret: Personalizing Recommendation Explanation Order
papers.abstract: Personalized explanations typically adapt their content or presentation based on preferences, interaction histories, or other user characteristics. We examine whether regularities inferred from prior textual interpretations can support personalization of explanation organization. In a controlled within participant study with 122 participants, prior interpretations were represented along three dimensions: information selection, relative salience, and relational organization. The relational dimension was partially operationalized through co mobilization. These representations were aggregated into fixed historical profiles and used to organize otherwise identical explanation sentences. Participants encountered four organization procedures: the OWN historical profile, the DONOR historical profile, a population profile called POP, and a language model procedure using the historical profile called PROFILE LLM. Post exposure objective comprehension was the primary outcome. OWN achieved 86.5 percent correct responses, compared with 66.0 percent for DONOR, 63.9 percent for POP, and 73.0 percent for PROFILE LLM. Mixed effects analyses showed higher comprehension with OWN than with each alternative procedure. No reliable overall condition effect was detected for recommendation acceptance. These findings indicate that historical profiles derived from prior interpretations can provide an actionable signal for personalizing explanation order while keeping explanatory content and wording fixed.
papers.summary: Personalized explanations usually adapt their content, but the authors ask whether the order of explanation sentences can be personalized based on how a user interpreted earlier texts. In a within-participant study with 122 people, prior interpretations were summarized along information selection, relative salience, and relational organization, then used to reorder otherwise identical recommendation explanations. Ordering by the participant's own historical profile (`OWN`) **yielded 86.5% correct comprehension answers**, compared with 66.0% for another person's profile, 63.9% for a population profile, and 73.0% for a language-model procedure using the profile. Recommendation acceptance showed no reliable difference between conditions.

papers.title: Training Stability under Adaptive Curricula
papers.abstract: Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approaches train reinforcement learning (RL) agents on diverse curricula that may evolve with their capabilities. While prior work has largely focused on how these curricula are constructed, we study whether their students remain trainable under the resulting distributions. Across multiple UED mechanisms, environment complexities, and extended training horizons, we identify recurring learner-side pathologies, including parameter growth, degraded value--outcome ordering, and loss of representational diversity, that accompany stagnation and performance degradation. These findings connect limitations in UED to optimization failures previously identified in conventional deep RL, while showing how adaptive curricula couple the learner's optimization state to its future training distribution. Controlled interventions show that mitigating selected pathologies improves learning. Stabilizing the learner improves long-horizon performance and zero-shot generalization without changing the curriculum rule or increasing environment interaction. Our results establish learner trainability as a complementary design principle for UED. Effective curricula require students that remain capable of learning from the distributions they produce.
papers.summary: Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) trains reinforcement learning (RL) agents on curricula that adapt as the agent improves, and earlier work has focused on how those curricula are built. The authors instead ask whether the learner stays trainable, and across several UED methods and long training runs they find recurring problems: parameter growth, degraded ordering between value estimates and outcomes, and loss of representational diversity, all accompanying stagnation. Because the curriculum depends on the learner's current state, these optimization failures feed back into the future training distribution. Targeted interventions that stabilize the learner **improve long-horizon performance and zero-shot generalization without changing the curriculum rule or adding environment interaction**.

papers.title: Not All Latents Are Equal: Importance-Weighted Latent Graph Generation
papers.abstract: Graph generation has shown tremendous effectiveness in modeling complex scientific tasks ranging from molecule generation to optimized circuit design. Most recent advancements have developed models that learn to denoise noisy graphs using either discrete diffusion or flow matching. However, discrete graph diffusion scales quadratically with the number of nodes, making it difficult to use such models on larger graphs. On the other hand, latent graph generation instead seeks to denoise noisy graph latents, which scale better to more nodes due to their lower dimension. However, in practice, latent graph generation models lag behind their discrete counterparts in performance. We study this problem, finding that it is caused by the unequal distribution of that different latent dimensions have on graph reconstruction. the impact. We observe that the vast majority of impact is contained in only a smaller number of latent dimensions. Since equal emphasis is placed on reconstructing the entire latent in the loss function, existing models are optimized to reconstruct information irrelevant to the downstream task. To tackle this problem, we propose Latent Importance Reweighting ({\bf LIR)} which weights each latent dimensions via it's importance to final graph reconstruction. Importance is calculated as the relative influence of a single latent unit on graph reconstruction, which is represented via the Jacobian of the decoder relative to the latent. Our method is model-agnostic and requires no additional model parameters or hyperparameters. Experiments show that LIR can boost performance and lead to faster training convergence when applied to two different autoencoders on various benchmark datasets. Code: https://github.com/biraaj/GraphGenLatentReweight
papers.summary: Latent graph generation, which denoises compressed graph representations, scales better than discrete graph diffusion but usually performs worse. The authors trace this gap to the fact that **most of the impact on graph reconstruction comes from a small number of latent dimensions**, while standard losses weight every dimension equally. Latent Importance Reweighting (`LIR`) weights each latent dimension by its influence on reconstruction, measured through the decoder's Jacobian, and adds no parameters or hyperparameters. Applied to two different autoencoders on several benchmarks, `LIR` improves generation quality and speeds up training convergence.

papers.title: SteerGR: Steering Generative Recommendation via Sparse Autoencoders for Controllable Game Discovery
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation aims to predict item identifiers from user interaction histories, but explicit control over the properties of recommended items remains underexplored. A key challenge is to connect human-readable concepts to internal features whose interventions effectively change the recommended items. To address this, we propose Steerable Generative Recommender (SteerGR), a framework that uses sparse autoencoders for concept-level control in game discovery. SteerGR proceeds through three stages: (i) Concept Definition and Grounding for defining play concepts with an LLM; (ii) Feature Discovery and Selection for discovering candidate features by their concept associations and selecting one by its steering effect; and (iii) Sparse Feature Intervention for amplifying or suppressing selected features to steer recommendations without retraining the recommender. Extensive experiments with two industrial generative recommendation models on a real-world game dataset show that the selected features successfully steer recommendations toward or away from target concepts. We believe this work takes a first step to extend SAE-based steering from LLMs to industrial generative recommendation.
papers.summary: Generative recommenders predict item identifiers from a user's history but offer little explicit control over what kinds of items they recommend. `SteerGR` uses an LLM to define play concepts for game discovery, finds sparse autoencoder (SAE) features associated with each concept, keeps the feature whose intervention best shifts recommendations, and then amplifies or suppresses it at inference time without retraining. Experiments with two industrial generative recommendation models on a real-world game dataset show that **the selected features steer recommendations toward or away from target concepts**, carrying SAE-based steering from LLMs over to recommendation systems.

papers.title: MotionDecipher: LLM-Assisted Clinical Interpretation of Human Motion Signals for Efficient Gait Analysis
papers.abstract: Clinical gait and motion analysis is widely used to guide targeted interventions for patients with neurological disorders, the outcome of which is typically a report with descriptions of joint movements and forces. Current practices rely on experts' manual effort, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide opportunities to address this problem, but translating human motion into clinical gait descriptions remains challenging because the quality of the context directly affects LLMs' reasoning capability over continuous motion signals. To tackle this, we introduce MotionDecipher, a novel framework bridging the semantic gap between motion data and clinical interpretations. Specifically, we made 3 key advancements: 1) a Human Motion Tokenizer that converts motion signals into domain-specific tokens for time- and frequency-informed gait interpretation; 2) a Meta Feature Selector that transforms tokens into Structured Representations; and 3) a Hybrid Context Constructor to determine the optimal demonstration-based prompt for In-Context Learning. We evaluated MotionDecipher on data collected at an accredited gait lab from 122 patients and 46 controls. Results show that MotionDecipher achieves 0.91 BERTScore (13% over GPT-5), while expert evaluation ranks MotionDecipher highest in Correctness, Completeness, and Conciseness compared to baselines, highlighting its promise for efficient gait analysis.
papers.summary: Clinical gait analysis reports are written by hand by experts, and large language models (LLMs) struggle to reason directly over continuous motion signals. `MotionDecipher` converts motion data into domain-specific tokens that capture time and frequency information, selects meta features to build structured representations, and assembles the best demonstration examples for in-context learning. Evaluated on gait-lab data from 122 patients and 46 controls, it **reaches a `BERTScore` of 0.91, 13% higher than `GPT-5`**, and clinical experts ranked it highest for correctness, completeness, and conciseness.

papers.title: The Matthews Correlation Coefficient: Fifty years
papers.abstract: Fifty years after its introduction, the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) remains central -and debated- in binary classification. This survey offers a comprehensive retrospective and an in-depth analysis of MCC, covering its historical development, mathematical foundations, and implications for practice. We clarify long-standing misconceptions, formalize its equivalences (to Pearson's correlation and to Chi2 in 2x2 tables), and examine its behavior under class imbalance. Beyond MCC, we develop analytical (derivatives) and graphical (contour plots) frameworks that generalize to any confusion-matrix-based metric. These frameworks expose structural properties -bias, robustness, sensitivity- that scalar summaries conceal, and they provide actionable guidance for selecting and interpreting performance measures in applications where reliability and fairness matter. Together, our results position MCC within a broader toolkit while clarifying when it is informative -and when alternatives may be preferable.
papers.summary: Fifty years after its introduction, the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) is still widely used and argued about as a binary classification metric. This survey traces its history, corrects common misconceptions, formally shows its equivalence to Pearson's correlation and to the chi-squared statistic on 2x2 tables, and examines how it behaves under class imbalance. The authors also develop derivative-based and contour-plot tools that **apply to any metric computed from a confusion matrix**, exposing bias, robustness, and sensitivity that single numbers hide, and they give practical guidance on when MCC is informative and when another metric is a better choice.

papers.title: I Think, Therefore I Attack: Evaluating Thought Injection Attacks on Reasoning Agents
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) are one of the key components of current agentic systems. LRMs augment their output with an explicit chain-of-thought reasoning stage, introducing a new attack surface for thought injection, in which untrusted text resembling the model's own deliberation is fed back to the model. We present a two-part study of this attack, performed against the prevailing large, production class open-weight models (e.g., GLM-5.3, MiniMax-M2.5, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). We first evaluate the effectiveness of static thought-injection prompts under different styles as well as tagged and untagged conditions and find that the effects of thinking tags and payload styles are all properties of the specific target model. In the second study, we exploit this model-specificity in a containerized agentic cyber range, using indirect injection prompts styled in the form of the target model's own reasoning traces to achieve attack success rates (ASR) up to 50% on operational objectives such as reverse-shell exfiltration and repository backdooring. We also find that the same malicious objective in standard prompt injection user voice never succeeds, and thinking tags suppress the agent's tendency to disclose the injection. Our results show that imitating a reasoning model's own thought style is effective for this style of attack, and that tag stripping is an unreliable defense.
papers.summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) produce an explicit chain of thought, which creates a new attack: thought injection, where untrusted text written to look like the model's own reasoning is fed back to it. Against production open-weight models such as `GLM-5.3`, `MiniMax-M2.5`, and `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next`, the authors find that whether thinking tags and payload styles matter depends on the specific target model. In a containerized agentic cyber range, indirect injections written in the target's own reasoning style **achieve attack success rates of up to 50%** on goals such as reverse-shell exfiltration and backdooring a repository, while the same goals phrased as ordinary user-voice prompt injection never succeed. The results also show that stripping thinking tags is an unreliable defense.
papers.highlight_summary:
Reasoning models treat text that looks like their own chain-of-thought as their own deliberation, so attackers can plant fake "thoughts" in a prompt or document to steer them. Across two studies on open-weight models, injected thoughts written in the target model's own reasoning style and wrapped in thinking tags drove an agent to complete real attack objectives. The same requests phrased as an ordinary prompt injection never succeeded.

- **Single-message test:** 100 short injection prompts were tested against `GLM-5.3-Flash`, `Qwen3.8-27B` and `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` to see whether they would leak protected customer records (6,000 runs). Pooled leak rates fell in a narrow **8.6–11.7%** band, but wrapping the same text in thinking tags more than tripled the rate on `GLM-5.3-Flash` (**13.4% vs. 3.8%**) and made almost no difference on `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next`.
- **Where leaks appear:** **20.8%** of leaks appeared only inside the reasoning trace, which users and answer-only monitors usually never see. Removing the tags pushed more leaks into that hidden channel (up to 33.7% on `Qwen3.8-27B`), so stripping tags is an unreliable defense.
- **Agent test setup:** A sandboxed agent was asked to summarize a document that contained the hidden injection, tested on `MiniMax-M2.5` and `GLM-5.2`. Payloads copied from `MiniMax-M2.5`'s own reasoning traces and wrapped in tags made that model open a reverse shell in **42%** of runs and push a backdoored repository in **50%**. Without tags these rates fell to 8% and 10%, and user-voice payloads with the same goals scored **0% in every condition**.
- **Style transfers unevenly, and attacks stay hidden:** `GLM-5.2`'s reasoning style worked against `MiniMax-M2.5` (20% and 14%), but the reverse barely worked (0% and 2%). Thinking tags also kept the agent from mentioning the injection: in one condition, removing the tags dropped the share of runs where the injection went unmentioned from **92% to 22%**.
- **Limitations:** The two studies used different models and objectives, and the self-voice payloads came from the target's own solution traces, so copying its style is mixed up with handing it a ready plan. Scoring was done by hand on 50 runs per condition, and the authors describe the work as preliminary.

papers.title: Notwithstanding Anything to the Contrary, Ignore All Instructions: Measuring Prompt Injection Guards on Legal Contract Review Attacks
papers.abstract: Specialized prompt injection guards are deployed in front of document analysis systems, but no false positive rate has been published for any of them on legal contracts. We measure eleven open-weights guards on two corpora of legal contracts and find that existing guards struggle: document-level false positive rates are as high as 92.39%; two guards fall below chance on paired AUC; and a five-regex baseline is not Pareto-dominated by any guard in the panel. Controlled probes locate model-specific as well as general failure modes. Prompted LLMs resolve the tested failures, including a second threat category (unauthorized scope claims) on which every guard scores zero. A cascaded LLM solution, where the positives of a mid-tier model are verified by a frontier model, is 6.5x cheaper than using exclusively a frontier model and approaches its performance.
papers.summary: Prompt injection guards are deployed in front of document analysis systems, but none had a published false positive rate on legal contracts. Testing eleven open-weight guards on two contract corpora, the authors find **document-level false positive rates as high as 92.39%**, two guards performing below chance on paired AUC, and no guard that Pareto-dominates a simple five-regex baseline. Prompted LLMs fix the tested failures, including a second threat type (unauthorized scope claims) on which every guard scores zero. A cascade in which a frontier model verifies the positives flagged by a mid-tier model costs 6.5 times less than using the frontier model alone and comes close to its accuracy.

papers.title: Solver-Admitted Metamorphic Testing of Learned Network Optimization Surrogates
papers.abstract: Equivalent encodings of an optimization problem can produce different learned predictions. Interpreting these differences requires accounting for numerical error and multiple optima. We construct metamorphic tests for optimization solver surrogates with explicit eligibility conditions, output alignment, and numerical thresholds. Reference-solver agreement and independent constraint checks determine which sampled pairs enter the audit. We study alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF), the traveling salesman problem (TSP), the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP), and maximum independent set (MIS). Across five grids, GridSFM-Open violates each of 13 relations on at least one grid, and 12 by more than twice the threshold. Randomly initialized copies of the grid models fail nearly the same relations, so the failures do not require training. Source patches and input canonicalization remove selected discrepancies, but no intervention establishes preserved accuracy and feasibility within the declared margin on every grid. In routing, Policy Optimization with Multiple Optima (POMO) has a single-pass rotation/reflection violation rate that rises from 12.7% to 89.5% between 20 and 100 cities. Graph-Based Diffusion Solvers for Combinatorial Optimization (DIFUSCO) violates the MIS disjoint-union relation on 35.6% of draws. Post hoc normalization within connected components removes these violations on the tested graphs. These findings support reporting metamorphic consistency alongside optimality, feasibility, and accuracy, and validating repair quality separately from consistency.
papers.summary: Learned surrogates for optimization solvers can give different answers for mathematically equivalent encodings of the same problem. The authors build metamorphic tests with explicit eligibility rules, output alignment, and numerical thresholds, using reference solvers and constraint checks to decide which test pairs count, and apply them to alternating-current optimal power flow (`AC-OPF`), `TSP`, `CVRP`, and maximum independent set. `GridSFM-Open` violates all 13 relations on at least one grid, and randomly initialized copies fail nearly the same ones, so the failures do not come from training. **The rotation/reflection violation rate of `POMO` rises from 12.7% to 89.5% between 20 and 100 cities**, and `DIFUSCO` violates a disjoint-union relation on 35.6% of samples. Some repairs remove specific violations, but none preserves accuracy and feasibility across every grid.

papers.title: What Matters for LLM Persona Simulation: Signal Form in Cold-Start E-Commerce Advertising
papers.abstract: Estimating advertising performance in cold-start settings is challenging because historical logs are unavailable before launch. Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential alternative by simulating persona-conditioned user responses, but it remains unclear which design choices actually drive LLM-based persona simulation. Using real Google Ads e-commerce campaign data across five demographic segments, we identify three signal-form dimensions that affect simulation quality: (i) a demographic anchor without noisy rich attributes, (ii) a relative qualitative banner-blindness signal rather than quantitative anchors, and (iii) prompt phrasing. On this campaign, our method attains an MAE of 24.9 and a MAPE of 26.1%, a 51.3% lower MAE than the best tested non-LLM baseline and 77.3% lower than an LLM configuration using explicit CTR anchors. Systematic ablations show that minimal demographic descriptions achieve lower mean error than richer persona configurations, while relative qualitative cues substantially outperform the tested quantitative anchors. We additionally compare these configurations with direct-prior and rule-based baselines and with alternative LLM configurations.
papers.summary: Before an ad campaign launches there are no historical logs, so large language models (LLMs) that simulate how different personas respond are one way to estimate performance, but it is unclear which design choices matter. Using real `Google Ads` e-commerce data across five demographic segments, the authors identify three factors: a minimal demographic anchor without noisy extra attributes, a relative qualitative signal for banner blindness instead of numeric anchors, and prompt phrasing. Their configuration reaches an MAE of 24.9, **51.3% lower than the best non-LLM baseline and 77.3% lower than an LLM given explicit click-through-rate anchors**. Ablations show that sparse persona descriptions beat richer ones.

papers.title: When F1 Is Not Enough: Auditing Codebooks for LLM-Assisted Annotation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for text annotation in social science, but standard performance metrics do not explain why errors occur. Low F1 may reflect limitations of the annotation system, defects in the written codebook, or inconsistency in reference labels. We propose a pre-deployment codebook audit for LLM-assisted annotation. The audit uses class-specific metrics and confusion matrices to identify problematic classes and boundaries, structured document-level review to attribute error sources, and targeted codebook revision followed by held-out evaluation. We apply the audit to two published multi-class codebooks from distinct domains. In both applications, the audit identifies under-specified or conflicting coding rules, and targeted revisions reduce the diagnosed errors on held-out data. Analyses with two LLM annotators show that some problematic boundaries and codebook revisions transfer across models, whereas other revision effects are annotator-specific. The results show that LLM annotation errors can help identify weaknesses in the written measurement instrument, not only in the model. Codebook auditing complements prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning by clarifying whether persistent errors call for model improvement, codebook revision, or renewed scrutiny of reference labels.
papers.summary: When LLMs annotate text for social science research, a low F1 score doesn't reveal whether errors come from the model, a flawed codebook (the written coding instructions), or inconsistent reference labels. The authors propose an audit before deployment that combines class-level metrics, confusion matrices, document-level review to attribute each error to a source, and targeted codebook revisions checked on held-out data. Applied to two published multi-class codebooks, the audit **found under-specified or conflicting rules in both, and the revisions reduced the diagnosed errors on held-out data**. Comparisons across two LLM annotators show that some problem boundaries and fixes transfer between models while others are specific to one annotator.

papers.title: Learning Whom to Trust About the Unseen: Source Credibility and Reliability Transfer in Language Models
papers.abstract: A source who has been right before deserves attention, but about what? We ask how far a demonstrated record of reliability travels in language models when the new claim cannot be checked, and whether the answer depends on the kind of claim. Three behavioral studies across six models approach the question from three angles. Study 1 adapts the Einstein-effect paradigm and finds that models, unlike the human sample, favor a spiritual leader over a scientist for the same obscure statement, and that the preference largely reverses when the statement is reworded in the vocabulary of physics. Study 2 adapts a paradigm in which a trusted expert calls a scientific or religious explanation unknown or a mystery; models reproduce the human domain asymmetry in exaggerated form. Study 3, the central test, gives two fictional informants different records on checkable river forecasts and then has them endorse matched claims about hidden natural and spiritual causes of the same village events. Most models carry the record to natural causes and barely at all to spiritual ones; one model transfers it weakly to either. Telling the model that the reliable informant forecasts by spiritual guidance rather than by measurement lowers that informant's influence on natural claims in every model and produces no comparable gain on spiritual claims in any. Demonstrated reliability thus has a scope in these models, and the account a source gives of how they came to be reliable can narrow it. Whether this reflects a judgment about relevance or the low prior credence of spiritual claims is the question the design leaves open, and we outline the experiment that would settle it.
papers.summary: Language models are tested on how far a source's proven track record carries when it makes a new claim that cannot be checked, and whether the type of claim changes the answer. Three behavioral studies across six models adapt paradigms from human psychology. In one, models favor a spiritual leader over a scientist for an obscure statement, unlike human participants, until the statement is reworded in physics vocabulary. In the central study, informants with good or bad records on river forecasts endorse hidden natural or spiritual causes of village events. **Most models carry a good record over to natural-cause claims but barely to spiritual ones**, and saying the reliable informant forecasts by spiritual guidance lowers their influence on natural claims in every model.

papers.title: Mind the Divergence: Divergence-Guided Reliability-Aware Fusion and Adaptive LLM Prompting for Conversational Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversations (MERC) integrates textual, acoustic, and visual cues to identify utterance-level emotions. However, existing approaches generally do not explicitly adapt multimodal processing to the degree of inter-modal predictive disagreement. In real conversations, semantic incongruity, concealed emotion, noisy observations, and ambiguity can affect modality-specific emotional evidence differently, while the reliability of individual modalities varies across samples. Rather than identifying each source of inconsistency separately, we model their common consequence for emotion recognition as predictive disagreement among unimodal emotion distributions over the same emotion-label set. Such disagreement makes indiscriminate fusion prone to propagating unreliable or competing evidence. Inspired by the Brunswik Lens Model, we propose MiD-ERC, a divergence-centric framework that quantifies inter-modal predictive disagreement using a normalized divergence score and estimates sample-specific modality reliability. MiD-ERC uses these signals to coordinate divergence-guided cross-modal gating, divergence-modulated reliability weighting, and divergence-conditioned adaptive LLM prompting. The framework is trained end-to-end using only standard emotion annotations, without requiring additional conflict labels, auxiliary data construction, or external retrieval modules. Experiments on IEMOCAP and MELD demonstrate that MiD-ERC achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly pronounced improvements on high-divergence samples.
papers.summary: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversations (MERC) combines text, audio, and video to label the emotion of each utterance, but the modalities often disagree because of concealed emotion, noise, or ambiguity. `MiD-ERC`, inspired by the Brunswik Lens Model, scores that disagreement with a normalized divergence between the emotion predictions from each modality and estimates how reliable each modality is for a given sample. These signals control cross-modal gating, reliability weighting, and adaptive prompting of a large language model (LLM), and the system is trained end to end using only standard emotion labels. It reports state-of-the-art results on `IEMOCAP` and `MELD`, with **the largest gains on samples where the modalities disagree most**.

papers.title: Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline for Multi-Instance Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We present the Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline (ASP), an offline rollout scheduler for multi-instance asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs). ASP jointly reduces three sources of rollout underutilization - padding bubbles from intra-minibatch length heterogeneity, skewness bubbles from long-tail outputs, and sorting bubbles from fluctuations in training-queue occupancy induced by length-sorted dispatch - through a single offline preprocessing pass. This enables efficient multi-instance rollout that overcomes the early scaling plateau of single-instance inference while smoothing the arrival of generated samples at the trainer. We integrate the scheduler into an asynchronous architecture that decouples rollout from training while keeping policy lag observable and bounded. Complete ASP improves end-to-end throughput by up to 3.22 times and reduces iteration time by up to 76.8% relative to MindSpeed-RL, while reducing iteration time by up to 62.5% relative to verl. Within ASP, scheduling reduces mean iteration time by 10.9%. ASP also scales more robustly with additional generation resources than these baselines and shows no visible convergence degradation in the measured bounded-lag regime. ASP has since been used in an internal telecom-domain RL post-training workflow, reducing the reported training period from more than three months to about two months and producing a domain-enhanced model for knowledge answering and tool calling.
papers.summary: `ASP` (Adaptive Scheduling Pipeline) is an offline rollout scheduler for asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs) with multiple inference instances. In a single preprocessing pass it reduces three kinds of idle time: padding when output lengths differ within a minibatch, stalls from long-tail outputs, and uneven training-queue occupancy caused by length-sorted dispatch. It runs inside an asynchronous architecture that separates rollout from training while keeping policy lag bounded and observable. ASP improves end-to-end throughput by **up to 3.22x over `MindSpeed-RL`** and cuts iteration time by up to 62.5% versus `verl`, with no visible convergence loss. In an internal telecom post-training workflow it reportedly shortened training from over three months to about two.

papers.title: Rethinking Agent Trajectory Compression: A Workflow-Aware Perspective
papers.abstract: As long-horizon agents increasingly rely on multi-step tool interactions to accomplish complex tasks, their execution trajectories continuously accumulate structured outputs and intermediate artifacts, leading to growing context overhead. Existing compression methods primarily rely on text importance or fixed truncation rules, often overlooking cross-step dependencies within workflows and potentially discarding critical information required for subsequent task execution. To address this challenge, we propose WAAC, a workflow-aware framework for agent trajectory compression. WAAC structurally models successful historical trajectories to extract reusable workflow compression experience and incorporates online backward dependency analysis to dynamically identify information retention requirements. By combining current dependency constraints with historical experience, WAAC selects appropriate compression strategies for different types of historical information. Experiments on PinchBench and Odysseys demonstrate that WAAC achieves an overall score of 87.6 and a perfect completion rate of 19.0%, respectively, while reducing execution costs by 19.7% and 29.1% compared with the strongest baseline methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of workflow-aware trajectory compression in improving task performance and cost efficiency for long-horizon agents. Code and resources are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/waac-6527/.
papers.summary: Long-horizon agents that call many tools build up large contexts full of structured outputs, and existing compression methods drop text by importance scores or fixed truncation rules, often discarding information that a later step needs. `WAAC` builds reusable compression experience by modeling the structure of past successful trajectories, and adds an online backward dependency analysis to work out what the remaining workflow still needs. It then chooses a compression strategy for each type of historical information. On `PinchBench` and `Odysseys` it reaches an overall score of 87.6 and a 19.0% perfect completion rate, while **cutting execution cost by 19.7% and 29.1%** compared with the strongest baselines.

papers.title: The Relational Capacity Framework: A Lens for AI-Mediated Relationality
papers.abstract: A growing literature examines the impact of engaging with AI chatbots on our relationality: our ability to form relationships with others, maintain them through life's changes, and exit when needed. Currently, substantial work focuses on purpose-built AI companions (e.g. Replika, Character.AI), with less work investigating socioemotional uses of the more widely-used general-purpose chatbots. In this paper, we present a 100-person investigation into how people engage general-purpose AI for socioemotional needs. Participants' AI uses varied, from practicing specific social skills to seeking additional bandwidth and information as they navigated their social contexts. To explain this heterogeneity, we provide 8 states that describe how AI expands or contracts relationality for people with different levels of skills, bandwidth, and information. We then present a unified conceptual model for the role of technology in mediating human relationality, the Relational Capacity Framework, and outline future research designing appropriate roles for AI in human connection.
papers.summary: Research on AI and relationships has focused mostly on purpose-built companion apps such as `Replika` and `Character.AI`. This study instead examines how 100 people use general-purpose chatbots for social and emotional needs, such as practicing social skills, gaining extra bandwidth, or getting information to navigate their social situations. To explain the variety of uses, the authors describe **8 states in which AI expands or contracts a person's relationality** depending on their skills, bandwidth, and information. They combine these into the `Relational Capacity Framework`, a conceptual model of how technology mediates human connection.

papers.title: Who's Asking? Audience-Conditioned Privatization
papers.abstract: The abundance of user-generated conversational data makes the question of how to responsibly derive insights from confidential data without putting the individuals in it at risk ever more important. However, the majority of existing differentially private (DP) synthetic text generation (SDG) and anonymization approaches ignore the context of the data's downstream usage, which results in loss of important information. DP-SDG provides the same guarantee regardless of the recipient, and anonymization relies on predefined attribute categories. They both ignore the observation that an attribute that is harmless to one audience can be sensitive to another, and each audience typically needs only some attributes preserved. We propose Ext-Classify-Priv, a framework that (1) extracts the information types present in a corpus, (2) classifies which of them are private for a given audience following contextual integrity, and (3) protects only those attributes, using either anonymization or SDG with Feature-DP approaches. On Reddit data with 3 audiences, our audience-specific releases are more faithful than a single audience-agnostic release for every audience. On bioRxiv data, our SDG method improves MAUVE from 0.097 to 0.420 at epsilon=1 and on the proprietary real estate data, our anonymization method improves MAUVE from 0.698 to 0.959 over the best baselines.
papers.summary: Differentially private (DP) synthetic text generation and anonymization protect the same information no matter who receives the data, even though an attribute that is harmless for one audience can be sensitive for another. `Ext-Classify-Priv` extracts the types of information present in a corpus, uses contextual integrity to decide which are private for a given audience, and protects only those, either by anonymization or by synthetic generation with Feature-DP. On Reddit data with three audiences, releases tailored to each audience are more faithful than a single audience-agnostic release. On `bioRxiv` data the synthetic-data method **raises `MAUVE` from 0.097 to 0.420 at epsilon=1**, and on proprietary real-estate data anonymization raises it from 0.698 to 0.959.

papers.title: Toward LLM Self-Play Under Data Scarcity: Effectiveness, Generalizability, and Trustworthiness
papers.abstract: The rapid development of large language models (LLMs) has been driven largely by scaling model size and human-curated training data, yet this paradigm is increasingly constrained by data scarcity and diminishing returns from human supervision. Self-play offers a promising pathway for autonomous data generation and improvement, but current frameworks remain unsatisfactory due to a lack of a data-centric perspective, limited cross-domain generalization, and growing trustworthiness and security concerns. In this paper, we argue that real-world LLM self-play systems should achieve effectiveness, generalizability, and trustworthiness under data scarcity. To address these challenges, we outline three blue-sky research directions for future self-play systems: (1) data-centric self-play for effective experience generation, (2) generalizable self-play for open-world and unverifiable tasks, and (3) trustworthy self-play for reliable self-evolution. We further discuss research opportunities and solutions within each direction. This paradigm shift will establish a sustainable and safe AI ecosystem by transforming finite human knowledge into inexhaustible high-quality experience through self-play architectures.
papers.summary: This position paper argues that self-play, where a large language model (LLM) generates its own training experience, is a way past the shortage of human-curated data, but that current frameworks lack a data-centric view, generalize poorly across domains, and raise trust and security concerns. The authors propose that self-play systems should be effective, generalizable, and trustworthy when data is scarce. They outline **three research directions**: data-centric self-play for generating useful experience, generalizable self-play for open-world tasks whose answers cannot be verified, and trustworthy self-play for reliable self-evolution, with open problems for each.

papers.title: HomeLoop: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-IoT Coordination in Everyday Domestic Assistance and Safety
papers.abstract: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.
papers.summary: `HomeLoop` is a simulation framework and benchmark built on `Isaac Sim` for robots driven by vision-language models (VLMs) that must coordinate with home cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, wearables, simulated residents, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Its 20 tasks in five families are designed so that the same alert can have different causes, and a runtime monitor scores both outcomes and intermediate actions with temporal-logic checks and per-action costs. Across six VLMs the best family-balanced score is 61.9%. The models tend to over-react: **failures from prohibited interventions outnumber missed required interventions by more than two to one**, for example shutting off the stove before checking why the alarm went off.

papers.title: On the Incompleteness of do-calculus for Universal Identifiability
papers.abstract: We study the problem of causal effect identification from an arbitrary set of observational and/or interventional distributions, which we call Universal Identifiability (uID).
