The uID problem generalizes existing classical identifiability (ID) and general identifiability (gID) problems, which considered the identification problem from either mere observational distributions or a specific type of interventional distributions. Prior research has established graphical criteria to determine when a causal effect is identifiable in ID and gID problems. Moreover, algorithms that leverage do-calculus and basic probability manipulations have been proposed to compute these effects. Consequently, it has been shown that do-calculus is both sound and complete in these problems. Despite these well-established results, a formal definition of what it means for the do-calculus to be complete does not exist. We propose a rigorous formalization for the completeness of the do-calculus and show that the completeness results in previous work remain valid. However, for more general problems, such as uID, the rules of do-calculus are no longer complete. This is perhaps the reason why the uID problem has remained open thus far.
papers.summary: Universal Identifiability (uID) asks whether a causal effect can be identified from any combination of observational and interventional distributions, which generalizes the classical identifiability (ID) and general identifiability (gID) problems. The do-calculus has been described as complete for ID and gID, but completeness was never formally defined. The authors give a rigorous definition and confirm that the earlier completeness results hold under it. They then show that **the do-calculus is not complete for uID**, which may explain why the problem has remained open.

papers.title: Frame: Form-Restricted Authoring with Model-Based Evaluation
papers.abstract: Many professional reports reuse the structure of prior editions while updating the content. We formalize this setting as form-restricted report generation: given a sample report and new grounding documents, generate a report that preserves the sample's form while accurately reflecting the new evidence. We introduce FRAME, a benchmark of 120 EDGAR- and arXiv-derived instances across Financial Quarterly, Financial Annual, Academic Simple, and Academic Complex categories, built with a temporal three-snapshot pipeline. We evaluate outputs with three human-validated metrics: structural similarity via semantic tree-edit distance, coverage via information unit recall, and faithfulness via claim-level grounding verification. Across five LLMs, open-source models nearly match proprietary models on structure but lag on coverage and faithfulness; all models perform better on financial than academic reports, and performance declines with longer outputs and more complex grounding.
papers.summary: Many professional reports keep the structure of earlier editions while updating the content, a task formalized here as form-restricted report generation: given a sample report and new source documents, produce a report with the same form that accurately reflects the new evidence. `FRAME` is a benchmark of 120 instances built from EDGAR filings and arXiv papers, covering financial and academic categories. Outputs are scored with three human-validated metrics for structural similarity, coverage, and faithfulness. Across five LLMs, **open-source models nearly match proprietary ones on structure but lag on coverage and faithfulness**, and all models do worse on academic reports, longer outputs, and more complex sources.

papers.title: Glyph: An Interpretability Engine for AI-Driven Scientific Discovery in Clinical Data
papers.abstract: Automated scientific discovery has the potential to advance understanding of disease mechanisms and accelerate identification of early disease markers. Manual data annotation is infeasible at population scale, motivating methods that automatically extract pre-defined phenotypes in multimodal and unstructured clinical data. Such pre-defined feature sets determine and limit which associations these approaches can discover. This limitation extends to agentic AI systems that use these tools to query population-scale data. In contrast, foundation models (FMs) trained on large volumes of clinical data can perform tasks beyond their training objectives. This suggests their latent embeddings may represent novel or unexplored features that could yield insights into disease mechanisms, yet such latent features remain difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, we introduce Glyph, an automated multistage framework that extracts features from multimodal and unstructured clinical data using FMs and sparse autoencoders, interprets them as coded clinical concepts, and evaluates their value for clinical scientific discovery. We applied Glyph to abdominal CT volumes, CT radiology reports and laboratory measurements from 41,628 patients across different institutions. We identified 397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations. Moreover, a majority of discovered associations were automatically reproducible in held-out cohorts across different sites. Glyph concepts provided complementary associations to literature-derived markers, leading to gains in predictive power. We envision that interpretability can extend beyond a mechanistic understanding of neural networks to connecting implicitly learned features with clinical knowledge and establishing their significance for patient outcomes. We release Glyph at https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/Glyph.
papers.summary: Automated discovery from clinical data is usually limited to predefined phenotypes, while foundation models (FMs) trained on clinical data may encode useful features that are hard to interpret. `Glyph` extracts features from multimodal clinical data with FMs and sparse autoencoders, maps them to coded clinical concepts, and tests whether they are associated with patient outcomes. Applied to abdominal CT scans, radiology reports, and lab measurements from 41,628 patients at several institutions, it found **397 predictive concepts supported by 4,463 Bonferroni-significant associations**, most of which were automatically reproduced in held-out cohorts from other sites. The concepts added predictive power beyond markers taken from the literature.

papers.title: DRAFT-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Agents Across the Professional Design Lifecycle
papers.abstract: Can frontier general-purpose agents understand client intent, explore creative directions, execute revisions, and prepare production deliverables? We introduce DRAFT-Bench (Design Reliability Across Feedback and Tasks), a lifecycle-oriented evaluation of requirement elicitation, creative exploration, constrained editing, iterative revision, and production handoff. Its Requirement-to-Artifact framework links evolving requirements, protected properties, artifact versions, and delivery obligations. We compare native Codex/Astra and Claude Code across 35 design briefs under 43 conditions, alongside a separate 40-scenario RFQ track. Astra completes 43/43 design conditions and Claude 35/43. All scored core runs receive full structural credit, yet on the 28 core conditions scored for both systems, semantic checks flag violations in 11 for Astra and 5 for Claude; these are model judgments, not expert-confirmed failure rates. RFQ coverage is high, but success ordering changes across cohorts. SKU expansion, revision dependencies, and White ink files expose ambiguity among unmet obligations, missing inputs, and evaluator interpretations. These findings separate execution, requirement compliance, and professional acceptance. Unpaired tracks and different tools preclude claims of RFQ-to-delivery success, factory acceptance, or a pure model ranking.
papers.summary: `DRAFT-Bench` tests whether general-purpose frontier agents can handle the full professional design lifecycle: eliciting requirements, exploring creative directions, constrained editing, iterative revision, and preparing production deliverables. It compares `Codex`/`Astra` and `Claude Code` on 35 design briefs under 43 conditions, plus a separate 40-scenario request-for-quotation (RFQ) track. **Astra completed 43 of 43 conditions and Claude 35**, and all scored runs received full structural credit. However, model-based semantic checks flagged requirement violations in 11 of 28 shared conditions for Astra and 5 for Claude. The authors say these flags are not expert-confirmed failure rates and that the setup does not support a clean model ranking.

papers.title: Ordered Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (\textsc{OPO}). In each minibatch, \textsc{OPO} sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines.
papers.summary: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) clips the importance ratio between the new and old policies with one fixed range for every sample, which cannot tell harmful extreme ratios apart from large but acceptable changes. `OPO` (Ordered Policy Optimization) sorts the importance ratios in each minibatch, picks out the extreme ones most likely to dominate the update, and gives them adaptive per-sample clipping radii derived from a target tail profile. The method stays first-order and needs only a sort and a modified policy loss. On `MuJoCo` and `Atari` benchmarks, **this small change performs strongly against established baselines**.

papers.title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents
papers.abstract: Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.
papers.summary: `Flex-RSI` is a benchmark for recursive self-improvement, in which an agent improves not just its answer but its own harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop it works through. In each round an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores better on validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself, all under a fixed budget and starting from the same general-purpose harness. Across vision and robotics tasks, self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, and feedback that records only success or failure holds back open-weight models. Paired runs show that **editing the harness itself contributes to the gains**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Agent performance depends on the harness (the prompts, tools, memory and control loop around a model) as much as on the model itself, yet most benchmarks keep the harness fixed. `Flex-RSI` measures whether frontier agents can improve both their task solution and their own harness under a fixed budget, across 24 vision and robotics tasks.

- Each round, an executor edits the solution, and the edit is kept only if its score on hidden validation data beats the previous one by a noise margin; an improver then rewrites the executor's prompts, tools and workflow along with its own instructions, and every run starts from the same general-purpose harness and is scored once on a hidden test split.
- Across 18 models (11 closed-source, 7 open-weight), self-improvement raised the validation score in **150 of 177 runs (85%)**, by a median of **10.4 points**, with `Claude Opus 5.5` ranking first overall (**91.6**) and gains largest on tasks where the agent must build its own solution, such as `3D Tracking`, where the median rose from 19.4 to 62.2.
- Feedback granularity separates model classes: on tasks scored only as success or failure, open-weight runs gained a median of **1.6 points** against **16.9** for closed-source runs, and on `Scene from Video` no open-weight model placed a single object that stayed physically stable, against **70.7%** for `Claude Opus 5.5`.
- In paired runs that differed only in whether the improver was active, editing the harness raised the test score in **six of seven pairs** and tied in the seventh (for example, `Qwen3.8-Flash-Next` on `Active Search` went from 21.0 to 59.3), while extra token spending showed no link to score (rank correlation **−0.05**).
- Limitations: each model ran once per task, model coverage is uneven (some models ran on only nine tasks), the evidence that harness editing helps rests on just seven pairs, and some low-starting tasks like `ARC-AGI-3` barely improved at all.

papers.title: More with Less: Efficient Parallel Scientific Code Translation via an Agent-Skill Workflow
papers.abstract: Translating parallel scientific codes between HPC programming frameworks is a critical but labor-intensive task. Existing LLM-based approaches rely on fixed sequential pipelines with undifferentiated repair strategies and correctness criteria that do not match scientific computing practice. We present an agent-skill framework that separates translation, compilation diagnosis, and execution validation into three autonomous agents coordinated by a verdict-driven orchestrator, routing each failure to a targeted repair skill rather than retrying blindly. An automated output check drives the self-correction loop, complemented by an offline LLM-based verification that exposes false positives escaping compiler and runtime checks. We evaluate the framework on 30 HeCBench kernels translated bidirectionally among CUDA, OpenMP, and SYCL with three open-source LLMs. Our framework attains the higher verified correctness rate in all 18 model and direction combinations over a state-of-the-art baseline while consuming up to 52.4% fewer tokens, remaining consistent across models and directions without architectural modification.
papers.summary: Translating parallel scientific code between high-performance computing (HPC) frameworks is laborious, and existing LLM pipelines run fixed sequential steps and retry repairs without targeting the specific failure. This framework splits translation, compilation diagnosis, and execution validation across three agents coordinated by an orchestrator that sends each failure to a targeted repair skill, and adds an offline LLM check to catch false positives that slip past the compiler and runtime. On 30 `HeCBench` kernels translated in both directions among `CUDA`, `OpenMP`, and `SYCL` with three open-source LLMs, it achieves **higher verified correctness in all 18 model-and-direction combinations** than a state-of-the-art baseline while using up to 52.4% fewer tokens.

papers.title: PhysioWave-T: Token-Efficient Wavelet Foundation Models for Biosignals
papers.abstract: We present PhysioWave-T, a token-efficient wavelet foundation model family for EEG, ECG, and sEMG. Dynamic scale folding recombines J+1 wavelet subbands prior to tokenization, compressing sequence length from (J+1)CS to CS tokens for J levels, C channels, and S temporal patches. Route-specific front ends and learned channel-name embeddings allow one Transformer per modality to handle diverse montages and sampling rates, while unseen setups reuse the backbone via lightweight adapters. We pre-train a 30M-parameter EEG model on over 15M windows (19--128 channels), alongside ECG (30M) and sEMG (12M) encoders. Across four EEG routes, scale folding cuts Transformer latency by 4.0--7.2x and peak memory by 6.8--12.7x over scale expansion without accuracy loss. Our EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, and surpasses LUNA-L on wearable seizure detection with fewer parameters. Reliability-aware latent fusion (RALF) further integrates summary tokens from independently pre-trained encoders via sample-adaptive weights. On SeizeIT2, RALF raises event sensitivity at 11 false alarms/h from 61.4% to 74.4% and window AUPRC from 0.321 to 0.399 over the best unimodal baseline, outperforming weighted-logit and concatenation fusion across all variants. PhysioWave-T also achieves state-of-the-art sEMG accuracies and top macro-F1 on PTB-XL Super and Chapman-Shaoxing. Code and models: https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/PhysioWave.
papers.summary: `PhysioWave-T` is a family of wavelet-based foundation models for EEG, ECG, and surface EMG (sEMG) signals. Its scale-folding step merges wavelet subbands before tokenization, so sequence length no longer grows with the number of decomposition levels, and learned channel-name embeddings let one Transformer per modality handle different electrode layouts and sampling rates. Scale folding **cuts Transformer latency by 4.0-7.2x and peak memory by 6.8-12.7x without accuracy loss**, and the 30M-parameter EEG encoder leads 8 of 9 metrics against prior EEG models. A reliability-aware fusion method (`RALF`) raises seizure event sensitivity on `SeizeIT2` from 61.4% to 74.4% at a fixed false-alarm rate.
papers.highlight_summary:
Wavelet front ends are a good fit for non-stationary biosignals, but giving each of the J+1 subbands its own token row multiplies the Transformer's sequence length, which gets expensive for dense EEG arrays. `PhysioWave-T` merges the subbands into one signal before tokenization (**dynamic scale folding**) and uses route-specific front ends with learned channel-name embeddings, so one backbone per modality can handle many different channel counts and sampling rates.

- Folding blends the subbands with softmax weights predicted per channel and time block from subband statistics, refined by learned synthesis filters, cutting tokens from (J+1)·C·S to C·S; across four EEG routes this reduces Transformer latency by **4.0–7.2×** and peak memory by **6.8–12.7×** with no accuracy loss (128-channel batches drop from about 32 GB to **2.5 GB**).
- A 30M-parameter EEG encoder pre-trained on **15.4M windows** (19–128 channels) leads on **eight of nine metrics** against `BENDR`, `BIOT`, `LaBraM`, and `EEGPT`, including Sleep-EDFx kappa of **0.737 vs 0.686**, and beats `LUNA-L` on wearable seizure detection (**61.4% vs 60.9%** sensitivity) with 25.4M versus 40.4M parameters.
- Reliability-aware latent fusion (`RALF`) gates frozen EEG, ECG, and EMG encoders with per-sample reliability scores; on `SeizeIT2` it raises window-level AUPRC from **0.321 to 0.399**, ahead of weighted-logit fusion (0.372) and concatenation (0.347), and stays at or above 0.33 under every tested single-modality corruption.
- The ECG and sEMG encoders set new highs on several benchmarks, including **70.9%** macro-F1 on `PTB-XL` Super, **56.7%** on `Chapman–Shaoxing`, and **89.78%** accuracy on `GRABMyo` with a 12M-parameter model.
- Some results are mixed: weighted-logit fusion beats `RALF` on event sensitivity at 11 false alarms per hour (78.9% vs 74.4%), `PhysioWave-L` keeps the higher macro-AUROC on `PTB-XL` and `CPSC 2018`, and the frozen probe falls below training from scratch on `KaggleERN` and `EPN-612`.

papers.title: Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly aggregate judgments across model instances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure. We study a setting in which LLMs shift their public decisions after observing ambiguous social signals while reporting inaccurate estimates of what other agents privately judged, even when the group's recorded private judgments do not support the apparent consensus. We call this failure phantom consensus and study it as a pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives. To measure this phenomenon, we introduce PHANTOM-Bench, a benchmark that separates isolated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited estimates of the group's private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and controls for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, ambiguous public signals consistently degrade decision quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public collective outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points, and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. We observe substantial errors in reported group-private beliefs alongside public-stage failures, while control conditions reveal model-dependent differences in susceptibility to ambiguous and explicit peer signals. Revealing the agents' recorded private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although recovery varies across models. Our results show that evaluating multi-agent LLM systems requires measuring not only final agreement, but whether that agreement reflects independently measured private judgments or an apparent consensus.
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems combine judgments from many model instances, but agents can change their public decisions after seeing ambiguous social signals even when the group's private judgments do not support the apparent consensus. The authors call this phantom consensus and introduce `PHANTOM-Bench`, which separates private judgments, public decisions, agents' estimates of what others privately think, and control conditions. Across nine models, ambiguous signals consistently hurt decisions, with **public accuracy dropping by up to 47.8 percentage points**, and agents misjudge what the group privately believes. Showing agents each other's recorded private decisions fixes many failures without revealing the answer, though how much it helps varies by model.

papers.title: LEF-JEPA: Denoising-Trained Latent Energy Fields for Spatial Representation Learning
papers.abstract: A joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) that applies prediction supervision only at masked positions struggles to clearly capture object shapes and boundaries in its latent representations. We further observe that some existing methods improve spatial structure while also retaining rich variations in texture and color. However, preserving more low-level visual information does not necessarily make representations better suited to prediction and action. This raises a key question: how can we strengthen the spatial structure in latent representations that supports prediction and action without over-encoding these details? We introduce LEF-JEPA, which learns spatial structure through target-guided latent recovery and transfers this supervision to the visual encoder through a relative-energy constraint; the energy module is used only during pretraining and adds no inference overhead. To reduce the cost of energy optimization during pretraining, we further construct a conditional Ising Hamiltonian that allows low-energy-state search to be performed by specialized Ising solvers. On physical hardware, we validate the feasibility of achieving lower forward latency with fewer local updates. Under a unified CIFAR-10 pretraining and frozen-encoder evaluation protocol, both realizations outperform V-JEPA2.1 in image classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.
papers.summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) that supervise prediction only at masked positions capture object shapes and boundaries poorly, while some alternatives also keep texture and color detail that does not help prediction or action. `LEF-JEPA` learns spatial structure by recovering latents guided by targets and passes this supervision to the encoder through a relative-energy constraint that is used only during pretraining. The authors also cast the energy optimization as a conditional Ising Hamiltonian that specialized Ising solvers can minimize, and show on physical hardware that this can lower forward latency. With `CIFAR-10` pretraining and a frozen encoder, **both versions outperform `V-JEPA2.1`** on classification, foreground segmentation, and visual planning.

papers.title: Rethinking Optimization Methods for Hierarchical Feature Selection
papers.abstract: Rare-event forecasting often depends on interpretable conjunctions: a single keyword, location, or temporal cue may be weak, while their joint occurrence can identify a meaningful precursor. Hierarchical-Task Numerical conjunctive feature Learning (HTNL) selects Numerical Conjunctive Features (NCFs) through a structured sparsity objective. However, the resulting optimization problem is challenging, making optimization design critical to its practical performance. We give a unified diagnosis of four HTNL optimization families: original majorization-minimization (MM), variational quadratic form (VQF), alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), and weighted group lasso (WGL). Our analysis distinguishes three key factors that jointly determine HTNL optimization behavior. First, VQF and MM are algebraically equivalent under matched variational updates and optimize a squared-penalty formulation. Second, ADMM optimizes the unsquared objective through consensus splitting; we replace its truncated FISTA proximal solver with a scalar bisection update (ADMM-Bisect) for more accurate treatment of near-threshold blocks. Third, WGL targets the same unsquared objective, while all methods face rapidly decaying active-set admission scores. Across two synthetic datasets and 11 civil-unrest and flu-surveillance tasks, VQF achieves the highest mean AUC with the most compact non-collapsing supports. ADMM-Bisect reduces measured runtime, while calibrated WGL avoids the empty-support failures of its original scale. Synthetic results further show how proximal accuracy, pruning, and search budget affect candidate recovery, especially for longer conjunctions. Code will be made publicly available upon publication.
papers.summary: Hierarchical-Task Numerical conjunctive feature Learning (`HTNL`) picks interpretable combinations of features for forecasting rare events, but its structured-sparsity objective is hard to optimize. The authors compare four families of optimizers for it: majorization-minimization (MM), variational quadratic form (VQF), ADMM, and weighted group lasso. They show that MM and VQF are algebraically equivalent, and they replace ADMM's inner solver with a scalar bisection update. Across synthetic data and 11 civil-unrest and flu-surveillance tasks, **VQF gets the highest mean AUC with the most compact supports**, while the bisection variant of ADMM runs faster.

papers.title: Same Facts, Different Remedy: Linguistic Profiling and Arbitrariness in LLM and System One Decisions
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to resolve consumer complaints, and the way complainants write varies with age, education and socioeconomic status (SES). We audit three remedy-decision systems using sociolinguistic rewrites of US consumer financial complaints that are instructed to preserve every fact: two generative LLMs that return a single label (GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini) and a probabilistic "System One" model that returns a distribution over remedies (Jev). Using pre-registered hypotheses tested once on held-out complaints, we separate two phenomena that single-label audits conflate. At the group scale, older, college-educated and higher-SES styles receive slightly more generous remedies; these effects replicate but are small, with every monetary-remedy gap within 0.5 percentage points. At the individual scale, two style versions of the same complaint receive different monetary decisions 2.6-6.3% of the time. In a variance-component analysis of the probabilistic model, persona components shared across the two rewrite models account for about 1.6% of within-complaint variation. The persona gaps are associated mainly with delivery (vocabulary, grammar, politeness) rather than content. Positive controls show that all three systems respond 49-387 times more strongly to remedy-relevant facts than to style. Rewriting every complaint into one standard style reduced GPT-4o-mini's education and SES gaps by 94% and 87% while retaining fact sensitivity, but reversed two of the probabilistic model's gaps and did not make individual decisions more stable. Independent LLM auditors flagged material fact changes in 3.3% and 11.7% of rewrites, and instability persisted among unflagged rewrites. Fairness audits of LLM decision systems should report group disparities and individual instability as separate outcomes.
papers.summary: LLMs increasingly help resolve consumer complaints, and people's writing style varies with age, education, and socioeconomic status (SES). The authors audit `GPT-4o-mini`, `GPT-5-mini`, and a probabilistic model called `Jev` using rewrites of US consumer financial complaints that change style but are meant to keep every fact. In pre-registered tests, styles associated with older, college-educated, and higher-SES writers receive slightly more generous remedies, but every monetary gap is within 0.5 percentage points. **Two style versions of the same complaint receive different monetary decisions 2.6-6.3% of the time**, while all three systems respond 49-387 times more strongly to relevant facts than to style. Rewriting complaints into one standard style shrank `GPT-4o-mini`'s group gaps but did not make individual decisions more stable.

papers.title: Seeing vs. Counting: Complexity Twins Show Where Multimodal LLMs Fail on Diagrams
papers.abstract: When a multimodal LLM miscounts in a diagram, does it fail at seeing or at counting? Existing visual graph and puzzle benchmarks vary visual density and algorithmic hardness together, confounding the two. We pair counting questions about the same drawing that sit in different counting-complexity classes, such as its spanning trees (a determinant) and its simple paths (#P-complete), and use a transcription probe and a text-only control to separate reading from computing. We test Gemini, Gemma and Qwen3-VL models; for the Gemini models, the answer depends on how the model computes. In chain of thought, most of them read small drawings correctly and then fail at counting, at a rate set far more by the size of the answer than by its complexity class (for the primary model, the odds of an exact answer fall 2.38-fold per decade of the answer). Given code and an exact transcription, the primary model counts correctly even on 10x10 grids, and reading becomes the bottleneck: a single view misses horizontal edges, and a second reading of a rotated copy with crop checks reads 86/96 large grids exactly, against 57/96 when the upright reading is simply repeated.
papers.summary: Benchmarks of diagram reasoning usually make images denser and problems harder at the same time, so it is unclear whether multimodal LLMs fail at reading the picture or at computing the answer. The authors pair counting questions about the same drawing from different complexity classes, such as spanning trees (computable via a determinant) and simple paths (#P-complete), and add a transcription probe and a text-only control to separate reading from computing. With chain of thought, `Gemini` models mostly read small drawings correctly but then miscount, and the size of the answer predicts failure far better than its complexity class: for the primary model, **the odds of an exact answer fall 2.38-fold for each tenfold increase in the answer**. When the model is given code and an exact transcription it counts correctly even on 10x10 grids, so reading becomes the bottleneck; adding a second reading of a rotated copy with crop checks reads 86 of 96 large grids exactly, against 57 of 96 when the upright reading is simply repeated.

papers.title: Capital Efficiency, Isolation, Risk, and Ruin in Generative AI Inference Serving Infrastructure
papers.abstract: Generative AI serving is an extremely capital-intensive endeavor that demands rapid, step-change improvements in capital efficiency to prevent industry wide increases in the cost of capital from limiting growth plans. Keeping pace with the economic necessities will increasingly require infrastructure providers to confront operationally-inconvenient realities of production serving, including the extreme heterogeneity of generative AI request costs. We have explored workload isolation as a foundational, fleet-level lever for increasing capital efficiency. Isolation is the practice of intelligently grouping "like" requests before execution. Rather than exposing every replica to the full heterogeneous workload distribution, isolation deliberately reshapes the workload presented to the hardware by assigning requests with different cost characteristics to different portions of the fleet. Workload isolation on its own does not make expensive requests cheaper; it prevents a costly portion of the workload from unnecessarily determining the operating point and capital efficiency of the entire fleet. It additionally lays the foundational groundwork that can serve as a launching point for compounding gains via narrow-band optimizations (tailoring) and custom silicon designs while also informing up on pricing policy. This paper uses representative production data and experience to convey the motivation behind isolation as a fleet-level lever for increased capital efficiency.
papers.summary: Generative AI serving needs a lot of capital, and the cost of individual requests varies enormously, so a small share of expensive requests can set the operating point for a whole fleet. Drawing on representative production data and operating experience, the paper argues for workload isolation: grouping requests with similar cost profiles and sending them to separate parts of the fleet instead of exposing every replica to the full mix. The authors say isolation does not make expensive requests cheaper, but it keeps them from dragging down **fleet-wide capital efficiency**. They also present it as groundwork for further gains from narrow-band tailoring, custom silicon, and pricing policy.

papers.title: FoundaRF: A Physics-Informed Foundation Model Framework for Radio-Frequency Passive Components
papers.abstract: Designing RF/mmWave passive components is a time-consuming process that relies heavily on expert knowledge and iterative EM simulations. Although recent ML surrogate models have shown great promise in accelerating passive design, they remain task-specific and lack generalization. This paper presents FoundaRF, a foundation model framework that unifies passive layout modeling across diverse layout structures and technologies. It combines a self-supervised encoder with adaptive layout processing and physics-aware decoders to enable few-shot transfer. Experiments across four semiconductor technologies show strong generalization to unseen structures, outperforming baselines with up to a 3.3x reduction in prediction error, reducing labeled-data requirements by up to fourfold, and substantially shortening design turnaround. FoundaRF establishes a scalable and data-efficient solution for RF/mmWave passive design automation.
papers.summary: Designing radio-frequency and millimeter-wave passive components relies on expert knowledge and repeated electromagnetic simulation, and existing machine-learning surrogate models only work for the task they were trained on. `FoundaRF` is a foundation-model framework that combines a self-supervised encoder, adaptive layout processing, and physics-aware decoders so it can be transferred to new layout structures and technologies with few examples. Across four semiconductor technologies it generalizes to unseen structures, with **up to a 3.3x reduction in prediction error** over baselines, up to four times less labeled data, and shorter design turnaround.

papers.title: Did I See It or Think It? Probing Reality Monitoring in Vision-Language Models with Concept Injection
papers.abstract: Recent work tests whether language models can introspect by injecting a concept direction into their activations and asking whether they notice it and can name it. These studies are text-only. Vision-language models (VLMs) face an additional problem, known in cognitive psychology as reality monitoring: they must keep internally generated content separate from what they actually see. We therefore ask: can VLMs distinguish injected concepts from image content? We introduce a paradigm that varies the image and the injected concept independently. On each trial, the model reports what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. This design scores both whether the model identifies the concept and which source it assigns to it. Across six VLMs, only Gemma-3-27B reliably identifies injected concepts (35% vs. 3% for steering alone), with almost no false alarms. Even then, the source it reports is fragile. Strong or visual-pathway injections are reported as seen, and a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports. The same failure appears in ordinary captioning, where injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs. Evaluating multimodal self-reports therefore requires checking both their content and their reported source.
papers.summary: Earlier introspection studies inject a concept direction into a language model's activations and ask whether the model notices it. This work extends that test to vision-language models (VLMs), which must also do reality monitoring: telling internally generated content apart from what is actually in the image. The paradigm varies the image and the injected concept independently and asks the model what it sees, whether a thought was injected, and what that thought is. Of six VLMs, only `Gemma-3-27B` reliably identifies injected concepts (35% versus 3% for steering alone), but it often attributes them to the wrong source: strong or visual-pathway injections get reported as seen, and a visible object nearly eliminates correct thought reports. The same confusion shows up in ordinary captioning, where **injected objects appear in up to 87% of captions of real photographs**.

papers.title: SIMBAD: Spatio-Temporal Traffic Forecasting Robust to Aperiodicity
papers.abstract: Accurate traffic prediction is essential for urban planning but remains challenging due to the irregular patterns caused by unexpected events. While Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNNs) effectively model periodic data, they often struggle with these aperiodic fluctuations. To address this, we propose SIMBAD, which improves generalization irregular patterns via two key mechanisms: 1) adaptive regulation of periodic signals to prioritize recent signals, and 2) dynamic spatial modeling that adjusts influence between connected nodes based on contextual relations. Built upon simple similarity metrics to adapt to aperiodic patterns, SIMBAD outperforms existing methods on real-world benchmark datasets, demonstrating superior performance in predicting unseen and irregular traffic events.
papers.summary: Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNNs) forecast regular, periodic traffic well but struggle with irregular fluctuations caused by unexpected events. `SIMBAD` handles these with two mechanisms built on simple similarity metrics: it adaptively down-weights periodic signals in favor of recent ones, and it adjusts how much connected road nodes influence each other based on context. The authors report that it **outperforms existing methods on real-world traffic benchmarks**, especially on unseen and irregular events.

papers.title: Optimal Probabilistic Answer Set Programming: Complexity and Implementations
papers.abstract: Probabilistic Answer Set Programming (PASP) extends Answer Set Programming with the possibility of representing uncertain data. Among the possible available semantics, we focus here on the credal semantics. In this setting, prior work has focused exclusively on plain ASP programs, i.e., programs without optimization constructs. However, many real world tasks define optimality criteria over the possible solutions, which cannot be conveniently modeled with existing probabilistic ASP frameworks. In this paper, we close this gap and propose optimal Probabilistic Answer Set Programming, which extends PASP by also allowing weak constraints, which are the standard optimization construct of ASP. We define the semantics of such programs, study the computational complexity of the inference and most probable explanation tasks, and propose practical implementations based on Algebraic Model Counting and Answer Set Programming with Quantifiers. An empirical evaluation of the proposed approach on three real world tasks confirms the applicability of our framework.
papers.summary: Probabilistic Answer Set Programming (PASP) adds uncertain data to Answer Set Programming, but under the credal semantics prior work covered only programs without optimization constructs, so tasks with optimality criteria could not be modeled. The authors introduce optimal PASP, which allows weak constraints (ASP's standard optimization construct). They define its semantics and **characterize the computational complexity of inference and most-probable-explanation tasks**. They also provide implementations based on Algebraic Model Counting and Answer Set Programming with Quantifiers, which they evaluate on three real-world tasks.

papers.title: Scout Before You Route: Predicting Task Success and Token Count from a Small LLM Prefill
papers.abstract: Routers typically choose a model per query by trading predicted correctness against cost. Most price each model at a fixed cost, as if every query used the same number of output tokens, but the output length of reasoning models varies by an order of magnitude across queries. When is per-query cost worth predicting? What factors drive cost? How cheaply can predictions be made? We predict both the success probability and the output length of candidate models from the prefill activations of a single small frozen LLM, the scout. With reasoning candidates, perfect per-query cost knowledge would save 29-61% of spending on eight of nine datasets, and much less with non-reasoning candidates on the same problems. On those eight datasets, our predicted costs save 9-33% at matched accuracy relative to median-length pricing, up to 69% of what perfect knowledge would save. They are significantly cheaper than each estimator we reimplemented or adapted from published work, including ZeroRouter and a MixLLM-style predictor, on a majority of datasets. Output length depends mostly on the problem. On most math and code datasets, harder problems are longer, so predicted success alone prices cost nearly as well. On knowledge and mixed-format datasets they are not, and predicted success falls well behind a probe trained on length. The probe keeps most of its saving with 20 labelled problems and transfers without labels to four of seven new benchmarks. On a mixture of all nine benchmarks, it saves 22% beyond pricing each benchmark at its own median length. Savings stop growing at about a 2B scout, so above 4B a larger scout costs more than it adds.
papers.summary: LLM routers usually charge each candidate model a fixed cost per query, even though reasoning models' output lengths vary by an order of magnitude from one query to the next. The authors use the prefill activations of one small frozen model, the scout, to predict both each candidate's chance of success and its output length. On eight of nine datasets, perfect per-query cost knowledge would save 29–61% of spending with reasoning candidates, and the predicted costs **save 9–33% at matched accuracy compared with median-length pricing**, beating reimplemented estimators such as `ZeroRouter` and a `MixLLM`-style predictor on most datasets. The length probe keeps most of its savings with only 20 labeled problems and transfers without labels to four of seven new benchmarks; savings level off at a scout of about 2B parameters, and above 4B a larger scout costs more than it adds.

papers.title: A Controlled Study of Models, Skills, Feedback, and Curriculum in Agentic Robotics
papers.abstract: Agentic robotics asks coding agents to implement and iteratively improve robot policies from simulated and real-world physical interactions. We study the self-learning loop of agentic robotics through a controlled simulation study spanning nine manipulation tasks, 631 different experiment configurations, and 28K coding agent rollouts, systematically varying model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum. The experiment data suggests that the bottleneck is often not the access to sufficient information, but interpreting it into the right policy update. Across these factors, a successful self-learning loop depends on how effectively agents attribute failures, reason task-relevant spatial and geometric structure, and selectively restructure code to improve policies.
papers.summary: In agentic robotics, coding agents write robot policies and improve them through repeated rounds of physical interaction. This controlled simulation study covers nine manipulation tasks, 631 experiment configurations, and 28K coding-agent rollouts, and varies model capability, skill priors, feedback structure, and curriculum. The data suggest that **the bottleneck is usually not access to enough information but turning it into the right policy update**. Self-improvement works when agents attribute failures correctly, reason about the task's spatial and geometric structure, and restructure code selectively.

papers.title: ToolDex: An Ego-Exo Human Demonstration Dataset for Creative Physical Tool Use
papers.abstract:
Creative tool use is a fundamental human capability and an important step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence. It requires agents to reason about object affordances, physical constraints, and manipulation strategies, especially when standard tools are unavailable. However, progress in this area is limited by the lack of real-world datasets that capture human tool-use behavior with sufficient scale, fidelity, and diversity. Existing benchmarks are often simulation-based, focus on simplified interactions, or lack detailed observations and annotations.
  We introduce ToolDex, a large-scale egocentric-exocentric (ego-exo) human demonstration dataset for creative physical tool use. ToolDex captures scenarios in which humans select, adapt, and repurpose available objects as tools. Using synchronized egocentric cameras and eight exocentric cameras, the dataset provides high-fidelity multi-view observations and rich annotations for hands, tools, target objects, and their deformable interactions. Beyond data collection, we establish a benchmark suite characterizing three core capabilities: physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D and 4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning. ToolDex provides a foundation for studying human tool-use behavior and developing embodied agents that can adaptively use tools in complex real-world environments.
  Dataset visualizations and benchmarking results are available at https://tooluse-dataset.github.io/.
papers.summary: Research on creative physical tool use, where an agent selects, adapts, or repurposes objects when the standard tool is missing, lacks large, high-fidelity real-world data. `ToolDex` is a human demonstration dataset recorded with synchronized egocentric (first-person) and eight exocentric (external) cameras, annotated for hands, tools, target objects, and their deformable interactions. It comes with **a benchmark suite covering physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D and 4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning**.

papers.title: Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection for Reasoning Distillation
papers.abstract: Training smaller language models on reasoning solutions generated by a larger teacher model is the prevailing approach for transferring mathematical reasoning capabilities. However, the student tends to overfit the output distribution of the teacher and generalizes poorly when its own behavior at inference time deviates from the training data. Recent methods attempt to bridge this gap by incorporating error data, yet the corrective trajectories still reflect the reasoning patterns of the teacher, which the student cannot reliably reproduce, leaving the distribution mismatch largely unresolved. We propose a method, Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection (FPRT), built on the insight that effective training data should be jointly determined by what the student fails on and what it can realistically learn. Our method first profiles the failure behavior of the student on each problem through repeated sampling, characterizing it in terms of error rate and error consistency to reveal qualitatively distinct failure modes. Each mode demands a fundamentally different training signal. The diagnosed mode then guides candidate generation from the teacher via distinct prompting strategies tailored to each failure type. Among the correct candidates, our method selects the one whose initial reasoning steps after the point of divergence are most reproducible by the student. These first corrective steps constitute the primary bottleneck, while the remaining steps follow an already corrected context and can therefore be continued more readily. This contrasts with standard reranking approaches, which score the trajectory as a whole and thereby dilute the signal at the critical reasoning transition. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves the SOTA performance across the five benchmarks on both student backbones.
papers.summary: Small models trained on a larger teacher's reasoning traces tend to overfit the teacher's style and break down when their own reasoning drifts, and adding corrective traces does not fully fix this because the corrections still follow the teacher's patterns. Failure Profiling and Reachable Trajectory Selection (`FPRT`) samples the student repeatedly on each problem and classifies its failure mode by error rate and error consistency. It then prompts the teacher with a strategy suited to that mode and, among the correct candidates, keeps the one whose first steps after the point of divergence the student can most reliably reproduce. This contrasts with reranking methods that score whole trajectories, and the authors report **state-of-the-art results on five math reasoning benchmarks with two student backbones**.

papers.title: Equidistribution of Solution Gradients in Physics-Informed Neural Networks via Coordinate Transformations
papers.abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) often struggle to approximate solutions with sharp gradients due to optimization difficulties and spectral bias. Motivated by the principle of gradient equidistribution from the stretching approach in grid generation, which redistributes solution gradients to reduce functional complexity, we propose Coordinate Transformation PINNs (CTPINNs), which incorporate learnable coordinate transformations to map the physical domain into a computational domain where the physical solutions become approximately affine, making them easier for neural networks to learn. We propose two constructions of the transformation: an explicit construction based on Majorants and an implicit construction based on invertable neural networks. Experimentally, the explicit construction can improve accuracy for PDEs with available explicit coordinate transformations, and the implicit construction can be combined with other advanced PINN models as an efficient plug-in module to improve performance across a range of challenging PDE benchmarks.
papers.summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) struggle with solutions that have sharp gradients, because of optimization difficulties and spectral bias. Borrowing gradient equidistribution from grid generation, Coordinate Transformation PINNs (`CTPINNs`) learn a coordinate transformation that maps the physical domain to one where the solution is approximately affine and therefore easier to fit. The transformation can be built explicitly from majorants or implicitly with invertible neural networks, and **the implicit version works as a plug-in module that improves other advanced PINN models** across challenging PDE benchmarks.

papers.title: ProtoCouncil: Multi-Encoder Anatomical Prototypes for Prostate Cancer Detection in Micro-Ultrasound
papers.abstract:
Purpose: Micro-ultrasound ($\mu$US) is a promising modality for prostate cancer (PCa) detection, but identifying suspicious tissue depends heavily on clinical experience. Models trained on sparse, noisy core-level pathology offer little insight into their decisions and can fail under domain shift. Clinical use needs a traceable decision process and a flag for uncertain predictions.
  Methods: We introduce ProtoCouncil, in which three foundation encoders (MedSAM, DINOv3 and V-JEPA 2.1) learn case-based prototypes at three anatomical levels: whole gland, needle track and gland sectors. Prototypes are projected onto real training-core regions, and label-free fusion keeps every class logit as a bias plus an exact sum of prototype similarity contributions. Encoder disagreement triggers selective prediction.
  Results: In five-fold patient-level cross-validation (6,588 cores, 693 patients), ProtoCouncil reaches 82.9% AUROC for clinically significant PCa (csPCa, Grade Group $\geq$3), 4.3 points above the best previously published method. In zero-shot evaluation on two external cohorts, ProtoCouncil achieves higher all-cancer and csPCa AUROC than all previous methods. Nearest same-class exemplars match test-core tumor involvement better than random same-class cases. Externally, csPCa accuracy falls from 79% when encoders agree to 27% when two oppose the fused call. Abstaining on disagreement raises balanced accuracy by 7 and 15 points, while retaining 58% and 54% of the cores.
  Conclusion: ProtoCouncil grounds core-level predictions in exact similarity-based evidence from real, anatomically indexed training cases, which makes its reasoning interpretable. It achieves the highest csPCa AUROC across three cohorts and identifies unreliable predictions through encoder disagreement.
papers.summary: Detecting prostate cancer on micro-ultrasound depends heavily on clinical experience, and models trained on sparse, noisy biopsy-core labels are hard to interpret and brittle under domain shift. `ProtoCouncil` has three foundation encoders (`MedSAM`, `DINOv3`, and `V-JEPA 2.1`) learn case-based prototypes at the whole-gland, needle-track, and gland-sector levels, projects them onto real training-core regions, and fuses them so each class score is an exact sum of prototype similarities. In patient-level cross-validation on 6,588 cores from 693 patients it reaches **82.9% AUROC for clinically significant cancer, 4.3 points above the best previously published method**, and it leads prior methods zero-shot on two external cohorts. When the encoders disagree, accuracy drops sharply, and abstaining on disagreement raises balanced accuracy by 7 and 15 points on the two external cohorts while keeping 58% and 54% of the cores.

papers.title: UniRGBA: Unifying RGB and Alpha in Pretrained Video Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have achieved remarkable photorealistic RGB synthesis, yet generating videos with a native alpha channel remains an open challenge. Existing approaches often rely on matting-style data and non-native RGBA designs, causing them to specialize in real-object scenes and to degrade severely on visual-effect content whose semi-transparency is spatially non-local and non-elliptical. We present UniRGBA, a unified framework whose key insight is that RGBA generation does not require a dedicated alpha encoder or complex latent-space restructuring---a minimal, targeted extension of the existing RGB pathway is sufficient. UniRGBA-VAE extends a causal video VAE to 4-channel RGBA via zero-initialized channel expansion, symmetric selective layer unfreezing (5% trainable), and a six-term progressive reconstruction loss anchored by a KL reference loss that prevents latent drift, followed by a two-stage schedule that introduces a lightweight GAN objective. We then apply standard DoRA to the pretrained DiT, reusing the unified 4-channel latent without any alpha-specific architectural changes. On a visual-effect RGBA benchmark, UniRGBA substantially outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA reconstruction while preserving RGB fidelity. For generation, UniRGBA outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA text-to-video tasks and matches or surpasses the original pretrained Wan2.1 backbone on RGB-only metrics, demonstrating that native alpha support can be integrated without compromising the underlying RGB prior or the model's architectural versatility.
papers.summary: Video diffusion models produce photorealistic RGB video but cannot natively generate an alpha (transparency) channel, and existing approaches trained on matting data degrade on visual-effect content with non-local semi-transparency. `UniRGBA` extends a causal video VAE to four channels by zero-initializing the new channel and unfreezing only about 5% of layers, trained with a progressive multi-term reconstruction loss and a KL anchor that prevents latent drift. It then fine-tunes the pretrained diffusion transformer with standard `DoRA` and no alpha-specific architecture changes. It **outperforms `Wan-Alpha` on RGBA reconstruction and text-to-video generation while matching or exceeding the original `Wan2.1` on RGB-only metrics**.

papers.title: Large Language Model Deployment on Resource-Constrained Edge Devices: A Practitioners Survey
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed many areas of artificial intelligence (AI), but their substantial resource requirements limit their deployment on mobile and edge devices. Although LLMs have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various applications, the next challenge is deploying these models on resource-limited edge devices. Recent innovations in software optimizations and specialized hardware have made it feasible to deploy LLMs on edge devices. Edge deployment offers benefits including local data processing, cost savings, reduced latency, and personalized responses. This paper reviews the latest techniques that make the deployment of LLMs on edge devices feasible.
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) need substantial compute and memory, which limits their use on mobile and edge devices. Aimed at practitioners, this survey reviews the software optimizations and specialized hardware that **make on-device LLM deployment feasible**. It frames the benefits as local data processing, lower cost, lower latency, and personalized responses.

papers.title: GlobalPuzzle: Globally Informed Genetic Search for Eroded Jigsaw Puzzle Reassembly
papers.abstract: Jigsaw puzzle reassembly remains a highly challenging task, particularly when piece boundaries are irregularly eroded to simulate damage to cultural artifacts. On the GAP benchmark, existing methods achieve a perfect assembly accuracy of only 0.3% on $5 \times 5$ puzzles, whereas humans can solve jigsaw puzzles with remarkably high accuracy. Humans typically approach puzzle solving by identifying potentially adjacent pieces, evaluating the current assembly, and iteratively performing complex operations such as adding pieces, replacing incorrectly placed pieces, and moving entire connected groups of pieces. However, existing methods face a fundamental limitation: approaches that leverage global visual information typically predict piece arrangements directly, making it difficult to explicitly perform such complex iterative operations, while search based methods can rearrange pieces but primarily rely on pairwise boundary compatibility, lacking global visual information to evaluate and guide the search process. To bridge this gap, we propose GlobalPuzzle, a jigsaw puzzle reassembly framework that integrates global canvas level evaluation, action guidance, and genetic search. By incorporating global visual information into the evaluation and optimization of candidate assemblies, GlobalPuzzle aims to resolve ambiguous adjacency relationships that are difficult to determine from irregularly eroded piece boundaries alone, enabling flexible, globally informed reconstruction.
papers.summary: Reassembling jigsaw puzzles whose piece edges are eroded, as a stand-in for damaged cultural artifacts, remains very hard: on the `GAP` benchmark, existing methods assemble only **0.3% of 5x5 puzzles perfectly**. The authors note that global visual methods predict arrangements in one shot and cannot iteratively fix mistakes, while search methods can rearrange pieces but rely only on pairwise edge compatibility. `GlobalPuzzle` combines canvas-level evaluation of whole candidate assemblies with action guidance and genetic search, so it can add, replace, and move groups of pieces the way a human solver would. The abstract describes the design but reports no quantitative results for the method itself.

papers.title: Training-Free Active Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language models (VLMs) is usually studied in a fully unsupervised regime, where adaptation relies on pseudo-labels, confidence scores, or entropy computed by the model itself. This is a severe restriction on hard shifted samples: the model is asked to repair its own uncertain predictions without any external evidence. At the other extreme, supervised online adaptation assumes labels can directly train or correct the model. We study the intermediate deployment regime between these two extremes. In Active Test-time Adaptation for VLMs (Active VLM-TTA), a pretrained VLM may spend an explicit labeling budget on selected test samples, but the prediction for the current sample must be emitted before its label can be used; queried labels are therefore costed, delayed evidence for future samples rather than free correction for the present one. Under this future-only constraint, the central question is how to reuse sparse labels conservatively. We instantiate this setting with ACTive VLM-TTA for Online Retrieval (ACTOR), a training-free plug-in module that routes uncertain samples among base prediction, label query, and memory-based correction using a consistency-and-reliability check over previously queried labels. Across ten cross-domain benchmarks and a domain-transfer benchmark based on ImageNet, ACTOR consistently improves strong VLM-TTA baselines on ResNet and ViT backbones with negligible inference overhead. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/kaist-dmlab/ACTOR.
papers.summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language models (VLMs) usually relies only on the model's own pseudo-labels, which gives it little to go on for hard samples under distribution shift. The authors define Active VLM-TTA, where the model can spend a labeling budget on selected test samples, but a queried label arrives only after the current prediction and can therefore help only future samples. Their training-free plug-in `ACTOR` sends each uncertain sample to the base prediction, a label query, or memory-based correction, depending on a consistency-and-reliability check against previously queried labels. Across ten cross-domain benchmarks and an `ImageNet`-based domain-transfer benchmark, it **consistently improves strong VLM-TTA baselines on ResNet and ViT backbones with negligible inference overhead**.

papers.title: The Invisible Gap: Romanized Indic Generation Fails Where Automatic Metrics Succeed
papers.abstract: Hundreds of millions of Indians communicate with digital systems in romanized Latin characters -- typing "aap kaise hain" rather than native script -- yet romanized Indic generation is absent from NLP benchmarks and evaluation frameworks. We demonstrate that automatic metrics (BGE-M3, BERTScore) systematically misrepresent the quality of romanized Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada generation. We evaluate four LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 2.5-flash, Qwen3.5-35B) on 142 OpenAssistant query-response pairs. On a 72-response diagnostic subset, native speakers rate GPT-5.5 1.43 points higher than Claude Opus 4.8 on a 12-point rubric, whereas their full-dataset BGE-M3 means differ by only 0.004. Two distinct model-specific failure modes emerge: Gemini produces script spillage (16.9% of Telugu responses leak native script), while Qwen collapses to English-only output (16.2% of Kannada responses). We introduce a failure-aware evaluation policy that assigns zero to empty outputs, script-corrupted responses, and instruction collapses -- revealing failures metrics alone cannot detect. Our results show that evaluating romanized Indic generation requires a coordinated bundle: semantic similarity, script compliance, failure coverage, and native-speaker acceptability.
papers.summary: Hundreds of millions of people type Indian languages in Latin script, yet romanized Indic generation is missing from NLP benchmarks. The authors evaluated four LLMs (`Claude Opus 4.8`, `GPT-5.5`, `Gemini 2.5-flash`, `Qwen3.5-35B`) on 142 `OpenAssistant` query-response pairs in romanized Hindi, Telugu, and Kannada. On a 72-response diagnostic subset, native speakers rated `GPT-5.5` 1.43 points higher than `Claude Opus 4.8` on a 12-point rubric, **while their full-dataset `BGE-M3` similarity means differed by only 0.004**. They also found model-specific failures the metrics miss, namely `Gemini` leaking native script into 16.9% of Telugu responses and `Qwen` falling back to English in 16.2% of Kannada responses, and they propose a failure-aware scoring policy that combines semantic similarity, script compliance, failure coverage, and native-speaker acceptability.

papers.title: When Routine Operations Break Architectural Pattern Relationships in LLM Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: LLM agent harnesses distribute tool mediation, state management and safety guardrails across native services, independently written plugins and configuration. Routine operations can change the runtime order or retained state that architectural pattern relationships require, without any code change. We study five relationships associated with the Guardrail Enforcement Point, Autonomy Controller and Blackboard patterns across five released harnesses, analysing a main sample of fourteen independently written plugins. Using PatternOps, our assessment procedure, we trace requirements from pattern descriptions, provider documentation and deployment profiles to the providers that realise them and the records that decide them. We then compare alternative allocations under supported operations. Such operations broke relationships silently: after a plugin was reapplied or an allow rule saved, policy stopped evaluating edits while every plugin stayed active, and a prohibited edit executed. Which alternatives qualified depended on the requirement. Allocations that kept the required order, or kept or rebuilt the needed state, held on their tested paths and operation sequences, while others prevented prohibited effects but missed edits rejected elsewhere. In these harnesses, a pattern relationship is a property of the running system and its history, so architects should evaluate it against the decision paths, state lifetimes and operation sequences their deployments use.
papers.summary: LLM agent harnesses spread tool mediation, state management, and safety guardrails across native services, third-party plugins, and configuration, so routine operations can change execution order or retained state without any code change. Using an assessment procedure called `PatternOps`, the authors studied five relationships tied to the Guardrail Enforcement Point, Autonomy Controller, and Blackboard patterns across five released harnesses and fourteen independently written plugins. They found that **after reapplying a plugin or saving an allow rule, policy silently stopped evaluating edits and a prohibited edit executed**, while every plugin still appeared active. Allocations that preserved the required ordering or rebuilt the needed state held up on the tested paths, which leads the authors to argue that these properties must be checked against real decision paths, state lifetimes, and operation sequences.

papers.title: AdaAlloc: Adaptive Visual Token Allocation for Long-Video Question Answering
papers.abstract: Long-video question answering forces multimodal large language models to reason under strict visual-token budgets, creating a tradeoff between broad temporal coverage and fine-grained spatial detail. Uniform sampling preserves coverage but often obscures decisive local cues, while caption-based or frame-similarity retrieval operates over lossy proxies that can miss motion, state changes, and before-after relations. We recast long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem: given a fixed budget, decide how much to spend on global context versus high-resolution local evidence, and where in the video to draw that local evidence from. We introduce AdaAlloc, a training-free inference framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between a global video overview and localized visual detail. AdaAlloc first plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to locate candidate evidence segments and refines them into a compact temporal memory. The selected policy controls both frame sampling density and resolution, combining sparse, lower-resolution global frames with denser, higher-resolution local frames drawn from the refined memory. The final answerer reasons over the allocated global context and refined local evidence. Across LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench, AdaAlloc improves over budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points and outperforms the compared frame-selection and agentic methods on their reported benchmarks.
papers.summary: Answering questions about long videos forces multimodal LLMs to choose, under a fixed visual-token budget, between broad temporal coverage and fine spatial detail. `AdaAlloc` is a training-free inference framework that first decides how to split the budget between a global overview and local detail, then uses temporal grounding to find candidate evidence segments and refine them into a compact temporal memory. It answers from sparse, low-resolution global frames combined with dense, high-resolution local frames. Across `LVBench`, `MLVU`, `VideoMME`, and `LongVideoBench` it **improves on budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points** and beats the compared frame-selection and agentic methods on their reported benchmarks.

papers.title: AlienBench: A Benchmark of Structural Novelty in Language Model Outputs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for creative tasks such as writing, design, and idea generation. For these uses, it matters whether a model's ideas depart from familiar examples or stay close to them. Novelty is one standard measure of creativity, and current creativity evaluations ask human experts or LLM judges to rate how novel an output is. However, these ratings have no fixed reference for what counts as novel (or, in other terms, departure from the familiar). Measuring this departure requires a task with known familiar defaults. The structured imagination task from cognitive psychology is such a task. In this creativity test, people imagine a creature from another planet. The departure from features of Earth animals, such as bilateral symmetry and legs as mode of locomotion, is used as measure of creativity. We introduce AlienBench, a benchmark that adapts the structured imagination task to language models. Models describe alien creatures, and a panel of three LLM judges extracts ten biological features from the description and labels them as either Earth-typical or a departure. The sum of feature departures is the score of a description, from 0 to 10. Each model describes alien creatures under six prompt conditions that vary the framing of the task and the planetary environment. Each model generates 30 descriptions per condition (180 in total), and its overall score is the mean across these descriptions. We evaluate 10 language models, from frontier to open-weight models. Overall scores range from 3.28 (GPT-6 Luna) to 6.55 (Ministral 3 14B). Interestingly, open-weight models score higher than proprietary models in this task (5.40 vs. 4.58). Under the baseline prompt, the models depart from Earth defaults more often on average than 100 human participants on every feature. We release all prompts, generations, judge outputs, and scores.
papers.summary: Creativity evaluations of LLMs rely on human or LLM-judge novelty ratings that have no fixed reference for what counts as familiar. `AlienBench` adapts the structured imagination task from cognitive psychology: models describe creatures from another planet, and a panel of three LLM judges scores how many of ten biological features (such as bilateral symmetry or legs) depart from Earth norms. Ten models each produced 180 descriptions across six prompt conditions, with scores ranging from 3.28 (`GPT-6 Luna`) to 6.55 (`Ministral 3 14B`). **Open-weight models scored higher than proprietary ones (5.40 versus 4.58)**, and under the baseline prompt the models departed from Earth defaults more often than 100 human participants on every feature.

papers.title: CARGO: Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Preventive Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving
papers.abstract: This study presents Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Optimization (CARGO), a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for cooperative on-ramp merging in mixed traffic. A shared latent-context posterior and an action-conditioned response model estimate directed behavioral influence, with posterior uncertainty propagated into interaction-edge selection. Complementary attribution mechanisms couple signed influence with marginal team utility for cooperative reward shaping and assign responsibility from positive excess tail risk relative to a safe reference policy. Conditional diffusion generates future responses for action-dependent risk estimation. Responsibility-guided preventive optimization calibrates agent-specific risk-reduction requirements to local capacity within a policy trust region, using reserved safety margins, adaptive requirement scaling, and joint feasibility verification. Theoretical analysis establishes risk monotonicity and sufficient local conditions for non-decreasing environmental return under explicit assumptions. Experiments in highway-env across three traffic densities, together with controlled graph-recovery and attribution studies, support the effectiveness of the framework. Under high-density traffic, CARGO increases the success rate by 66.04\% and reduces the crash rate by 56.23\% relative to the best evaluated baseline for each metric.
papers.summary: Cooperative on-ramp merging in mixed traffic requires autonomous vehicles to coordinate while avoiding crashes, and the authors frame this as a safe multi-agent reinforcement learning problem. `CARGO` (Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Optimization) estimates directed behavioral influence between agents, uses it to shape cooperative rewards, and assigns each agent responsibility for excess tail risk relative to a safe reference policy, with conditional diffusion generating future responses for risk estimation. Each agent's risk-reduction requirement is then calibrated to its local capacity within a policy trust region, and the authors prove risk monotonicity under explicit assumptions. In high-density traffic in `highway-env`, `CARGO` raises the success rate by **66.04%** and cuts the crash rate by 56.23% relative to the best baseline for each metric.

papers.title: SPDMX: Large-Scale Open Stem Audio From Symbolic Music
papers.abstract: Large public datasets have driven recent progress in machine learning, from text and vision to speech and general audio. Music remains an outlier, as copyright blocks redistribution of training audio, while many modern tasks need individual stems rather than mixtures. Existing multitrack resources trade off realism, scale, and licensing, while synthetic alternatives rely on proprietary VSTs or naive open rendering that yields weak stems. We introduce SPDMX, a listening-guided rendering of public-domain PDMX scores into an openly-licensed stem corpus with aligned scores and an open render pipeline: $253{,}982$ songs, $490{,}159$ mono stems, and $5{,}469$ song-hours at $44.1$ kHz under CC BY 4.0, with paired MIDI and identifiers linking to PDMX metadata. $88{,}403$ songs ($34.8\%$; $2{,}734$ song-hours) provide multitrack supervision. To our knowledge, this is the largest openly-licensed synthetic multitrack subset by song-hours, enabling source separation, stem-conditioned synthesis, MIDI-to-audio, transcription, and joint symbolic-audio modeling. We release the corpus, metadata, and open pipeline for reuse on other symbolic collections. Demos and experimental notes are on the project page.
papers.summary: Copyright makes it hard to redistribute music training audio, and many modern tasks need individual instrument stems rather than full mixes. The authors render public-domain `PDMX` scores into audio through an open pipeline tuned by listening, producing `SPDMX`: 253,982 songs, 490,159 mono stems, and 5,469 song-hours at 44.1 kHz under CC BY 4.0, with paired MIDI.
