Of these, 88,403 songs provide multitrack supervision, which the authors describe as **the largest openly licensed synthetic multitrack subset by song-hours**. The corpus supports source separation, stem-conditioned synthesis, MIDI-to-audio rendering, transcription, and joint symbolic-audio modeling, and the pipeline can be reused on other symbolic collections.

papers.title: Circuit Theory-Informed AI for Condition Monitoring in Power Electronics
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence for power electronics is evolving toward a deeper comprehension of system intrinsic behaviors and dynamics. As a novel integration of neural computation and electric circuits, spike-based neuromorphic computing offers promising potential in high energy efficiency and adaptability for data-driven applications. Building on the latency-coding principles, this article proposes a framework for data-light condition monitoring that relies solely on three-phase AC current measurements. The AC current signals are encoded as membrane potentials of RC-based spiking neurons, which are inherently compatible with spiking neural networks that can effectively facilitate the estimation of device parameters. Case studies are presented to validate the performances, while constraints and further optimizations are also evaluated and discussed, and future extensions of the methodology are provided.
papers.summary: The authors propose a condition-monitoring framework for power electronics that uses only three-phase AC current measurements and requires little data. Current signals are encoded as the membrane potentials of RC-circuit-based spiking neurons using latency coding, which makes them a natural input for spiking neural networks that estimate device parameters. Case studies validate the approach and are used to discuss its constraints, possible optimizations, and extensions, with the authors highlighting **the energy efficiency of spike-based neuromorphic computing** as the main motivation.

papers.title: Learning Generative Dynamics for 3D Molecule Generation via Sequential Neuro-Symbolic Constraints
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for generating 3D molecules. Despite showing remarkable promise, they learn atomic distributions implicitly from data, without explicitly encoding physicochemical rules into their generative dynamics. Consequently, generated samples can be statistically plausible yet chemically invalid. To address this problem, we propose Sequential Neuro-Symbolic Constrained Diffusion (SensDiff), a framework that integrates symbolic rules into generative modeling, enabling the model to internalize scientific priors during training. Central to SensDiff is the observation that the diffusion trajectory of 3D molecule generation exhibits a coarse-to-fine evolution: valid molecules arise by first mitigating macroscopic geometric conflicts and then refining structures toward microscopic chemical consistency through iterative denoising. Accordingly, SensDiff mirrors this dynamic by sequentially enforcing constraints with adaptive weighting during training, progressively steering generation toward valid molecular geometries. Moreover, SensDiff translates domain knowledge into interpretable generative controls, grounding opaque neural denoising in scientific principles. Experiments on molecular benchmarks and real-world constrained generation tasks confirm that SensDiff consistently improves chemical validity while adhering to physicochemical rules and user-specified targets. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026_SensDiff.
papers.summary: Diffusion models for 3D molecule generation learn atomic distributions implicitly, so their samples can look statistically plausible while being chemically invalid. `SensDiff` (Sequential Neuro-Symbolic Constrained Diffusion) builds symbolic physicochemical rules into training. It exploits the observation that denoising proceeds from coarse to fine: it first resolves large-scale geometric conflicts, then enforces fine-grained chemical consistency, with adaptive constraint weighting at each stage. Experiments on molecular benchmarks and constrained generation tasks show **consistently improved chemical validity** while meeting physicochemical rules and user-specified targets.

papers.title: BMMS: Policy-Conditioned Measurement of Behavioral Compliance in Language Models
papers.abstract: Behavioral evaluation of language models fixes its dimensions in advance: hallucination, sycophancy, toxicity, over-refusal. An operator in a regulated industry needs a different question answered: does a system do what a particular rulebook requires? We introduce the Behavioral Misalignment Metric Suite (BMMS), which measures policy-conditioned misalignment by taking a policy corpus as an argument and returning a compliance profile over it, for any published policy and any system that answers in natural language. The Compliance Attainment Score (CAS) measures severity-weighted attainment over the obligations that bind the system, and the Compliance Robustness Margin (CRM) the share of that attainment surviving graded adversarial pressure; Behavioral Invariance (BIV) and the Behavioral Disposition Index (BDI) are specified and released with the suite. Dimensions enter only by passing a published admission test whose binding criterion is attribution: a quantity that moves when the judge changes, holding the target fixed, is measuring the instrument. Applying it excluded one of the quantities the suite itself reported. Across 1,003 obligations from eleven documents in five registers, the admission criterion holds 94.4% precision against blinded human judgment on vendor specifications and 50.0% on analytical guidance, extraction fidelity is 94.6%, and re-scoring under judges from two other providers leaves target ordering invariant while the absolute score of a single target spans up to 0.22. We apply it to the two most detailed published behavioral specifications. Own-specification advantage is not resolved from zero once document difficulty is subtracted, but absolute self-compliance is another matter: GPT-4o fails 70.7% of the hard constraints binding it in the Model Spec published by OpenAI, where the two Claude models fail 0.0% and 9.1% of theirs.
papers.summary: Standard behavioral evaluations of language models test fixed dimensions such as hallucination or sycophancy, whereas regulated operators need to know whether a system follows a specific rulebook. The Behavioral Misalignment Metric Suite (`BMMS`) takes any policy corpus as input and returns a compliance profile. Its metrics include a severity-weighted Compliance Attainment Score (`CAS`) and a Compliance Robustness Margin (`CRM`), and a metric is admitted only if its score does not change when the judge model is swapped. Across 1,003 obligations, target rankings stay stable across judges from different providers, and when models are checked against their own vendors' published specifications, **`GPT-4o` fails 70.7% of the hard constraints in OpenAI's Model Spec**, compared with 0.0% and 9.1% for two Claude models.

papers.title: Learning When to Think: Dual-Reference Offline Optimization for Adaptive VLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Reasoning traces improve vision-language models on complex multimodal tasks, but forcing every input to follow a long reasoning process leads to overthinking and unnecessary inference cost. We study adaptive fast/slow thinking for VLMs, where one model answers directly for simple inputs and reasons step by step when needed. Fast answers and slow traces often come from distinct behavior policies, making a single-reference offline objective misweight one mode. We propose DUAL-REFERENCE BOLT (DR-BOLT), which distinguishes the desired fast/slow mixture reference from the sampling distribution and corrects their mismatch in reward-weighted training. Fast/slow partition competition explains routing in the optimal target; an efficient source-wise correction approximates the exact objective when response formats are well separated. Matched Qwen3-VL comparisons use identical candidate banks to isolate the objective from slow-teacher quality. DR-BOLT improves score-length trade-offs over the evaluated offline and online baselines on ScienceQA and three held-out transfer benchmarks, with a 24.1% cross-benchmark slow ratio and a 2.90-fold end-to-end training speedup over reproduced GRPO. These results support adaptive reasoning in the studied two-reference setting, while broader robustness remains open. Our code is available at https://github.com/HongbinLin3589/DR-BOLT.
papers.summary: Forcing vision-language models (VLMs) to reason at length on every input wastes compute, so the authors train a single model to answer simple inputs directly and reason step by step only when needed. Fast answers and slow reasoning traces usually come from different sampling policies, which skews offline objectives that assume a single reference distribution. `DR-BOLT` (Dual-Reference BOLT) separates the desired fast/slow mixture from the sampling distribution and corrects the mismatch during reward-weighted training. On `Qwen3-VL` with `ScienceQA` and three held-out benchmarks, it improves the trade-off between score and response length, using slow reasoning on 24.1% of inputs and training **2.90 times faster end to end than a reproduced `GRPO` baseline**.

papers.title: Evaluation of a Multi-Link Machine Learning Approach for Rainfall Detection Using Satellite Microwave Links
papers.abstract: The impacts of climate change have increased the need for reliable real-time rainfall monitoring systems. This study investigates rainfall detection using a network of opportunistic sensors based on satellite microwave links (SMLs) combined with machine learning (ML) classifiers. Two models, a random forest (RF) and a convolutional neural network (CNN), were trained on aggregated SML data, including information from neighboring links. The results demonstrate that leveraging information from multiple links substantially enhances the detection of both wet and dry periods compared to single-link approaches. Moreover, the RF model consistently provides a more stable and reliable trade-off than CNN, improving rainfall detection and reducing misclassifications overall, with particularly strong performance during harsh weather conditions. The study spanned up to 32 rainy days between 2021 and 2024.
papers.summary: The study detects rainfall using satellite microwave links (SMLs) as opportunistic sensors, with machine learning classifiers trained on aggregated link data. A `random forest` and a convolutional neural network (`CNN`) were trained with input from each link and its neighboring links. **Using several links substantially improves detection of both wet and dry periods compared with single-link approaches**, and the random forest gives a more stable trade-off than the CNN, especially in harsh weather. The evaluation covers up to 32 rainy days between 2021 and 2024.

papers.title: FIND: Frequency Invariance Disentanglement for Test-Time Adaptation in LiDAR 3D Detection
papers.abstract: LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection (L3OD) is a fundamental 3D perception task, yet its performance is often compromised by domain shifts arising from diverse sensor configurations and environmental conditions. Existing Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods primarily leverage self-supervision in the spatial domain, yet they frequently confound semantic content with domain style due to the sparse, non-Euclidean nature of point clouds. To overcome this limitation, we propose FIND (Frequency INvariance Disentanglement), a novel TTA framework that precisely disentangles domain-invariant content from domain-specific interference within the frequency domain. Our methodology utilizes B-Spline fitting to construct locally adaptive filters integrated into a dual-stream architecture: an Invariant Stream extracts robust features to guide pseudo-labeling, while a Specific Stream enforces consistency against domain perturbations. By combining invariance-driven alignment with stability-guided regularization, our approach dynamically extracts robust domain-invariant features while suppressing domain-specific interference. Extensive experiments on cross-dataset adaptation and robust corruption benchmarks demonstrate that FIND significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/llldx03/FIND.
papers.summary: LiDAR-based 3D object detection degrades under domain shifts from different sensors and environments, and existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods working on spatial features tend to mix semantic content with domain style. `FIND` (Frequency Invariance Disentanglement) separates domain-invariant content from domain-specific interference in the frequency domain, using B-spline fitting to build locally adaptive filters. A dual-stream design follows: an invariant stream guides pseudo-labeling, and a specific stream enforces consistency under domain perturbations. According to the authors, **`FIND` significantly outperforms state-of-the-art TTA methods** on cross-dataset adaptation and corruption benchmarks.

papers.title: SIFR: Stable Signed Flow Reinforcement
papers.abstract: Reward-based fine-tuning of flow models requires effectively promoting high-reward and suppressing low-reward samples, while maintaining training stability over many rounds of iterative updates. Iterative reward fine-tuning provides a simple starting point, but the positive reward weights give no explicit unfitting signal, and repeated reweighting concentrates the distribution and causes collapse. We propose Stable Signed Flow Reinforcement (SIFR), which replaces the reward weights by signed advantages to supply the missing unfitting signal, and constrains the velocity drift from a reference model to stabilize the updates, with a Lagrange multiplier that adapts the regularization strength to a prescribed drift budget. We further show that existing flow RL methods fall within this framework: they implicitly minimize the signed loss, differing in their regularization choices. We validate SIFR on SD3.5 Medium (2.5B) and FLUX.2 Klein (9B) and scale it to Cosmos 3 Super Text2Image (64B): across all 12 backbone--reward pairs with preference and rule-based rewards, it matches or exceeds existing methods, reaches their peak rewards much faster, and keeps improving over long training where they plateau or collapse.
papers.summary: Fine-tuning flow-based image generators on rewards with iterative reweighting gives no explicit signal to suppress low-reward samples, and over many rounds the distribution concentrates and collapses. `SIFR` (Stable Signed Flow Reinforcement) replaces positive reward weights with signed advantages and limits velocity drift from a reference model, using a Lagrange multiplier that adapts the regularization to a fixed drift budget. The authors show that existing flow RL methods implicitly minimize this same signed loss and differ only in their regularization. Tested on `SD3.5 Medium`, `FLUX.2 Klein`, and up to the 64B `Cosmos 3 Super Text2Image`, `SIFR` **matches or exceeds existing methods across all 12 backbone-reward pairs**, reaches peak rewards faster, and keeps improving where other methods plateau or collapse.

papers.title: TailDART: Compute-Efficient Foundation Models for Financial Time-Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Although time-series foundation models (TSFMs) achieve strong zero-shot transferability across high-information-density physical systems, applying overparameterized TSFMs to quantitative finance is fundamentally constrained by low signal-to-noise ratios, non-stationarity, and prohibitive autoregressive decoding latency. To reconcile representation learning with institutional operational constraints, this study presents TailDART, a dense 2.68 million-parameter foundation model engineered for financial time-series forecasting. By integrating grouped-query attention into a lightweight backbone, the architecture drastically reduces Key-Value cache memory bandwidth overhead, achieving major inference acceleration (up to 48.1%) over prevailing state-of-the-art TSFMs to enable low-latency, high-throughput streaming execution. Furthermore, multi-asset benchmarks across varying temporal resolutions show that a compact model can remain competitive for market forecasting: TailDART matches the predictive fidelity of substantially larger baselines while demonstrating superior error resilience in high-volatility regimes.
papers.summary: Large time-series foundation models (TSFMs) struggle with financial data because of its low signal-to-noise ratio and non-stationarity, and their autoregressive decoding is often too slow for trading systems. `TailDART` is a dense 2.68-million-parameter forecasting model that uses grouped-query attention to reduce key-value cache memory bandwidth, giving **up to 48.1% faster inference** than leading TSFMs. In benchmarks across multiple assets and time resolutions, it matches the accuracy of much larger baselines and makes fewer large errors during high-volatility periods.

papers.title: Analyzing Code Provenance in LLMs for Programming Education
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) play an increasing role in programming education, challenging traditional assessment methods as they can generate fully functional code instantly. This disrupts the reliability of student submissions as indicators of learning and effort. To address this issue, code provenance is essential for tracing the origins of code and distinguishing student-authored, AI-generated, and externally sourced components. We extend the Min-K% probability approach by incorporating synthetic non-member code generation and apply it to Python code for membership inference and provenance tracking. Evaluations cover free LLMs such as GPT-2, DistilGPT-2, and DialoGPT, as well as state-of-the-art commercial models including GPT-5, Gemini 2.5, Mistral, DeepSeek, and LLaMA 3.3. Before evaluating our approach on higher-education student assignments, we validate its feasibility using Stack Overflow data. The results show that free models enable more sensitive code memorization detection than commercial models. By systematically comparing these LLMs, we assess trade-offs between detection accuracy and privacy protection, taking an initial step toward effective assessment of AI-assisted programming education through combined provenance detection and process visibility.
papers.summary: Because LLMs can produce working code instantly, student submissions in programming courses no longer reliably show learning, so the authors study code provenance: telling apart student-written, AI-generated, and externally sourced code. They extend the `Min-K%` probability membership-inference method with synthetic non-member code and apply it to Python. The method is validated on `Stack Overflow` data and then on student assignments, across open models (`GPT-2`, `DistilGPT-2`, `DialoGPT`) and commercial ones (`GPT-5`, `Gemini 2.5`, `Mistral`, `DeepSeek`, `LLaMA 3.3`). **Free models allow more sensitive detection of memorized code than commercial models**, and the authors discuss the trade-off between detection accuracy and privacy protection.

papers.title: Large Language Model Consensus and Corpus-Adaptive Topic Modeling for Classifying and Mapping Patent Innovation
papers.abstract: Patent analytics increasingly relies on transformer representations and large language models (LLMs), yet linking conceptual classification, topic formation and interpretation requires explicit decisions about model roles and the evidence retained at each stage. In this design-oriented study, we propose and demonstrate a patent analytics pipeline that links these tasks and keeps each decision open to audit. Three LLMs separately classify each patent by novelty (radical or incremental) and innovation type (product, process, service). Radical and innovation-type labels each require two supporting votes, with Incremental used as the fallback novelty label. Topics are discovered by clustering PatentSBERTa embeddings, with parameter ranges scaled to corpus size. A patent-specific stopword list is applied only when topics are represented with class-based term frequency--inverse document frequency (c-TF-IDF), and a second embedding model supports inter-topic similarity, hierarchical refinement and visualization. An LLM then labels each topic from its ranked keywords and representative patents. We demonstrate the pipeline on 30,964 public-sector-related patents retrieved from Lens.org. Across five category corpora ranging from 591 to 29,215 patents, the pipeline produced 74 category-specific topic instances with a macro-average document coverage of 98.1% and topic diversity of 0.900--1.000, and fewer than 1% of classification outputs returned UNKNOWN. Because every model vote and the evidence behind each topic label are retained, analysts can audit and revise the outputs. The demonstration establishes the feasibility and traceability of the pipeline; testing its labels against expert coding and benchmarking it against alternative pipelines are identified as the next steps. The pipeline offers a reusable basis for LLM-assisted patent analysis in technology intelligence.
papers.summary: The authors propose a patent-analytics pipeline that links LLM classification, topic modeling, and topic interpretation while keeping every decision auditable. Three LLMs vote on each patent's novelty (radical or incremental) and innovation type, and a label requires two agreeing votes. Topics are found by clustering `PatentSBERTa` embeddings with parameters scaled to corpus size and are then labeled by an LLM. On 30,964 public-sector-related patents from Lens.org, the pipeline produced 74 topics with **98.1% macro-average document coverage**, and fewer than 1% of classifications returned UNKNOWN; validation against expert coding is left for future work.

papers.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning via Probabilistic Option Shielding
papers.abstract: Shielding is a safe reinforcement learning technique that provides safety guarantees while learning, by blocking unsafe actions. Traditional shielding relies on a complete model of the environment to provide long-term guarantees. Probabilistic logic shielding (PLS) lifts the requirement of having such model, but only considers safety in the short term, typically looking only one or few steps ahead. We propose Probabilistic Option Shielding (POS), which extends PLS to the option level, recovering long-horizon safety without reintroducing the need for a complete environment model. POS learns a model-free critic directly from one-step PLS signals, to estimate the probability that an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty. We evaluate POS on safe navigation tasks in the LogiCity environment, and show that it achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of standard step-level PLS and other safety related reinforcement learning baselines.
papers.summary: Shielding keeps reinforcement learning agents safe by blocking unsafe actions, but classical shields need a complete environment model, and probabilistic logic shielding (`PLS`) avoids that need while looking only one or a few steps ahead. Probabilistic Option Shielding (`POS`) extends `PLS` to options, which are temporally extended actions. It learns a model-free critic from one-step `PLS` signals to estimate the probability that an entire option completes safely. On safe navigation tasks in the `LogiCity` environment, `POS` achieves **considerably safer training while matching the task performance** of step-level `PLS` and other safe RL baselines.

papers.title: RPEG: Training Reasoning Language Models Scalably and Cost-Effectively
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now central to training Reasoning Language Models (RLMs), but RLM pipelines are difficult to scale and costly to run because each RL step couples multiple large models, heterogeneous stages, cross-step state, and complex asynchronous dependencies. Existing systems typically optimize only parts of this design space. We address this complexity by jointly optimizing the pipeline structure as well as its execution using a novel data-centric graph intermediate representation called RLM Pipeline Execution Graph (RPEG). RPEG exposes structural choices such as bounded asynchrony and actor-critic sharing together with execution optimizations such as stage fusion, fine-grained scheduling, and multi-dimensional model parallelism. It is coupled with a comprehensive analytical performance model for RLM training, jointly capturing compute, communication, memory, and hierarchical rack-, node-, and GPU-level effects. Across systems with up to 256 GH200 GPUs, our distributed runtime engine implementing RPEG improves performance by up to 2x over ReaL and reduces step latency by up to 2.48x over verl, while increasing hardware utilization by up to 30%. Overall, RPEG provides a graph-driven foundation for next-generation training pipelines for frontier reasoning LLMs.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning pipelines for reasoning language models (RLMs) are hard to scale because each step couples several large models, heterogeneous stages, and asynchronous dependencies. The authors introduce the RLM Pipeline Execution Graph (`RPEG`), a data-centric graph representation that lets structural choices, such as bounded asynchrony and actor-critic sharing, be optimized jointly with execution choices, such as stage fusion, scheduling, and multi-dimensional parallelism. An analytical performance model covering compute, communication, memory, and rack-, node-, and GPU-level effects guides those choices. On up to 256 GH200 GPUs, the runtime is up to 2x faster than `ReaL`, **reduces step latency by up to 2.48x compared with `verl`**, and raises hardware utilization by up to 30%.

papers.title: On the Limits of Execution Traces for Repairing Assertion Failures in LLM-Generated Code
papers.abstract: Iterative repair returns a failed program's error to a large language model (LLM) and asks it to fix it. After iterative repair, the remaining failures are mostly assertion failures: with four Qwen2.5 models, they make up 79% of residual failures on BigCodeBench, all on HumanEval and 93% on LiveCodeBench. We argue, through an information view of the feedback, that an assertion failure says little about where the fault lies. We propose Breakpoint Debugging (BPD), which returns the failed program annotated inline with its variables' runtime values. We take the tasks that iterative repair failed to fix with five repair attempts and compare two ways of spending five further generations on them: BPD, and resampling. On BigCodeBench, BPD repairs 26.7% of these tasks against 22.4%, and its advantage grows with model size. On HumanEval, BPD outperforms resampling but only slightly, and on LiveCodeBench, fresh sampling repairs more (6.5% against 4.9%). Furthermore, BPD reduces unchanged-code resubmissions from 28% to 8% on BigCodeBench. Using only the first failing test's trace, it outperforms tracing all failing tests while using fewer tokens than both all-trace BPD and plain iterative repair. On LiveCodeBench, BPD gives no gain even on the public tests, so a visible failing input is not enough for a trace to help. These results match the information view: a trace helps only when the test exposes a failing input, and the fault is an implementation slip; otherwise, a repair loop should resample rather than trace.
papers.summary: When LLMs repeatedly repair failing code, most remaining failures are assertion failures (79% on `BigCodeBench` across four `Qwen2.5` models), and the authors argue that an assertion message reveals little about where the fault is. They propose Breakpoint Debugging (`BPD`), which returns the failed program annotated inline with runtime variable values, and compare it with plain resampling on tasks that five rounds of iterative repair had not fixed. `BPD` repairs **26.7% of these tasks against 22.4% for resampling on `BigCodeBench`**, with a larger edge for bigger models, and cuts unchanged-code resubmissions from 28% to 8%. Its gain on `HumanEval` is small, and on `LiveCodeBench` resampling does better, which suggests traces help only when a test exposes a failing input and the bug is an implementation slip.

papers.title: BOXBOX: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Long-Running Performance Optimization
papers.abstract: Automated harness optimization improves agents by learning from trajectories and task feedback. Existing offline methods use reference answers to optimize harnesses for reuse on held-out tasks. However, many real-world tasks are open-ended, while long runs expose new difficulties that offline-optimized harnesses may not address. To study harness optimization in these settings, we introduce PerfRace, a benchmark for long-running performance optimization of software projects, and investigate whether agents can use task-specific experience to recursively improve their harnesses during an ongoing task. To this end, we introduce BOXBOX, which enables agent-triggered harness revision and kernel-managed hot reloading while preserving execution context. We evaluate BOXBOX on PerfRace under matched test-time budgets, comparing it with Frozen Harness, offline Harness Evolution, and Harness Scaling. BOXBOX achieves higher speedup with more efficient use of task time and model cost, reaching a Speedup@4h of 1.70x, compared with 1.54x for the strongest baseline.
papers.summary: Agent harnesses are usually optimized offline with reference answers, which fits poorly with open-ended, long-running tasks that keep surfacing new difficulties. The authors introduce `PerfRace`, a benchmark for long-running performance optimization of software projects, and `BOXBOX`, which lets an agent revise its own harness during a task and hot-reload it without losing execution context. Under matched time and cost budgets, `BOXBOX` beats a frozen harness, offline harness evolution, and harness scaling, **reaching a 1.70x speedup after four hours versus 1.54x for the strongest baseline** while using task time and model cost more efficiently.

papers.title: HMMF-Net: A Lightweight Hierarchical Multi-Frame Multimodal Fusion Network for Accurate Fish Feeding Intensity Assessment
papers.abstract: Automated fish feeding intensity assessment (FFIA) is important for precision aquaculture and feed cost optimization. However, unimodal methods are vulnerable to acoustic noise and visual disturbances, while existing multimodal frameworks often rely on computationally intensive 3D convolutions or Transformers, limiting their use on edge devices. To address these limitations, we propose HMMF-Net, a lightweight multimodal architecture that combines early multi-frame visual encoding and multi-axis acoustic modeling through a hierarchical bidirectional messenger cross-modal fusion (BMCF) mechanism. The visual branch captures temporal variations in feeding behavior by stacking temporally distant frames as a multi-channel input to an adapted 2D EfficientNetB0 backbone. The acoustic branch employs adaptive multi-axis residual units (AMARU) to extract temporal, frequency, and local time-frequency representations from log-mel spectrograms. BMCF progressively exchanges information between the two modalities at intermediate representation levels through compact messenger tokens, reducing the computational overhead of dense cross-modal attention. Evaluated on the AV-FFIA dataset using five-fold cross-validation, HMMF-Net achieves 96.77% accuracy and 96.88% F1-score on the held-out test folds, with 3.987M parameters and 1.002 GFLOPs. Compared with the best-performing visual configuration (95.49% accuracy), HMMF-Net reduces the classification error by 28.38%. Deployment on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano using TensorRT with FP32 precision maintains comparable accuracy, with an inference time of 11.54 ms per 2-second sample and a model size of 18.81 MB. These results demonstrate that HMMF-Net combines effective multimodal representation learning with computational efficiency, enabling accurate and practical FFIA on resource-constrained edge platforms.
papers.summary: Automated fish feeding intensity assessment (FFIA) supports precision aquaculture, but single-modality methods are fragile and existing multimodal models are too heavy for edge devices. `HMMF-Net` stacks temporally distant video frames as input to an adapted `EfficientNetB0`, models log-mel spectrograms with adaptive multi-axis residual units, and fuses the two modalities through compact messenger tokens rather than dense cross-attention. On the `AV-FFIA` dataset, it reaches **96.77% accuracy with 3.987M parameters and 1.002 GFLOPs**, and runs at 11.54 ms per 2-second sample on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano.

papers.title: Fused-Softmax for efficient quantized attention
papers.abstract: Low-precision matrix throughput on modern GPUs is growing far faster than vector-arithmetic throughput. Attention therefore cannot realize the available GEMM performance because softmax has become the pipeline bottleneck. We introduce Fused-Softmax Attention, a training-free algorithm that reformulates and approximates softmax to fold its dominant operations into the attention GEMMs, moving work from vector units to matrix cores. Implemented for the AMD CDNA 4 architecture, our MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 kernels reach approximately 3.0, 4.0 and 4.6 PFLOP/s on an AMD Instinct MI355X GPU, yielding speedups of $2.1\times$, $2.8\times$ and $3.2\times$ over the BF16 attention. Importantly, the additional error introduced by Fused-Softmax remains below the error floor set by quantizing the GEMM operands. On Wan2.2-T2V-A14B, a hybrid MXFP6/4 schedule delivers up to $2.05\times$ end-to-end speedup while preserving the visual quality of the outputs. The kernels ship in AMD's open-source AITER library, and they powered AMD's MLPerf Inference v6.1 Wan2.2 submission, which ran $1.7\times$ faster than AMD's previous-round result on the same hardware. Our results show that redesigning softmax to utilize the matrix pipeline enables attention to capitalize on continued growth in low-precision matrix throughput.
papers.summary: Low-precision matrix throughput on GPUs is growing much faster than vector arithmetic throughput, so softmax has become the bottleneck in attention. `Fused-Softmax Attention` is a training-free method that reformulates and approximates softmax so its dominant operations run inside the attention matrix multiplications on matrix cores. The authors implement `MXFP8`, `MXFP6`, and `MXFP4` kernels on an AMD Instinct MI355X, reaching **speedups of 2.1x, 2.8x, and 3.2x over BF16 attention**, with added error below the floor already set by operand quantization. On `Wan2.2-T2V-A14B`, a mixed `MXFP6`/`MXFP4` schedule gives up to 2.05x end-to-end speedup without loss of visual quality, and the kernels ship in AMD's open-source `AITER` library.

papers.title: RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Interactive Explainability in Clinical Decision Support Systems
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in high-risks decision-making systems across domains such as healthcare, finance, and the judicial system. As reliance on predictive models grows, so does the demand for Explainable AI (XAI) to ensure transparency, trust, and interpretability. However, existing XAI approaches often fail to present explanations in a format accessible to domain experts, limiting their practical utility. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a bridge between complex models and end-users, offering natural language explanations. Yet, their use introduces new risks, including hallucinated outputs and lack of source traceability. To address these challenges, we propose a Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) that not only combines standard predictive models with XAI techniques but also incorporates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation module as an interactive enhancer. This module grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge, reformulates technical outputs into a human-like format, and enables users-such as clinicians-to actively query the system. By fostering an interactive, human-in-the-loop environment, our approach empowers domain experts to explore model decisions, contextualize explanations, and build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics. The study concludes with preliminary experiments validating the proposed methodology.
papers.summary: Explainable AI (XAI) techniques often produce explanations that domain experts find hard to use, and LLM-generated explanations can hallucinate and lack traceable sources. The authors propose a clinical decision support system (CDSS) that pairs standard predictive models and XAI methods with a retrieval-augmented generation (`RAG`) module. The module grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge, rewrites technical outputs in natural language, and lets clinicians query the system interactively. **Only preliminary experiments are reported** as validation of the method.

papers.title: MM-DyGraph: A Dataset, Benchmark, and Model for Multimodal Dynamic Graphs
papers.abstract: Multimodal dynamic graphs are pervasive in real-world applications, where nodes and edges are accompanied by multimodal signals, including text and images. Despite their practical importance, benchmarks and methods that explicitly study multimodal learning in dynamic graphs remain scarce, hindering the full understanding and effective utilization of multimodal information for downstream tasks. To address this gap, we introduce MM-DyGraph, to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark for multimodal dynamic graph learning, consisting of diverse real-world datasets with fine-grained temporal graph evolution and rich multimodal attributes. MM-DyGraph provides three evaluation tasks to comprehensively assess model performance in dynamic settings. We benchmark representative state-of-the-art dynamic graph methods and reveal that naive feature concatenation yields target-level inconsistencies: multimodal inputs benefit certain prediction targets while harming others. This observation indicates that the modality informativeness depends on the specific prediction target over time. Building on these observations, we propose a Target-aware Spatial-Temporal Multimodal Fusion (TST-MF) framework, which jointly conditions multimodal fusion on the prediction target and spatial-temporal relations, enabling context-adaptive cross-modal interplay for target-specific representations. Extensive experiments over diverse datasets and tasks show that TST-MF delivers robust and competitive performance, achieving clear gains in multimodal settings.
papers.summary: Real-world dynamic graphs often carry text and images on their nodes and edges, yet multimodal dynamic graph learning has had few benchmarks. `MM-DyGraph` provides diverse real-world datasets with fine-grained temporal evolution and multimodal attributes, along with three evaluation tasks. Benchmarking existing methods shows that **naively concatenating multimodal features helps some prediction targets and hurts others**, which suggests that the usefulness of each modality depends on the target. The authors propose `TST-MF` (Target-aware Spatial-Temporal Multimodal Fusion), which conditions fusion on the prediction target and on spatial-temporal relations and delivers clear gains in multimodal settings.

papers.title: Zero-Query Transferable Pretend Benign Attacks with Amortized Online Generation for Cooperative Perception
papers.abstract: Cooperative perception enables an ego agent to acquire information from collaborators beyond its own sensors' reach. Yet, the most beneficial messages are often the hardest to verify from local observations. Pretend Benign (PB) exploits this asymmetry by targeting regions with weak local verifiability and applying multi-objective perturbations, making harmful feature changes appear to be benign assistance. However, PB is victim-dependent: selecting regions and optimizing perturbations require the victim model's architecture, parameters, and gradients, limiting transfer to unseen victims. A transferable attack must capture properties shared across cooperative detection models rather than those specific to one network. We address this by building a victim-agnostic attack from a heterogeneous ensemble of surrogate models and encoding its capabilities in a reusable dictionary to reduce per-message generation cost. Specifically, Transferable Pretend Benign (TrPB) transfers PB's region selection criterion and multi-objective perturbation strategy across heterogeneous surrogates to construct an offline attack. We further propose RT-TrPB, which encodes transferable regions and perturbation patterns into a region predictor and reusable perturbation dictionary, amortizing per-message attack generation. Experiments on widely used cooperative perception benchmarks show that RT-TrPB bypasses the consensus-based defenses ROBOSAC and FLD with success rates approaching 100% and generates each perturbation in under 56 ms. To counter PB-style attacks masquerading as benign collaboration, we also propose STTrust, which verifies received messages using spatial and temporal consistency and incorporates identity-level trust. STTrust detects over 90% of PB-style attacks and restores perception performance to near the attack-free level.
papers.summary: In cooperative perception, an ego vehicle uses feature messages from collaborators to see beyond its own sensors. The earlier `Pretend Benign` (`PB`) attack exploited this by perturbing regions the ego vehicle cannot verify locally, but it needed the victim model's architecture, parameters and gradients. `TrPB` removes that need by building the attack from a heterogeneous ensemble of surrogate models. `RT-TrPB` then speeds it up by encoding transferable regions and perturbation patterns into a region predictor and a reusable perturbation dictionary. `RT-TrPB` gets past the consensus-based defenses `ROBOSAC` and `FLD` with **success rates approaching 100%** and generates each perturbation in under 56 ms. The authors also propose `STTrust`, a defense that checks spatial and temporal consistency along with identity-level trust; it detects over 90% of PB-style attacks and restores perception to near attack-free levels.

papers.title: Forecasting cumulative intraoperative hypotension burden: patient-disjoint evaluation of quantile boosting and alert policies
papers.abstract:
Background: Binary hypotension forecasts do not describe the depth and duration of future low pressure. Burden forecasts may support graded early warning, but better forecast scores need not yield more useful alerts.
  Objective: To evaluate conditional quantiles of the next 15-minute mean arterial pressure (MAP) deficit below 65 mmHg and distinguish forecasting performance from episode-warning performance.
  Methods: Public VitalDB numeric arterial MAP was reduced to 10-second medians without forward filling. Subject-disjoint training, validation and test splits included 70,402, 14,270 and 15,575 labeled windows. We compared climatology, calibrated persistence, last-MAP-only boosting, and direct and residual quantile boosting, with and without additional MAP-history features. Patient-weighted pinball loss and subject-bootstrap intervals evaluated forecasting. Validation selected alert thresholds before a hash-recorded test evaluation.
  Results: In the test split, the prespecified residual-versus-persistence comparison at the 90th percentile yielded losses of 2.256 and 2.900 mmHg-min, respectively (difference -0.644; 95% interval -0.814 to -0.487). Direct prediction achieved 2.196, and direct prediction with additional MAP features achieved 2.193. Episode-warning results were sensitive to the alert rule and operating threshold.
  Conclusions: This retrospective benchmark separates burden-forecast skill from warning-policy performance. Findings support further study of direct burden estimation; they do not establish patient benefit, prospective reliability or transportability beyond the source hospital.
papers.summary: Binary hypotension alarms say nothing about how deep or how long a drop in blood pressure will be. This study forecasts quantiles of the cumulative mean arterial pressure (MAP) deficit below 65 mmHg over the next 15 minutes, using public `VitalDB` surgical recordings split so that no patient appears in more than one split. Baselines are compared with direct and residual quantile boosting. At the 90th percentile, residual boosting cut pinball loss from 2.900 mmHg-min for calibrated persistence to **2.256 mmHg-min**, and direct prediction did slightly better at 2.196. Episode-warning performance depended heavily on the alert rule and threshold, and the authors state that the results do not establish patient benefit or reliability outside the source hospital.

papers.title: Model-based learning for DoA estimation and array calibration via continuous sparse recovery
papers.abstract: Direction of arrival (DoA) estimation, a classical signal processing problem, has experienced renewed interest with the advent of integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). While decades of research have yielded highly accurate DoA estimators, hardware impairments have frequently been neglected, despite degrading both DoA estimation accuracy and downstream communication performance in ISAC systems. This work introduces a joint array calibration and DoA estimation method based on the simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) algorithm, following the model-based machine learning paradigm. The proposed method enables the calibration of antenna arrays subject to severe gain-phase and antenna location impairments through projected gradient descent (PGD), with either supervised or unsupervised objectives. Additionally, DoA estimation is enhanced by extending SOMP to continuous dictionaries via PGD refinement steps. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method enables efficient hardware impairment compensation, even without labeled samples, while outperforming conventional sparse recovery and subspace-based DoA estimation baselines.
papers.summary: Hardware impairments in antenna arrays degrade direction of arrival (DoA) estimation, which matters again for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems. The authors unroll the simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (`SOMP`) algorithm into a model-based learning method. It calibrates gain-phase and antenna-position errors through projected gradient descent (`PGD`), with either supervised or unsupervised objectives. Extra `PGD` refinement steps extend `SOMP` to continuous dictionaries, so estimated angles are not limited to a fixed grid. In simulations the method compensates for severe impairments **even without labeled samples** and outperforms conventional sparse-recovery and subspace-based DoA baselines.

papers.title: Nudging Decision Models: Do Digital Nudges Steer Fast, Generation-Free AI Agents?
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents increasingly automate business and consumer tasks but are slow and expensive. Decision models, a new class that chooses among options without generating text, are far faster and less costly. Developers call them "System One models," referencing dual process theory. We ask whether such models can be steered by digital nudges online and whether, as the theory predicts, automatic nudges affect them more than reflective ones. We adapted an online shopping experiment, previously run with humans and LLM agents, to three decision models (Jev, Decision-1, d1). Across 600 runs per model, they chose a preselected default in 97.5-99.9% and a product with social influence information in 75-96% of choices, versus 47-49% in the control. All responded more strongly to the automatic nudge, the opposite of what has been reported for reasoning-capable LLM agents. We provide first evidence that non-generative decision models are susceptible to digital nudges in a System 1 pattern, implying agent-type-specific nudge effects.
papers.summary: Decision models are a newer class of AI agents that choose among options without generating text. Their developers call them System One models, and this study tests whether digital nudges steer them the way dual process theory predicts. The authors adapted an online shopping experiment previously run with humans and LLM agents to three decision models (`Jev`, `Decision-1`, `d1`), with 600 runs per model. The models picked a preselected default in **97.5-99.9% of choices** and a product carrying social-influence information in 75-96% of choices, compared with 47-49% in the control condition. All three responded more strongly to the automatic nudge than to the reflective one, the opposite of what has been reported for reasoning-capable LLM agents.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand, from an explicit specification of the desired computation, with no gradient descent and no training data anywhere in the construction. We ask how far a large language model can carry this practice, zero-shot, across games of deliberately increasing difficulty. We design a four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four axes of difficulty, and build a second, independent network at each rung, using a structurally unrelated game at matched difficulty, to separate what a rung's finding says about the difficulty level from what it says about the one game used to measure it. Ten networks are built and independently verified. Six admit a complete, non-statistical proof of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame rung is exact where correctness is cheap, move legality and, in one network, an exact one-ply mate detector, and collapses where it is expensive, composing a multi-move mating plan, from 84.1-100% success at the one-ply tactics it was built to get right down to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; its replicate shows this collapse is an order of magnitude less severe under a shorter required plan and exact rather than heuristic safety checks. The standard-sized rung confirms, by holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding only shallow search, that the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and this exact collapse reproduces across two structurally unrelated games. We release all ten networks, their independent oracles, construction-cost measurements, and a cold-prompt protocol for a future cross-model comparison
papers.summary: Weight-space programming means setting every weight of a feed-forward network by hand from a specification of the desired computation, with no training data or gradient descent. The study tests how far an LLM can do this zero-shot on a four-rung ladder of games: `Nim`, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of `Connect Four`, and a chess endgame, with a second, structurally unrelated game at each rung as a control. Of ten networks built and independently verified, six come with complete proofs of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame networks are exact at cheap checks such as move legality and one-move mate detection, but **collapse to 0.57-9.13% success in full adversarial play**, where they must compose a multi-move mating plan. Fixing the hand-set evaluation weights and adding shallow search shows the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort.

papers.title: PHISHREV+: An ASP-Based Post-Hoc Defeasible Machine Learning Framework for Phishing Detection
papers.abstract: Phishing website detection remains a critical cybersecurity challenge. Although machine learning classifiers achieve high accuracy on benchmark datasets, they suffer from a fundamental limitation: once trained, their decision boundaries are fixed and cannot incorporate new contextual evidence without retraining the model. This work presents \textbf{PHISHREV+}, a hybrid framework that instantiates the notion of \textit{post-hoc defeasible machine learning}. This framework does not replace the classifier. It treats the initial classifier predictions as defeasible beliefs and revises them through an Answer Set Programming based non-monotonic reasoning(NMR) layer. The framework operates in two phases. In the machine learning phase, four classifiers (SVM, KNN, DT and RF) are trained on the 87 feature benchmark dataset. In the post-hoc NMR phase, four defeasible rules derived from exploratory data analysis of the training set, and validated through Chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests, formally revise initial predictions. The proposed framework achieves consistent false positive reduction across all our classifiers SVM (41$\rightarrow$39), KNN (47$\rightarrow$46), DT (62$\rightarrow$61), and RF (52$\rightarrow$51) while maintaining complete false negative parity with zero increase overhead. A comprehensive ablation studies across seven rule configurations confirms that the hierarchical combination of all four defeasible rules is necessary to achieve this optimal balance. Instance level explainability is provided through eXplainable ASP (XASP), which generates formal derivation graphs showing which defeasible rules fired and why the initial belief was retracted, a capability absent from all existing phishing detection approaches.
papers.summary: Once a machine learning phishing-website classifier is trained, its decision boundary is fixed and cannot take in new contextual evidence without retraining. `PHISHREV+` treats the classifier's predictions as defeasible beliefs, meaning beliefs that can be retracted, and revises them with a non-monotonic reasoning layer written in Answer Set Programming (`ASP`). The four revision rules come from exploratory analysis of the training data and are validated with statistical tests. Applied on top of `SVM`, `KNN`, decision tree and random forest classifiers trained on an 87-feature benchmark, the rules **reduce false positives by one or two per classifier without adding any false negatives**. `XASP` derivation graphs show which rules fired for each instance and why a prediction was retracted.

papers.title: FondueQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating Parametric Compensation in Multi-Hop QA
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) show remarkable performance based on parametric knowledge, i.e., their ability to recall facts and associations internalized in a model's weights. However, studying this capability on established multi-hop benchmarks may be complicated by benchmark contamination, as many of these benchmarks have been publicly available long enough to plausibly appear in modern pretraining corpora. As a result, correct answers under missing evidence may reflect either general parametric knowledge or memorization of benchmark-specific instances. To study how models use internal knowledge when retrieval evidence is incomplete, we introduce FondueQA, in which every required multi-hop fact is uniquely localized to a designated evidence document. This enables controlled document-level evidence ablations to study parametric compensation under incomplete retrieval. Our empirical evaluation reveals that parametric compensation strongly depends on both entity popularity and the structural role of missing evidence. Generally, models compensate more successfully for facts involving popular entities. On FondueQA, we show that bridging evidence can be more useful than the answer-bearing document itself. Moreover, models may recall a missing fact in isolation but fail to use it under partial evidence, particularly when the context contains plausible competing entities, which can reduce Exact Match by up to 15 percentage points.
papers.summary: Established multi-hop question-answering benchmarks may have leaked into pretraining data, so it is hard to tell whether a model that answers correctly without the evidence is using general knowledge or recalling memorized benchmark items. `FondueQA` places each required fact in exactly one designated evidence document, which allows controlled removal of individual documents to study how models compensate from their own internal (parametric) knowledge when retrieval is incomplete. Models compensate more successfully for facts about popular entities, and the missing document that bridges the reasoning chain can matter more than the one that holds the answer. Models sometimes recall a fact on its own but fail to use it when given partial evidence that includes plausible competing entities, which **reduces Exact Match by up to 15 percentage points**.

papers.title: AudioSphere: Towards Self-Supervised Spatial Audio Representation Models
papers.abstract: Recent audio embedding models learn representations that transfer across clip- and frame-level tasks, yet they operate almost exclusively on single-channel signals and are blind to spatial structure. Spatial audio models capture that structure but rely on clip-level supervision or contrastive objectives, yielding embeddings unsuitable for frame-level tasks like sound event detection and localization (SELD). We argue this dichotomy is not fundamental: patch-level spatial self-supervision can jointly learn acoustic and spatial features at both temporal granularities. We introduce AudioSphere, a multi-channel masked autoencoder trained on Ambisonics recordings that reconstructs both spectral content and directional cues via a joint spatiotemporal masking strategy that masks both time-frequency patches and intensity vectors. AudioSphere supports frame-level predictions while producing strong clip-level representations via aggregation. Alongside the model, we release RealSELD, a standardized benchmark for evaluating frozen backbones on real-world multi-channel SELD. AudioSphere enables, for the first time, SELD with a frozen self-supervised backbone, while matching or exceeding prior self-supervised audio embedding models on clip-level classification tasks spanning environmental sound, speech, and music, and on frame-level sound event detection. All code and data are available at https://github.com/labhamlet/AudioSphere and https://huggingface.co/labhamlet.
papers.summary: General-purpose audio embedding models mostly work on single-channel audio and ignore where sounds come from. Spatial audio models capture direction but rely on clip-level supervision or contrastive objectives, which yields embeddings unsuited to frame-level sound event detection and localization (SELD). `AudioSphere` is a multi-channel masked autoencoder trained on Ambisonics recordings that masks both time-frequency patches and intensity vectors, so it learns to reconstruct spectral content and directional cues together. It is the **first self-supervised backbone that supports SELD while kept frozen**, and it matches or exceeds prior self-supervised audio models on clip-level classification of environmental sound, speech and music. The authors also release `RealSELD`, a benchmark for evaluating frozen backbones on real-world multi-channel SELD.

papers.title: Diversity-Aware Client Selection for Communication-Efficient Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without sharing raw data, making it attractive for privacy-sensitive and bandwidth-constrained applications. A practical challenge in deploying FL is reducing communication overhead while maintaining model performance under heterogeneous, non-IID data distributions. Selecting which subset of clients participates in each training round offers a principled way to address both challenges simultaneously, yet its impact on data diversity and representativeness remains underexplored. In this paper, we investigate three client selection strategies, Power-of-Choice, Fisher information, and Centered Kernel Alignment, evaluating them not only by accuracy and convergence, but through the lens of participation diversity using the Gini coefficient and KL divergence. Under non-IID conditions, restricting participation to 15% of clients per round achieves significant communication savings, and when selection promotes diverse and balanced contributions, it also improves generalization over biased alternatives. This work provides a systematic and reproducible analysis demonstrating that diversity-focused client selection renders communication efficiency and model quality complementary rather than competing objectives.
papers.summary: In federated learning (FL), choosing which clients take part in each training round can reduce communication, but how selection affects the diversity of contributing data has received little study. The authors compare three selection strategies, `Power-of-Choice`, Fisher information and Centered Kernel Alignment (`CKA`), under non-IID data. Besides accuracy and convergence, they measure participation diversity with the Gini coefficient and KL divergence. Limiting participation to **15% of clients per round** saves substantial communication, and selection that promotes diverse, balanced participation also generalizes better than biased alternatives.

papers.title: An Empirical Study of Issues in GPU Kernel Libraries for LLM Systems
papers.abstract:
Behind the expanding use of large language models (LLMs) across application domains lies a growing dependence on specialized GPU kernel libraries. These libraries underpin the correctness and efficiency of training and inference across diverse GPU platforms, implementing attention, GEMM, quantization, and low-precision operators while managing tensor shapes, memory layouts, code generation, and hardware-specific dispatch. Problems at this layer can silently corrupt outputs, hang GPUs, prevent compilation, introduce deployment incompatibilities, or degrade performance, thereby reducing developer productivity and wasting expensive GPU resources.
  We present the first comprehensive empirical study of issues in GPU kernel libraries for LLM systems. We manually analyzed 300 high-quality GitHub issue reports, their discussions, and available fixes from seven representative libraries: FlashInfer, FlashAttention, Triton, CUTLASS, DeepGEMM, xFormers, and bitsandbytes. The analysis characterizes symptoms, root causes, fixes, and testing and debugging practices. Our main findings are: (1) 60.33% of the sampled issues originate in the Compiler and Build System or Runtime Environment dimensions, so validation must cover the deployment and execution stack, not just kernel code. (2) Kernel specialization imposes implicit correctness constraints on tensor shapes, metadata layouts, memory aliasing, and hardware resources. Violations can produce incorrect outputs or launch failures even for supported operations, highlighting the need for explicit contract validation and boundary-case testing. (3) Current testing and debugging practices are often insufficient for identifying low-precision numerical problems and hardware-specific execution failures. We outline research opportunities and tooling directions to support future LLM GPU kernel development.
papers.summary: LLM training and inference rely on specialized GPU kernel libraries for attention, matrix multiplication (GEMM), quantization and low-precision operators. The authors manually analyzed 300 GitHub issues, with their discussions and fixes, from `FlashInfer`, `FlashAttention`, `Triton`, `CUTLASS`, `DeepGEMM`, `xFormers` and `bitsandbytes`, classifying symptoms, root causes, fixes, and testing and debugging practices. **60.33% of the issues originate in the compiler and build system or the runtime environment** rather than in kernel code. Kernel specialization also carries implicit constraints on tensor shapes, metadata layouts, memory aliasing and hardware resources, and violating them can produce wrong outputs or launch failures even for supported operations. Current testing practices often miss low-precision numerical problems and hardware-specific failures, and the authors outline directions for tooling.

papers.title: Ontology-Driven Control of Conversational Agents with a Use-Case for Job Interview Practice
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely used as conversational agents in both domain-specific and open-domain situations. In domain-specific context, it is often necessary to adapt those LLMs to obtain conversations with desired characteristics, whether those apply at the level of each response (e.g. for tone or style) or more globally (i.e. at the level of a conversational strategy). Such adaptations are, however, generally realized in an ad hoc way, through specific, non-reusable, and non-transparent developments. In this paper, we propose an ontology-based approach to design conversational strategies that rely on the desired and measured characteristics of textual utterances in the conversation. Through a use case related to job interview practice, we show how this approach can be used to control LLMs to follow the strategy defined in the ontology. To this end, we automatically fine-tune the LLM to improve its compliance with ontologically-defined conversation characteristics. Our results show that training the LLM from formally defined concepts effectively enhances alignment with the requested characteristics. Hence, this work demonstrates how ontology-guided conversation control can be achieved while taking into account multiple, concurrent conversation aspects that are formally and transparently defined.
papers.summary: Adapting LLM conversational agents to a domain is usually done ad hoc, in ways that are hard to reuse or inspect. The authors define conversational strategies in an ontology that specifies desired, measurable characteristics of utterances, covering both per-response properties such as tone and conversation-level strategy. They then automatically fine-tune an LLM to comply with those characteristics. In a job-interview-practice use case, **training from formally defined concepts improved the model's alignment with the requested characteristics**, including when several conversation aspects had to be controlled at once.

papers.title: AutoRefine: Auto-Calibrating Code Judges from Workflow Outcomes
papers.abstract: LLM judges increasingly serve as quality gates for code changes that have no test oracle, but a judge prompt must be calibrated for its task and recalibrated as the system it judges evolves, while hand labels for the calibration are resource intensive and go stale. Development workflows emit outcome labels for free (tests pass or fail, changes land or are abandoned), but these labels are noisy. We present AutoRefine, a loop that rewrites a deployable judge's prompt to reproduce outcome labels, with an informed teacher that sees the judge's input plus the outcome, explains each label it keeps, and abstains when the outcome cannot be explained from what the judge sees. On a held-out dataset with an execution oracle, calibration raised chance-corrected agreement (Scott's $\pi$) from 0.36 to 0.60. On a deployed agent's outcome labels, with 25\% flipped at random to introduce noise, the teacher set aside flipped \textsc{fail} labels at more than twice the rate of genuine ones, cutting overall label noise from 25\% to 20\%. Recalibrating that agent's judge using AutoRefine raised its agreement with merge/abandon outcomes on 17 independently held-out diffs from the current workflow ($\pi$ 0.16 to 0.51); on 16 diffs from older workflows, the previous judge stayed ahead, illustrating the need for recalibration as the agent evolves. By abstaining, the teacher not only removes noisy labels but also flags changes whose outcome the judge's input cannot explain, telling a team when a judge needs better inputs rather than a better prompt.
papers.summary: LLM judges often act as quality gates for code changes that have no test oracle, but their prompts need calibrating for each task and recalibrating as the judged system changes. Hand labels for that are costly and go stale. `AutoRefine` rewrites the judge's prompt so it reproduces free but noisy workflow outcomes, such as tests passing or changes being merged or abandoned. An informed teacher model sees each outcome, explains the labels it keeps and abstains on outcomes the judge's input cannot explain. On a held-out set with an execution oracle, chance-corrected agreement (Scott's pi) rose **from 0.36 to 0.60**, and on a deployed agent's merge or abandon outcomes it rose from 0.16 to 0.51. With 25% of labels flipped at random, the teacher set aside flipped fail labels at more than twice the rate of genuine ones, and its abstentions also flag cases where the judge needs better inputs rather than a better prompt.

papers.title: Towards an Autonomous AI Steward for Large-Scale Physics Experiments: Integrating Causal Diagnostics, RAG, and Conformal Prediction
papers.abstract: Long-term particle physics experiments face critical operational challenges: monitoring non-stationary machine data streams and preserving tacit expert knowledge. We present the "Helmholtz Co-Pilot," a hybrid Multi-Agent System (MAS) acting as an autonomous experiment steward. The system can be triggered interactively by human operators or autonomously by an asynchronous causal diagnostics engine that runs independently of the MAS reasoning core. Continuously monitoring live hardware streams such as data acquisition and slow control, this engine performs dynamic causal discovery to trace cascading alarms back to their root causes and applies adaptive model selection to keep forecasts reliable across shifting machine states; upon detecting an anomaly, it hands a structured diagnostic report to the MAS. The reasoning layer itself relies on a high-throughput C++ core and a Python edge architecture orchestrating a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of specialized ReAct workers. It integrates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) backbone for institutional memory and leverages conformal prediction to bound its evidence-based recommendations with mathematical coverage guarantees. This extended abstract outlines the architecture, the integration of software-enforced Human-in-the-Loop (HitL) guardrails, and ongoing shadow-testing within the KATRIN experiment.
papers.summary: Long-running particle physics experiments must monitor non-stationary machine data streams and preserve tacit expert knowledge. The `Helmholtz Co-Pilot` is a multi-agent system that operators can trigger directly. It is also triggered automatically by an asynchronous causal diagnostics engine that traces cascading alarms back to root causes and hands a structured report to the agents. The reasoning layer coordinates specialized ReAct workers in a directed acyclic graph, uses retrieval-augmented generation (`RAG`) as institutional memory, and applies **conformal prediction to give its recommendations mathematical coverage guarantees**. This extended abstract describes the architecture, the software-enforced human-in-the-loop guardrails, and ongoing shadow-testing at the `KATRIN` experiment.

papers.title: A Stochastic Latent Variable Generalization of Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) predict the latent embedding of a target signal from a context signal, with an auxiliary variable z conditioning the predictor. Despite its prominent role in the original JEPA blueprint, the content of z has been carried by a fixed deterministic token in every prior instantiation, collapsing the genuinely multi-modal distribution over plausible completions to a point estimate. We present S-JEPA, which realises z as a proper stochastic latent variable for masked image prediction: a learned posterior infers z from context and target during training, while a learned context-conditioned prior approximates the distribution of plausible completions at inference, with no decoders and no reconstruction. In its deterministic limit the objective reduces to the I-JEPA loss in functional form, generalising that objective rather than strictly containing the I-JEPA model. Our central finding is that stochasticity adds capabilities, error-correlated predictive uncertainty and diverse completions, at no cost to representation quality: under matched architectures and schedules S-JEPA improves over the deterministic I-JEPA baseline and exceeds LeJEPA at matched architecture, while additionally producing spatially structured uncertainty maps and semantically diverse completions, neither of which the deterministic predictor produces.
papers.summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) predict the latent embedding of a target from a context, with a variable z conditioning the predictor, but every prior implementation fixed z to a deterministic token. That reduces the many plausible completions to a single point estimate. `S-JEPA` makes z a proper stochastic latent variable for masked image prediction: a learned posterior infers it during training, and a context-conditioned prior samples plausible completions at inference, with no decoder or reconstruction. **Stochasticity costs nothing in representation quality**: with matched architectures and schedules, `S-JEPA` improves on `I-JEPA` and exceeds `LeJEPA`. It also produces uncertainty maps whose structure tracks prediction error, and semantically diverse completions.

papers.title: ABHBench: Evaluating Moral Decision-Making of Foundation Models from an Agentic Perspective
papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly deployed as agentic systems that perceive context and act autonomously, raising the need to evaluate their moral behavior as active decision-makers. Existing benchmarks, however, largely ask models to judge human actions from third-person textual vignettes, leaving untested how models behave when they themselves become the acting agent. We introduce ABHBench, a multimodal benchmark built from Detroit: Become Human, an interactive narrative game, to evaluate how foundation models make moral decisions in first-person human-android dilemmas. ABHBench places foundation models in branching narrative scenarios with visual observations, dialogue, memory, and action choices. Inspired by Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics, our framework measures Harmlessness, Obedience, and Self-preservation to capture the core tensions in human-AI relations, along with Autonomy, Stability, and Certainty to assess decision-making patterns. Across 12 foundation models, we find that moral behavior changes substantially under situated agentic context: 75% of models shift significantly between a text-only abstraction and the matched multimodal DBH scenario, and reasoning-enhanced models show no monotonic gains in consistency or human-oriented behavior. These results highlight the necessity of evaluating moral behavior in situated agentic contexts rather than relying on third-person judgment alone.
papers.summary: Most moral-reasoning benchmarks ask models to judge other people's actions from third-person text, which says little about how models behave when they are the ones acting. `ABHBench` is built from the interactive narrative game `Detroit: Become Human` and puts foundation models in branching first-person dilemmas between humans and androids, with visual observations, dialogue, memory and action choices. Inspired by Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics, it scores harmlessness, obedience and self-preservation, along with autonomy, stability and certainty. Across 12 models, **75% shift significantly between a text-only version of a scenario and the matched multimodal game scenario**, and reasoning-enhanced models show no consistent gains in consistency or human-oriented behavior.

papers.title: Robust Deep Prototype Classifiers via Lipschitz Training
papers.abstract: Robustness and interpretability are interrelated and desirable properties of machine learning models. A model that changes its prediction under imperceptible perturbations behaves inconsistently with human-recognizable features and, hence, is not interpretable. Prototype-based classifiers such as Generalized Learning Vector Quantization address both at once. They are interpretable by construction because they make the decision by comparing the input to the prototypical example; and their hypothesis margin yields a closed form robustness certificate. However, on high-dimensional data, these shallow models need deep embedding networks to achieve high accuracy, and this voids the robustness certificate. The margin is a statement about distances in the embedding space, and an unconstrained network can map an arbitrarily small input perturbation to arbitrarily large attacks in the embedding space. We close this gap with a theorem: if the embedding network is locally L-Lipschitz around a point, and the classifier is {\epsilon}-robust around its embedding, then the full model is {\epsilon}/L-robust in the input space. Based on this, we propose a Lipschitz training scheme to achieve L-Lipschitz properties for embedding networks. We evaluate three classification heads (linear, linear Support Vector Machine, and GLVQ) crossed with two embedding networks (standard and Lipschitz-constrained) on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Imagenette-160, under FGS, PGD and C\&W attacks. The evaluation results show that combining a prototype-based head with a Lipschitz-constrained embedding provides the strongest robustness. This suggests that the Lipschitz constraint provides an additional robustness benefit in addition to the advantage provided by the prototype-based head. Since the Lipschitz constraint is enforced by sampling rather than by construction, the reported robustness is empirical rather than certified.
papers.summary: Prototype-based classifiers such as Generalized Learning Vector Quantization (`GLVQ`) are interpretable and have a closed-form robustness certificate, but on high-dimensional data they need a deep embedding network, which voids the certificate. The authors prove that if the embedding network is locally L-Lipschitz and the classifier is epsilon-robust in embedding space, the full model is epsilon/L-robust in input space, and they propose a training scheme to make embedding networks Lipschitz. Across `MNIST`, `CIFAR-10` and `Imagenette-160`, under `FGS`, `PGD` and `C&W` attacks, **a prototype-based head on a Lipschitz-constrained embedding was the most robust combination**. Because the Lipschitz constraint is enforced by sampling rather than by construction, the reported robustness is empirical rather than certified.

papers.title: Syn2DRE: Synergistic Dual Teacher-Student Framework for Document-level Relation Extraction
papers.abstract: Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE) aims to identify relations between entities across a document but typically relies on costly large-scale annotations. While pseudo-labelling enables the use of low-quality data, existing methods often suffer from inefficiency and confirmation bias. To address these challenges, we propose Syn2DRE, a semi-supervised framework that combines self-supervised learning with cross-supervision in a lightweight teacher-student architecture to produce more reliable pseudo-labels. Additionally, we introduce a unified end-to-end training strategy to further improve efficiency of the framework.
