The estimated structural parameters can also be used to build safety leaderboards that rank agent actions by risk, which helps prioritize audits. Experiments on `tau-bench Retail`, `ToolSandbox`, and `ImpossibleBench` show that **the benefit of intervening varies substantially across agent actions and states**.

papers.title: Test-Time Compute Scales Better with Parallel Agent Teams
papers.abstract: Test-time scaling improves the performance of a fixed model by spending more computation at inference. There are two common ways to spend it on agents when a verifier can score every attempt. Best-of-N sampling runs many independent agents and keeps the best result but saturates quickly. One large team of collaborating agents can score higher but stops improving as it grows. Can we get the best of both? Our method, parallel agent teams, does so by sampling many small teams in parallel and keeping the best team's result. We test it on 12 long-horizon tasks from GPU kernels and formal proofs to exploit development. With a 27B model and a budget of 100 agents, parallel teams of ten beat parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks and beat one team of 100 on all four tasks where we ran such large teams. At equal dollar cost the same parallel teams beat a frontier model on half the tasks. A simple statistical model shows that individual agents lose because their many samples have a low mean and that one large team loses because a single sample gets no gain from variance. Sampling many small teams in parallel balances a high mean with the gain from variance. Parallel agent teams thus offer a more effective way to scale test-time compute.
papers.summary: When a verifier can score every attempt, there are two common ways to spend extra inference compute on agents: best-of-N sampling of independent agents, which saturates quickly, and one large collaborating team, which stops improving as it grows. The proposed alternative, parallel agent teams, runs many small teams in parallel and keeps the best team's result. Across 12 long-horizon tasks, including GPU kernel writing, formal proofs, and exploit development, a 27B model with a budget of 100 agents organized as parallel teams of ten **beat independent parallel agents on 10 of 12 tasks and beat a single 100-agent team on all four tasks where that was tested**, and at equal dollar cost it beat a frontier model on half the tasks. A simple statistical model explains the result: independent agents have a low mean score, a single large team gets no benefit from variance, and many small teams get both a high mean and a benefit from variance.
papers.highlight_summary:
Best-of-N sampling over independent agents saturates quickly, and one large collaborative team stops improving as it grows. `parallel agent teams` sits between the two: it samples many small teams of agents that share a forum, then uses a verifier to keep the best team's result.

- Each team is a flat group with no manager, where agents work in separate sandboxes and post notes to a shared forum, so a budget of B agents buys B/k independent team samples.
- With `Qwen3.8-27B` on 12 long-horizon tasks, including GPU kernels, `Lean` proofs and exploit development, ten teams of ten beat 100 independent agents on **10 of 12 tasks**, averaging **27% higher**; on `Carleson Formalization` the score rose from 19.0 to **54.8**.
- On the four tasks where one big team was run, ten teams of ten beat a single team of 100 by **8% to 30%**, and at equal dollar cost the 27B teams beat `GPT-5.6-sol` on **4 of 8 tasks**.
- A simple model treats the expected best score as roughly μ + σ√(2 ln(B/k)): teams win by raising the mean score per sample (each team beats a single agent by 0.5σ to 4.4σ) while still collecting most of the gain that comes from drawing many samples, whereas one big team is a single sample and gets no such gain.
- Limitations: the model predicts the sign of the gain on only 9 of 12 tasks and breaks down when scores are far from normal, there are only 10 to 11 team runs per task, a manager-led team architecture did worse than the flat teams, and the whole method relies on having a verifier to pick the best team.

papers.title: When Instruction Files Go Stale: Documentation Debt and Hidden Cost in Coding Agents
papers.abstract: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, which are read in every agent session. As any documentation artifact, these files can fall behind the code and become stale (e.g., a test folder moves, but the file still points to the old one). In technical debt terms, such a stale instruction is documentation debt, and its interest is the cost it adds to every later agent session. Evaluations that check only task success can miss this cost, and the stale file can persist. In this study, we ask what leads agents to act on a stale instruction, how it affects their behavior and at what cost, and how they recover. We study three real-world stale instructions from active open-source repositories in depth, each a different kind of guidance: a test command, a code location, and a procedure for adding a component. Agents fix 22 maintenance tasks under three versions of each instruction (left stale, corrected to the current path, and removed), with the code and the task held fixed, and we analyze 732 trajectories of two models at the level of individual tool calls. We find that agents follow stale guidance when it is relevant to their tasks, sometimes even when correct information is available elsewhere. On the stale test command, Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, a third more than with the corrected command; in the other cases, we could not detect a difference. Although agents generally recovered from the immediate failures, none repaired the underlying instruction file. Correcting the instructions eliminated operations on obsolete paths, while removing them prevented most. Our findings show that task success alone can hide the costs of documentation debt, highlighting the need to evaluate agent behavior beyond final outcomes.
papers.summary: Coding agents such as `Claude Code` read repository instruction files like `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` in every session, and these files can fall out of date as the code changes, which creates documentation debt that is paid on every later run. The authors took three real stale instructions from open-source repositories (a test command, a code location, and a procedure for adding a component) and had agents fix 22 maintenance tasks with each instruction left stale, corrected, or removed, then analyzed 732 trajectories from two models at the level of individual tool calls. Agents followed stale guidance whenever it was relevant to the task, sometimes even when correct information was available elsewhere; with the stale test command, `Claude Sonnet 5.5` needed about two extra tool calls per run, roughly a third more than with the corrected command. Agents usually recovered from the immediate failures, but **none of them repaired the stale instruction file**, which shows that measuring only task success can hide these costs.

papers.title: Maya a1: Do the Options Read the Model, or Does Their Position? Order Sensitivity in a Non-Autoregressive Decision Model
papers.abstract: Laya answers typed multiple-choice questions in one forward pass by scoring a hidden state at one [MASK] marker per option. We re-engineer the checkpoint (421M parameters; a 2-layer option head with no positional tensor; a documented but unused parallel layout) and test whether the answer depends on where an option is listed. Presenting 951 Qwen-verified questions under every cyclic rotation of their options (or six random permutations for 12 options), the released checkpoint changes its answer for 25.8% [22.9-28.7] of questions (19.7% on the 605 English-language items alone); accuracy with the gold option first versus last differs by 10.1 points, and the flips concentrate where the model's own confidence is low (54% versus 8% across confidence terciles). Fine-tuning with Laya's trainer on 2,818 teacher-verified rows with option shuffling cuts the flip rate to 7.2%; the identical rows without shuffling give 11.4%, so shuffling is responsible for 4.2 points of the improvement. A confidence-weighted vote over orderings gives 69.7% against 69.1% for a single base pass at 4.1x the compute. Labels are LLM-made and the test sets are teacher-filtered. We also fine-tune with the authors' parallel layout on the same rows: flip rate 0.5%.
papers.summary: `Laya` is a 421M-parameter model that answers multiple-choice questions in a single forward pass by scoring a hidden state at one [MASK] marker per option. The authors test whether its answers depend on the order of the options by presenting 951 verified questions under every rotation of the options, and **the released checkpoint changes its answer on 25.8% of questions**, mostly where its own confidence is low. Fine-tuning on 2,818 verified rows with shuffled options cuts the flip rate to 7.2% (versus 11.4% without shuffling), and fine-tuning with the authors' documented but unused parallel layout brings it to 0.5%. A confidence-weighted vote over orderings barely improves accuracy (69.7% versus 69.1%) at 4.1 times the compute.

papers.title: Scaling Graph Similarity Learning with Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Graph similarity computation is an important task in graph mining with many real-world applications, such as chemical compound analysis, program dependence comparison, and social network analysis. The problem is computationally challenging: Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS), which quantify the distance between graphs and identify their largest shared subgraph, respectively, are NP-hard to compute exactly. To address these computational challenges, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been applied to this problem. However, existing GNN-based approaches have primarily focused on small-scale graph datasets, while scalability to larger scales remains underexplored. In this work, we propose FiLSim, a scalable GNN-based framework, and investigate whether a simplified GNN pipeline can maintain competitive performance on standard benchmarks while scaling to large graphs. We additionally propose a sequential graph-editing strategy to construct large-scale graph datasets with reliable GED labels to evaluate scalability. The proposed framework is evaluated on four benchmark datasets and four newly created large-scale datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability. FiLSim remains accurate on graphs with more than 150{,}000 nodes, where the baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.
papers.summary: Graph Edit Distance (GED) and Maximum Common Subgraph (MCS) are standard measures of how similar two graphs are, but both are NP-hard to compute exactly, and existing graph neural network (GNN) approximations have only been tested on small graphs. `FiLSim` is a simplified, scalable GNN pipeline for graph similarity. The authors also introduce a sequential graph-editing strategy that produces large datasets with reliable GED labels. On four standard benchmarks and four new large-scale datasets, **`FiLSim` stays accurate on graphs with more than 150,000 nodes**, where baseline methods run out of memory or fail to learn, and it scores all test pairs within seconds on a single GPU.

papers.title: Generative Latent Priors for Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Dominant methods for interpreting large models impose strong structural assumptions. Generative Latent Priors (GLP) are a complementary approach: a diffusion model that learns the distribution of a frozen model's activations directly, imposing no assumptions. We port GLP to ESM-2 activations (UniRef50) and evaluate it at two host scales (ESM-2-8M and -650M), both as a lens for protein representations and as a prior for editing them. Generation quality scales smoothly with depth and compute. As a lens, single GLP "meta-neurons" are the strongest probes of discrete Swiss-Prot concepts at both hosts, beating InterPLM's released SAE features, and lead on continuous properties at 8M though not at 650M; falsification tests show this is mostly concentration, not new information. As an editing prior, the on-manifold correction makes DiffMean steering of three biochemical properties effective and restores on-manifoldness, but only in isolation: re-embedding the sequences actually produced after several rounds of decoding, the structural plausibility is compromised. This is mainly reproduced in additional SAE-based clamping structural steering experiments, where only Helix motif succeeds. The naturalness failure is traced to the rewriting coverage and the decoder rather than the prior, highlighting what the method must clear before it can serve for both discovery-by-editing and discovery-by-exploration. Trained GLPs are released on huggingface.co/collections/HPAI-BSC/glprot.
papers.summary: Generative Latent Priors (GLP) are diffusion models trained directly on a frozen model's activations, which makes them an interpretability tool with no built-in structural assumptions. The authors apply GLP to the activations of the protein language models `ESM-2-8M` and `ESM-2-650M` (trained on `UniRef50`). Individual GLP "meta-neurons" are **the strongest probes of discrete `Swiss-Prot` concepts at both model sizes**, beating `InterPLM`'s sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, although falsification tests indicate this mostly concentrates existing information rather than revealing new information. Used as a prior for editing, GLP makes `DiffMean` steering of biochemical properties effective in isolation, but sequences produced after several rounds of decoding lose structural plausibility, a failure the authors trace to the rewriting coverage and the decoder rather than to the prior.

papers.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
papers.abstract: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.
papers.summary: Classical computers can only evaluate quantum algorithms on small or restricted instances, which limits automated discovery loops. The authors built a quantum program library in the `Lean` theorem prover, where teams of LLM agents write new programs against formal specifications and prove both their correctness and their cost; the agents share results through wikis and discuss ideas at organized conferences. The resulting programs improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), **quantum arithmetic (290x)**, and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry, and drug metabolism (11x, 8x, and 2.5x respectively).

papers.title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
papers.abstract: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. We present BitDecoding-FP4, an algorithm--system co-design for accurate and efficient native FP4 KV decoding. We mitigate three error sources: Dual-Residual Query Quantization splits queries into two FP4 tensors, cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%; Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling prevents E4M3 scales from rounding long-context probabilities to zero; and Outlier-Aware Key Quantization combines static smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search to suppress key outliers under token-wise scaling. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. In end-to-end serving on NVIDIA B300 with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, it delivers 2.4-3.0$\times$ higher peak serving throughput than BF16 KV. The implementation is available at https://github.com/OpenBitSys/BitDecoding-FP4.
papers.summary: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory use and bandwidth when serving LLMs with long contexts, and existing 4-bit floating-point (FP4) KV cache systems either lose substantial accuracy or rely on codebook lookups that slow decoding. `BitDecoding-FP4` co-designs the algorithm and the system: it splits queries into two FP4 tensors (cutting query logit error from 60% to 1%), scales probabilities to avoid underflow at long contexts, and suppresses key outliers with smoothing, Hadamard rotation, and scale search, while transposed softmax with fused quantization removes a kernel bottleneck. Across dense and mixture-of-experts models, accuracy stays within 0.5 points of a 16-bit KV cache with `NVFP4` and within 1 point with `MXFP4`. In end-to-end serving of `Qwen3-4B` and `Qwen3-30B-A3B` on NVIDIA B300 GPUs, it delivers **2.4–3.0x higher peak throughput** than a 16-bit KV cache.
papers.highlight_summary:
Existing FP4 KV-cache decoding either applies vanilla `NVFP4` and loses substantial accuracy on long contexts, or uses accurate codebook-based 4-bit schemes that are too slow on GPUs. `BitDecoding-FP4` closes this gap with an algorithm–system co-design that targets the three main FP4 error sources (queries, softmax probabilities and keys), so that both attention matrix multiplications run natively on Blackwell FP4 Tensor Cores.

- On the algorithm side, `Dual-Residual Query Quantization` stores the query as the sum of two FP4 tensors, cutting the query's share of logit error from **60% to 1%**; `Underflow-Aware Probability Scaling` folds a constant into the softmax exponent and adaptively picks a smaller scale maximum, lowering the E4M3 underflow floor **24×**; and `Outlier-Aware Key Quantization` combines static per-head mean subtraction, Hadamard rotation and a two-candidate block-scale search.
- On the kernel side, a transposed softmax assigns threads to keys instead of query-head rows, so reductions run as warp butterfly shuffles that also yield FP4 block scales for free, while a stacked query MMA packs the residual query into the zero padding of one FP4 MMA, keeping the accuracy recipe's overhead **within 4%**.
- Accuracy stays **within 0.5 points of BF16 KV with `NVFP4`** (67.27 vs. 67.69 on `Qwen3-4B`, 72.74 vs. 73.15 on `Qwen3-30B-A3B`) and within 1 point with `MXFP4`, beating `FP8 KV` and prior 4-bit methods, whereas `TRT-LLM-NVFP4` loses up to **8.5 points**; it also generalizes to 355B `GLM-4.7` with GQA and 770B `Hy4-preview` with MLA, and tracks BF16 KV during `DAPO` RL rollouts.
- Efficiency gains include up to **2.99× kernel speedup on B300** and **4.01× on RTX PRO 5000** over BF16 KV at 128K context, **1.81× lower** per-token decoding latency at 256K, a KV cache up to **3.5× smaller**, and **2.4–3.0× higher peak serving throughput** in `vLLM`, matching or exceeding `TRT-LLM-NVFP4`.
- The method requires Blackwell-class FP4 Tensor Cores and relies on offline calibration (static key means and the probability-scaling threshold); `MXFP4` trails `NVFP4` slightly, and no latency gains are reported for the sparse-MLA `Hy4-preview` model, where the benefit is mainly memory capacity.

papers.title: Can Agentic Systems Close the Gap in Radiology with Production AI Tools?
papers.abstract: Radiology AI has developed along two paths: specialized models that perform well on narrow tasks but cover few clinical findings, and generalist models that address a broader range of tasks but remain prone to hallucination and inaccurate measurements. Combining the two through agentic systems offers a route towards comprehensive radiology reporting, but published systems are tied to one modality or body part. We describe a radiology agentic framework that standardizes how an orchestrator calls modular tools to produce a structured report, and use it to measure what such a system can do with the tools from FDA-cleared radiology AI devices. Report generation is simulated on a large multi-modality report corpus, with the orchestrator given either a catalog of finding classes consolidated from the cleared devices, each available on the modalities it is cleared for, or an unlimited catalog in which any class can be requested, and planning either from the clinical indication or from the target report. Tool outputs are simulated from the reference report, so the comparison isolates tool availability and orchestration from tool error. With the cleared catalog and the indication alone, the orchestrator recovers under a third of the clinically actionable findings; recovery improves substantially with the unlimited catalog, and further when the plan is written from the target report. Attributing every missed finding to a cause shows that most are classes no cleared device offers for the study's modality, and that a third are classes or tools that were offered and not called. Adding the most frequently missing tools closes most of the gap to the unlimited catalog on held-out reports, whereas a smaller orchestrator with the unlimited catalog gives up the whole gain. Tool availability and effective orchestration are thus complementary constraints on comprehensive AI-assisted radiology reporting.
papers.summary: Radiology AI is split between specialized models that are accurate on a few findings and generalist models that cover more but hallucinate, and existing agentic systems that combine the two are limited to a single modality or body part. The authors define a framework in which an orchestrator calls modular tools to produce a structured report, and they simulate report generation on a large multi-modality report corpus using the finding classes offered by FDA-cleared devices, with tool outputs simulated from reference reports so that only tool availability and orchestration are measured. With only the cleared tools and the clinical indication, **the orchestrator recovers under a third of clinically actionable findings**. Most misses are findings that no cleared device covers for that modality, and a third are tools that were available but never called; adding the most frequently missing tools closes most of the gap, whereas a smaller orchestrator loses the gain.

papers.title: Ensemble Methodology for Reference-Free Confidence Estimation in LLM-based Code Summarization
papers.abstract: This paper describes an approach and use case to estimate the correctness of LLM-generated COBOL summaries without access to human-authored references. The core intuition is that inter-model agreement on semantics is informative about truth, and that an LLM-as-judge can provide higher-fidelity pairwise assessments than traditional string- or embedding-based metrics. We operationalise this intuition with (i) controlled summary generation from diverse models; (ii) a LLM evaluator that compares pairs of summaries and emits structured judgments; and (iii) a calibrated aggregation rule that combines supportive evidence while penalising only corroborated contradictions.
papers.summary: The authors estimate whether LLM-generated summaries of COBOL code are correct when no human-written reference summaries exist. Their premise is that agreement between different models on a summary's meaning is evidence of correctness, and that an LLM-as-judge compares summaries more faithfully than string-based or embedding-based metrics. The method generates summaries from diverse models under controlled conditions, uses an LLM evaluator to make structured pairwise judgments, and combines them with **a calibrated aggregation rule that adds up supporting evidence and penalizes only contradictions corroborated by more than one judgment**.

papers.title: Flow-Guided Target-Space Alignment via Path Consistency
papers.abstract: Many multimodal alignment problems require mapping a source modality into a fixed space defined by a target modality, where the target space is not merely an intermediate embedding but is used directly for downstream analysis. In this setting, successful alignment should preserve both the global structure of the target distribution and the instance-level correspondence observed in paired source--target training data. Existing objectives typically address only part of this goal: contrastive losses encourage relative similarity, distribution-matching losses improve marginal agreement, and pointwise regression fits each source sample to its paired target without explicitly modeling target-space path geometry. We propose FlowAlign, a flow-guided target-space alignment method that repurposes conditional flow matching as a training-time alignment signal rather than an inference-time transport model. FlowAlign uses the learned flow field to guide the alignment of source-side representations with the fixed target space, encouraging them to preserve paired correspondence while remaining compatible with the global target-space structure. We further provide theoretical analysis showing how FlowAlign helps improve paired correspondence by controlling endpoint accuracy and capturing local target-space geometry. Experiments on synthetic data, paired single-cell multiome benchmarks, and image--text alignment demonstrate that FlowAlign improves instance level correspondence while preserving target-space structure across different modality settings.
papers.summary: Some multimodal tasks require mapping one modality into a fixed embedding space defined by another, where that target space is used directly for downstream analysis, so the mapping must preserve both the overall structure of the target space and the pairing of individual samples. `FlowAlign` uses conditional flow matching as a training-time alignment signal rather than an inference-time transport model, guiding source representations toward their paired targets while keeping them consistent with the global target geometry. The authors' theoretical analysis shows how this controls endpoint accuracy and captures local geometry. Experiments on synthetic data, paired single-cell multiome benchmarks, and image–text alignment show **better instance-level correspondence while preserving target-space structure**.

papers.title: Grasp-TAGS: Task-Aware Grasp Selection via Critic Distillation for Prehensile Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Loco-manipulation, which requires mobile manipulators to coordinate locomotion and manipulation over long horizons, is a key capability for large-object rearrangement in applications such as service robotics and warehouse automation. Despite recent progress, reliably executing these tasks remains challenging because performance depends on complex robot-object and object-environment interaction dynamics. Existing approaches address this challenge either through model-based methods, which often require accurate dynamics models, or through learning-based methods, which reduce this requirement but typically assume a fixed or predefined initial grasp. However, different geometrically stable grasps can lead to substantially different downstream manipulation performance. Therefore, we propose Grasp-TAGS, a task-aware grasp selection framework for goal-conditioned large-object rearrangement. We train a unified PPO-based reinforcement learning policy across multiple initial grasp configurations and distill the learned critic into a lightweight grasp utility network that ranks candidate grasps using only the candidate grasp configuration and goal information. At inference time, we select the grasp with the highest predicted downstream utility for the downstream policy to complete the task, before even making a contact. Experiments demonstrate that Grasp-TAGS improves rearrangement success over both fixed single-grasp policies and random grasp selection, achieving an average success rate of 89.84% compared with 79.87% for the best-performing single-grasp policies, an improvement of 9.97 percentage points. Grasp-TAGS also reduces final orientation errors across all evaluated objects. For more qualitative results, refer to the supplementary webpage: https://rpm-lab-umn.github.io/Grasp-TAGS-web-page/
papers.summary: Mobile manipulators that rearrange large objects have to coordinate driving and manipulation, and the choice of initial grasp strongly affects whether the rest of the task succeeds, yet learning-based methods usually assume a fixed grasp. `Grasp-TAGS` trains a single `PPO` reinforcement learning policy across many initial grasp configurations, then distills its learned critic into a lightweight network that ranks candidate grasps using only the grasp configuration and the goal, so the best grasp is chosen before the robot touches the object. Rearrangement success **averages 89.84%, compared with 79.87% for the best single-grasp policies**, and final orientation errors drop on every evaluated object.

papers.title: GRAC: Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning for Surgical Scene Description
papers.abstract:
Purpose: Surgical operative reports support procedural documentation, surgical training, performance assessment, and workflow review. However, extracting meaningful information often requires extensive manual review and clinical expertise. Automated surgical scene descriptions could reduce this burden by leveraging recurring surgical activities and prior knowledge.
  Methods: We propose GRAC (Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning), a framework that represents surgical scenes as graphs capturing relationships among instruments, actions, and anatomical structures. Given an input scene graph, GRAC learns to retrieve relevant graph-caption pairs from training data. It compares instrument-tissue interactions between retrieved examples and the input scene, using comparison features to condition retrieved-caption representations during generation.
  Results: On the EndoVis-18 benchmark, GRAC achieved a CIDEr-D of 5.88, compared with 4.23 for SGT and 3.36 for the strongest conventional Transformer baseline. Exact instrument-action-target triplet-set accuracy reached 52.6%, compared with 32.7% for SGT and 26.2% for the strongest conventional baseline. These results demonstrate improvements in language quality and factual agreement. On TORS, GRAC achieved a CIDEr-D of 5.06, compared with 3.80 for the strongest baseline.
  Conclusion: GRAC demonstrates that combining structured surgical scene representations with retrieved examples improves surgical scene captioning and produces more contextually meaningful descriptions.
papers.summary: Automatically describing surgical scenes could reduce the manual work of writing operative reports. `GRAC` (Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Captioning) represents each scene as a graph of instruments, actions, and anatomical structures, retrieves similar graph–caption pairs from the training data, and uses the differences in instrument–tissue interactions between the retrieved examples and the input scene to condition caption generation. On `EndoVis-18`, it reaches a `CIDEr-D` score of 5.88 versus 4.23 for `SGT`, and **exact instrument–action–target triplet accuracy of 52.6% versus 32.7%**; on `TORS`, it scores 5.06 `CIDEr-D` versus 3.80 for the strongest baseline.

papers.title: On the Reliability of Majority-Vote Pseudo-Labels in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts pretrained language models to unlabeled target-domain data using self-generated pseudo-labels, whose reliability remains poorly understood. We analyze majority-vote supervision for TTRL with online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and decompose its error into population-majority bias and prompt-dependent finite-rollout variation. Because population-majority bias is generally unidentifiable without external supervision, we focus on mitigating the downstream effects of finite-rollout variation. We propose \emph{Prompt-Conditional Distributionally Robust DPO (PC-Dr.DPO)}, which conditions within-prompt robust reweighting on observed vote reliability to make updates from sampling-sensitive prompts more conservative. We further introduce a cache-based mechanism to reduce self-supervised forgetting during online adaptation. Across six mathematical and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five model backbones, PC-Dr.DPO matches or outperforms the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings.
papers.summary: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) adapts a language model to unlabeled data by training on its own majority-vote answers as pseudo-labels, but how reliable those labels are is poorly understood. The authors analyze majority-vote supervision under online Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and split its error into a bias in the population majority, which cannot be identified without external labels, and variation caused by drawing only a finite number of samples per prompt. Their method, `PC-Dr.DPO`, makes updates more conservative on prompts whose votes are unstable and adds a cache to reduce forgetting during online adaptation. Across six math and knowledge-intensive reasoning benchmarks and five base models, it **matches or beats the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings**.
papers.highlight_summary:
Majority-vote pseudo-labels in test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) can be wrong for two reasons: the model's population-level modal answer is itself incorrect (**population-majority bias**), or a finite sample of rollouts lands on a different majority than the population mode (**finite-rollout variation**). The first cannot be identified without external supervision. The authors prove that the second shrinks exponentially in the rollout count, and they propose `PC-Dr.DPO`, an online-DPO variant that makes updates more conservative on prompts whose votes look unstable.

- **Method:** `PC-Dr.DPO` applies distributionally robust reweighting within each prompt's rollout group rather than globally, with a per-prompt temperature `β_x = β_base · κ(x)`, where `κ(x)` is the fraction of the 32 rollouts that agree with the modal answer; for weak majorities this shifts weight toward preference pairs the policy already satisfies, which provably tightens a bound on the size of the update.
- **Supporting mechanisms:** A cache stores the rollouts of prompts that became unanimous, and if a later majority contradicts the cached answer it replays them with a likelihood loss instead of learning from the new pairs; answer selection also replaces frequency voting with summed likelihood-ratio scores between successive policies.
- **Main results:** Across six benchmarks (`AIME24/25`, `AMC23`, `MATH500`, `GPQA-Diamond`, `MMLU-Pro` math subset) and five backbones (`Qwen2.5` 1.5B/3B/7B/Math-1.5B, `Llama-3.2-3B`), it **matches or beats the strongest TTRL baseline in 24 of 30 settings**, with the largest gains on `MMLU-Pro`, where baselines often fall below the base model (e.g., **64.7% vs. 46.0%** for `TTRL` on `Qwen2.5-3B`, whose base model scores 53.6%).
- **Ablations:** On `Qwen2.5-3B`, a constant temperature drops `AMC`/`MATH500` accuracy from **45.8/73.3 to 42.0/72.3**, frequency voting drops it to 44.6/71.4, and removing the cache cuts `Llama-3.2-3B` on `MATH500` from **58.4% to 56.3%**.
- **Limitations:** The method does nothing about a confidently wrong population majority; the theory assumes binary answers; gains are often modest; it trails `TTRL` in some settings (e.g., 13.3 vs. 17.4 on `AIME25` with `Qwen2.5-7B`); and every method, including this one, collapses on `AIME25` for `Qwen2.5-1.5B` and `Llama-3.2-3B`.

papers.title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
papers.abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.
papers.summary: LLMs solve every problem from scratch even when they have already worked out how to solve that kind of task. Agentic reasoning caching turns LLM reasoning traces into agentic reasoning caches (ARCs), CPU-executable artifacts that apply a worked-out solution to new instances of the same task with little involvement from a language model. ARCs **perform on par with frontier LLMs on difficult math and science tasks while being 16–291x cheaper to invoke** than the source model, and the authors report that they are fully explainable, can keep being trained, and are robust to input perturbations.

papers.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
papers.abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.
papers.summary: Agentic manipulation policies (AMPs) let a generalist AI model command a robot arm directly and adjust its actions as the task unfolds, in contrast to specialist vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) trained on demonstrations. The reference harness `AMP1` runs unchanged on single-arm, bimanual, and mobile robots with no demonstrations, task-specific training, or built-in grasping or placing skills, and it **reaches 85.6% zero-shot success on `RoboLab-120`, versus 49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies**. It succeeds in 104 of 108 real-world trials across twelve tasks and three robots, and the agent develops its own strategies such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. Adding persistent memory across episodes cuts the failure rate on `RoboDojo` bimanual tasks by 4.6x compared with zero-shot deployment.
